Because sentient beings enter the Path primarily through the *Prajñāpāramitā*. What is the reason? It is because all ordinary people who fail to attain the Way do so due to...

Because the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) relies upon and adheres to [the truth] in order to correctly shatter the attachments of sentient beings, it is said that there is a dharma of non-reliance and non-attachment;
furthermore, the perfection of wisdom is itself true repentance. Thus, all Mahāyāna sūtras that elucidate true repentance rely upon the perfection of wisdom.
As the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from deluded conceptualization. If...
Those who wish to repent should sit upright and contemplate the reality-mark of *nirvāṇa*.

It is also said that if one hears of the King of Non-action and Non-reception, even grave offenses will certainly be extinguished. Therefore, although there are many different versions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, its essential point is this:
because sentient beings constantly suffer from the illness of attachment and dependence, the Buddha taught that by being without dependence, one attains the Dharma. As the *Dvīrātra-sūtra* states:

From the night of attaining the Way until the night of *nirvāṇa*, he constantly preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* during five periods to eight classes of beings; how could this be considered much? Question:
Since the *Prajñāpāramitā* consists of five periods and thus forms five sections, why does the *Avataṃsaka* consist of eight assemblies rather than eight sections?

Furthermore, since the eight assemblies are combined into a single work, why are the five periods not likewise combined? Answer: To speak in general terms, both cases can be considered analogous. Now...

Otherwise, the eight assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka* would not have their meanings mutually established from beginning to end as previously explained—namely, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages, along with the ocean of marks and characteristics.
Since these constitute a sequence of shallow and deep causes and effects, they can form a single division.
If it were not a sequence of shallow and deep stages from beginning to end, [the five periods of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*] would likewise not be so.
Because they are mutually established, each is divided into five periods.
The fifth [period] clarifies the sequence of the preceding and following questions regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Vajraprajñāpāramitā*.

As for which was taught first, some say that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* was taught first and the *Vajraprajñāpāramitā* was taught subsequently; others say that the *Vajraprajñāpāramitā* was taught first and the [other] was taught later.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, each [interpretation] uses textual evidence to establish its meaning, yet they result in only two views. Now, it is clarified that these two explanations cannot yet be used as definitive criteria;
furthermore, how can "teachings according to suitability" (*yathāyogam*) be fixed? First, regarding their sequence:

either they may be explained fully at once across multiple sections, or even within a single section, the sutra may be explained over a long period. This shall be explained in greater detail later in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Second, [regarding the nature of the teaching].
Since it is thus with both the preceding and succeeding [parts] of the sutras, the five periods and the eight classes of assemblies are likewise not fixed.

Not only is the sequence of the *Prajñāpāramitā* indeterminate, but all other scriptural teachings can be understood by this same principle; therefore, the sutra states that within each of the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭākārābhisambodhi*), all eight phases are fully present—how could their timing be fixed?
Sixth, distinguishing the tenets of the Northern and Southern traditions and the ancient and modern schools regarding the essence of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
some take the object as the tenet, some take wisdom as the tenet, some take the cause as the tenet, and some take the fruit as the tenet; these shall be omitted here for brevity. Question:
Is the interpretation of the Mountain Gate (the monastic community) the same as or different from others? Answer: If one seeks the origins of the various interpretations...
If one seeks the identity or difference of that which is attained through the gateway of possibility and finds it cannot be found, with what could it be identical or different?

Being able to be thus neither identical nor different, neither self nor other, without dependence and without attainment, and having nothing upon which to dwell—this is the profound essence of Prajñā.
Whatever has a basis for dwelling is not the school of Prajñā. Now it is clarified that Prajñā has no fixed characteristic; it accords with conditions.

He was skillful in meaning such that there was nothing he did not penetrate; yet, in true *prajñā*, there has never been the distinction between object and non-object, wisdom and non-wisdom, cause and non-cause, or effect and non-effect.
Through skillful means (*upāya*), he followed conditions: when present in the cause, he was called the cause; when present in the effect, he was called the effect;

when present in the object, he was called the object; and when present in the wisdom, he was called the wisdom. Thus, Master Zhao said: "To examine the fundamental nature of subject and object, and wisdom and its object..."
How could "causality" be something that can be grasped by the causality of object and cognition? It is simply because it is neither object nor cognition, yet it can be both object and cognition;
it is neither cause nor effect, yet it can be both cause and effect. Now, discussing this according to the text:

for the time being, we say that although *prajñā* is neither cause nor effect, its very essence is precisely causality; therefore, it is said that "cause is named *prajñā*, and effect is named [Buddhahood]."
"Sarvajñā" (all-knowledge) indicates its true essence as being neither cause nor fruit.

The seventh [section] clarifies that the Great Illumination of the Esoteric [Vehicle] has four gates for the single transformation [of beings]: first, revealing the Bodhisattvas through the Exoteric Teaching while the Śrāvakas are not esoteric—this is the *Avataṃsaka*;
second, revealing the Śrāvakas through the Exoteric Teaching while transforming the Bodhisattvas through the Esoteric—this is the *Tripiṭaka*.
Furthermore, because it is the third [of the three] to manifest [the truth], the bodhisattva’s secret transformation of śrāvakas is the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

because it is the fourth to manifest [the truth], the bodhisattva’s manifest transformation of śrāvakas is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Moreover, there are four gates consisting of the primary and the secondary:

first, the primary manifestation of the ultimate reality with the secondary opening of expedient means, which is the *Avataṃsaka*; second, the primary opening of expedient means with the primary concealment of ultimate reality, which is the Tripiṭaka.
Third, that which directly reveals the ultimate reality while incidentally opening the provisional means—namely, the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras.

Fourth, that which directly opens the provisional means and directly reveals the ultimate reality—namely, the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Question: In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is clarified that the three vehicles are provisional;

thus, it can reveal that the one vehicle is the ultimate reality. However, since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* does not yet distinguish that the three vehicles are provisional, how can it reveal the one vehicle?

Question: Is this [Mahāyāna] the ultimate truth? Answer: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals the real by contrast with the provisional, while the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* distinguishes the two vehicles as inferior and the Mahāyāna as superior;
therefore, the Mahāyāna is the ultimate truth. Question: Which passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that it is the ultimate truth? Answer:

The "Parable of the Entrustment" (*Śraddhāparivarta*) chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The secret treasury of all Buddhas is expounded only for the sake of Bodhisattvas to reveal its reality."

Regarding the matter, he did not explain this essential truth to me; this text clarifies it by referring to this very sūtra. Thus, we know that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom) has already revealed the reality.

Question: If the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* reveals the reality by showing that the Small Vehicle is inferior and the Bodhisattva path is superior, then since the Tripiṭaka also clarifies that the Two Vehicles are inferior and the Mahāyāna is superior, [is the reality not already revealed there as well?]
It should already have revealed that the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna) is the true answer, because it primarily elucidates the Mahāyāna while incidentally touching upon the Hīnayāna;
because it primarily reveals the true Tripiṭaka while incidentally touching upon the Lesser Vehicle;
and because it is not [merely] partial but fully and clearly explains the Buddha. Thus, it truly manifests the three [aspects of truth].
Because the Tripiṭaka conceals [the ultimate truth], although it elucidates the Buddha-vehicle, it remains a teaching of veiled meaning and thus does not directly manifest True Suchness (tathatā).

Because the Tripiṭaka elucidates that the Buddha was truly born in the royal palace and truly passed away at the Twin Trees, and that he attained sainthood from the state of an ordinary person, achieved Buddhahood under the King of Trees, and wore tattered rags as a householder—it is precisely this Buddha who is being described. Therefore, one knows that the reality has not yet been fully revealed.

Next, to clarify the specific citation from this sutra in contrast to the *Dharmaparyāya-śāstra* (Lotus Sūtra Treatise), the *Mahā-śāstra on Questions of the Esoteric and Exoteric* (Volume 100) states:

"If the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is not an esoteric teaching, yet it entrusts [the Dharma] to the śrāvakas, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is an esoteric teaching, reaching even to the bodhisattvas—how then can one distinguish between the esoteric and the non-esoteric?
The answer is: There are generally two gates for distinguishing between the esoteric and the non-esoteric. First, by means of the Great... [text ends].

Because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* reveals that the Secret Hīnayāna is not secret, it states therein that Arhats have severed their afflictions (*kleśa*) and are thus pure, whereas Pratyekabuddhas have not yet severed their afflictions and are therefore impure.

In the Secret Dharma, however, it is stated that Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) alone transcend the two vehicles; therefore, these Bodhisattvas are pure. This is...
First, because the Hīnayāna is shallow and superficial, it is not secret; whereas the Mahāyāna is profoundly deep, it is therefore called "secret.
Second, even within the Mahāyāna there are further distinctions of the secret, as stated in the hundredth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

since the *Prajñā* [sūtras] do not clarify that arhats become buddhas, they are not secret. [Objection: But the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that arhats become buddhas; why then is the *Prajñā* considered secret?
Question: Why is it that the Arhats becoming Buddhas, as explained in the *Dharmapada*, is not considered a secret? Answer:

Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* explains that Arhats become Buddhas in a manner that is extremely profound and difficult to understand, it is therefore "secret. In contrast, because the *Prajñāpāramitā* explains that Bodhisattvas become Buddhas in a way whose meaning is easy to understand, it is not "secret.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Regarding the Arhats becoming Buddhas, one understands this only upon reaching Buddhahood"; this is the correct interpretation of the treatise.

One may discuss other matters; since Nāgārjuna stated that they were not understood until one reached the stage of Buddhahood, it is clear that an Arhat’s attainment of Buddhahood is profoundly difficult to comprehend.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "As the Buddha has taught, all Arhats shall eventually attain nirvāṇa;
such a profound sphere of the Buddha's practice cannot be known by ordinary people of shallow and foolish intellect."

Therefore, one knows that it is difficult to understand how an Arhat can become a Buddha. Question: Why is this difficult to understand? Answer: This is considered difficult in light of the former teachings.
According to the former teachings, it is clarified that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of an Arhat have already been exhausted and will not arise again;
as it is said, "Once the husks of ignorance have fallen away, what remains in the field will not sprout again. Yet, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is clarified that Arhats do indeed become Buddhas.
Therefore, it was difficult [to explain] in the past; for whom was it difficult in the past? The answer is: it was precisely for the sake of the Śrāvakas that it was difficult.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A great physician is able to use poison as medicine, whereas a minor physician can only use medicine as medicine.
A Bodhisattva is able to transform the Two Vehicles into Buddhahood, just as one who understands how to use poison as medicine does. Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...

The entrustment is to the Bodhisattvas; whereas the Śrāvakas only understand that Bodhisattvas become Buddhas—just as one understands the use of medicine as being for the purpose of curing illness—the Prajñāpāramitā is entrusted to the Śrāvakas.

Question: If the Prajñāpāramitā only clarifies that Bodhisattvas become Buddhas and does not clarify that those of the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) become Buddhas, then the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* would be inferior and the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* would be superior. How can this be reconciled with the explanation given in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*?

Question: The "Chapter on the Vehicles" (*Yāna-parivarta*) enumerates ten great sūtras, among which the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the greatest. Since it is weighed as the greatest, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* would then be inferior;

thus, the two texts appear to contradict each other. Answer: The *Saddharmapuṇṇḍarīka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā* do indeed possess relative superiority and inferiority. If they are taught for the sake of śrāvakas to clarify that those of the two vehicles attain Buddhahood, then the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is superior and the *Prajñāpāramitā* is inferior.
However, if they are taught for the sake of bodhisattvas to clarify true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), [the *Prajñāpāramitā* is superior].

Expedient means (*upāya*) is the superior Dharma, while Prajñā is inferior. Why? Because the sixty-six chapters of the *Prajñāpāramitā* distinguish the inexhaustible wisdom of reality (*bhūtadhī*), whereas the twenty-four subsequent chapters concern expedient means.
These are the parents of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Prajñā is the mother of Bodhisattvas; expedient means is their father. All sentient beings... [text ends]
The Guides are all born from this; since the parents of the Dharmakāya have been extensively elucidated, it is the most profound and vast among all the Vaipulya sūtras.

Other sūtras do not correctly clarify this meaning and thus cannot equal the Prajñā[pāramitā], for the Prajñā extensively clarifies the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and is therefore the most profound and vast among all sūtras. The reason for this is that the three vehicles attain the Way through it.
Furthermore, the severance of delusions, the repentance of grave offenses, and these three meanings all rely upon the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
since the *Prajñāpāramitā* extensively and correctly elucidates the true mark, these three meanings are thereby established. Because other sutras do not clarify this, their *prajñā* is inferior.
Thus, because there is a distinction of superiority and inferiority between these two sutras, Nāgārjuna has two texts—one earlier and one later. This [latter] was produced in Guanzhong.

The Preface to the *Svalpikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by Dharma Master Rui states that this was not composed from a new conception. Question: If there is a distinction of superiority or inferiority between these two sutras, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further state that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is another name for the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
Answer: The *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are identical in being the Right Contemplation (*samyak-pratyavekṣaṇā*) and the Great Wisdom of Equality (*sama-mahāprajñā*).
Since they are no different in their manifestation of the Way, it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is another name for the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
As the treatise states: "Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of it by various names; he establishes these different terms according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Now, regarding the distinction between persons based on the teachings: the teaching of Prajñā is for bodhisattvas who proceed directly [to Buddhahood], while the Lotus teaching is for those bodhisattvas who turn from the Small Vehicle to enter the Great.
Although they differ in terms of the persons for whom the Buddhas act, there is no difference in their attainment of Buddhahood.

The Elder’s great house and its seven treasures remain fundamentally unchanged from beginning to end; it is simply that at the time of entrusting the wealth, it was not yet the time to hand over the family estate.
Regarding the question of whether the *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies that those of the two vehicles attain Buddhahood—this would constitute an "incomplete teaching" (*neyārtha*).
The answer is: the *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies that Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood; this matter is explicit (*nītārtha*), and it does not yet state that those of the two vehicles attain Buddhahood.
From one perspective, this meaning may also be considered an "unresolved question" (*avyākṛta-praśna*). If that is so, how can one explain the *Niyatāniyata-parivarta*, which states:
"Subhūti heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarify that all beings attain Buddhahood, yet he also heard the *Prajñāpāramitā* distinguish that bodhisattvas may regress;
therefore, he now asks the Buddha whether they are fixed (*niyata*) or unfixed. This is the question.

When [Vimalakīrti] carefully examined the similarities and differences between the two sutras, the Buddha replied: "A bodhisattva is 'definitively settled' (niyata). To be definitively settled means to be destined for the attainment of Buddhahood.

Since it is thus clarified that one is definitively destined for Buddhahood, there is only the Single Vehicle of the Buddha; the non-retrogression of the śrāvaka [vehicle] thereby reveals that there are no two vehicles.
This intent clarifies that the *Prajñāpāramitā* is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. How can it be said that the *Prajñāpāramitā* has not yet clarified this?

The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* explains that the two vehicles attain Buddhahood; however, it does not clarify this while discussing the initial stage in a single session at one time, and thus differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Later, it clearly elucidates the non-retrogression of bodhisattvas, revealing that there is only one vehicle and no second, which is largely identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
therefore, they do not contradict one another.

Eighth, the analysis of the teachings: the theories regarding the five periods (*pañca-kāla*) in the South and the four schools (*catur-nikāya*) in the North have already been examined in detail previously;

they are now omitted here as they would detract from the meaning. Indeed, the turmoil of the four modes of birth arises from a lack of empty-mindedness, and the proliferation of the six realms of existence truly stems from attachment and stagnation.
Thus we know that the circling within the ocean of suffering has dwelling and clinging as its source; to transcend it, one must abandon these.
However, the application of the other shore (pāra) takes non-attainment as its foundation; yet the accumulation of the faculties is not a single cessation, for there are many gateways to inversion:

some are great from beginning to end, some are small both at the start and the conclusion, some are small at the start and great at the end, some are great at the start and small at the end, and within a single moment, both the great and the small may be manifest.
Or, over immeasurable time, there may be only a single dharma, or one may speak of various dharmas.

The discrepancies between the earlier and later [teachings], or instances where the same doctrine is clarified yet differs in its initial and final formulations, arise precisely because the capacities for awakening are not uniform;
thus, the adaptation of the teachings is boundless and cannot be confined to five periods or limited to four doctrines.

As for what is called "greatness from beginning to end," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "When I first attained the Way, there were already bodhisattvas who asked about this meaning; I [taught it] to you..."
Because that which is asked is equal and without distinction, we know that just as Nirvana is explained later, this teaching is also explained at the beginning.

Regarding the case where both the beginning and the end are "small," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the first turning of the wheel of Dharma until the Great Parinirvāṇa, [the teachings] were compiled into the four Āgamas"—this refers precisely to such a case.
Regarding the case where the beginning is small and the end is great: at the Deer Park, the Small Vehicle was first taught, whereas at Vulture Peak...

This refers to clarifying the Great Dharma. "First great, then small" means that beneath the Bodhi tree he first preached the *Avataṃsaka*, and subsequently proceeded to the Deer Park to clarify the Small Teachings.
"Clarifying both the Great and Small within a single period" is as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The manifestation of the teaching gate refers to the few secret dharmas preached at Nairañjanā; the clarification of the Great refers to [the teachings] at the Deer Park."

Furthermore, there are cases where a single dharma is explained over immeasurable periods of time, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the *Prajñāpāramitā* was not taught in a single session or at one time.
Alternatively, there are cases where different dharmas differ according to their sequence;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Subhūti, having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, understood that all beings attain Buddhahood, yet upon hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he learned that bodhisattvas may regress. It is for this reason that he now asks.

Is this bodhisattva one who is destined for certainty (*niyata*) or not destined? The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā* are called "distinct dharmas," yet the *Prajñāpāramitā* may precede the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* or follow it;
thus, their sequence differs. Question: How is it known that [the *Prajñāpāramitā*] was before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further explains that three hundred bhikṣus took off their upper robes...
It is said that some claim: since the precepts were not established for twelve years, one knows that the *Prajñā* was taught before those twelve years;
yet the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was only expounded forty-odd years after his enlightenment.

Furthermore, the "Belief and Understanding" chapter clarifies that the entrusting of the wealth occurs after [the initial teaching], and thus the sons of the Buddha meet [the Buddha] later; this also shows that the *Prajñā* comes first and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* follows, as listed above.
Regarding the textual sequence of the *Bidingpin* (Chapter on Certainty), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* comes first and the *Prajñāpāramitā* follows later.

Alternatively, there are cases where the teaching is identical yet the sequence differs; for instance, within the five periods of teaching, all share the same *Prajñāpāramitā* dharma, yet the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang) states that the four kinds of *Prajñāpāramitā* were taught in the twenty-ninth year, while the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Renwang Prajñāpāramitā) was taught in the thirtieth year. Such matters cannot be detailed exhaustively.

Briefly citing one point to demonstrate that the holy teachings are without fixed direction and should not be restricted to five periods or four schools: Question: If this were so, then there would be no distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, and the shallow and deep would be in total confusion; how then could one discuss the two treasuries of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, or the opening of the two vehicles of Great and Small? Answer: Although the Buddha’s teachings are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, when examined from the perspective of their ultimate purpose, there is no discrepancy. Thus, while the provisional teachings may differ, they all converge upon the same ultimate truth. It is for this reason that we speak of the two treasuries and the two vehicles. Furthermore, the various sūtras and śāstras do not contradict one another; rather, they are mutually inclusive. Therefore, one should not arbitrarily limit the teachings to specific periods or schools. As it is said: "The Dharma is like the great ocean; its depths cannot be fathomed. To insist on a fixed sequence of five periods or four schools is to fail to grasp the boundless nature of the Buddha’s wisdom. Thus, while the teachings appear diverse in their manifestations, they are fundamentally one in their essence. This is why we can establish the distinctions between the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva treasuries, and the Great and Small vehicles, without falling into confusion. It is through skillful means (*upāya*) that the One Vehicle is revealed in manifold ways, yet all these ways lead back to the single destination of universal liberation.

Therefore, one must understand that the Buddha’s teaching is a seamless whole, and that its apparent diversity serves only to accommodate the varied capacities of sentient beings. To insist on a rigid classification is to miss the point of the Buddha’s compassionate intent. Thus, while we provisionally distinguish between the two treasuries and two vehicles, we must ultimately realize that they are non-dual in their ultimate reality. This is the true meaning of the Buddha’s teaching: vast, open, and beyond all limitations.

Regarding the first point, "not exhaustive": when teachings are given to those with limited capacities, they are called the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna); when taught to those with great capacities, they are designated as the "Great Teaching" (Mahāyāna).

However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the compilers of the Dharma-piṭaka categorized everything the Buddha taught during his lifetime that pertained to the Lesser Vehicle as the "Śrāvaka Piṭaka," and everything he taught at all times regarding the Mahāyāna as the "Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Thus, the distinction between the Great and the Small is based on their relative depth.
This distinguishes the profound teaching. Question: How is it known that there are two distinct baskets (*piṭaka*)? Answer: The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states:

"Previously, within the Śrāvaka-dharma, the twelve links of dependent origination were taught; subsequently, for those who have already practiced and are capable of receiving the profound Dharma, the characteristics of dependent origination according to the Mahāyāna-dharma were taught—namely, that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, neither identical nor different."
They are ultimately empty and non-existent, as explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Ānanda and Kāśyapa compiled the Tripiṭaka, while Maitreya, Ānanda, and Mañjuśrī compiled the Mahāyāna Piṭaka. Additionally, the *Dharmadhātu-vibhaṅga-śāstra* states:
"The eleven divisions of the sūtras are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, while the Vaipulya sūtras are called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. However, the Great...
The *Samparigraha*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*—these four sūtras all contrast the "small" of the past with the praise of the "great" of the present;

thus, one knows that within a single transformation, the two teachings of the great and the small are clarified. Question: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states, "There is only the One Buddha Vehicle.

Why, then, do you establish the categories of Great and Small? Answer: Because the Tathāgata accords with two types of conditions—the great and the small—he preaches the teachings of the Great and the Small. He speaks only of these two.
Since the teachings ultimately serve to reveal the One, the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "All phenomena are expounded through wisdom and skillful means;
all that is taught reaches the ground of omniscience. Thus, we know that there is no difference in the teachings, which signifies no difference in the conditions for awakening.
Nevertheless, because they are presented in contrast to what is different, their non-difference is clarified. Since difference itself does not exist, there is no non-difference.
Because they have also ceased, that sutra says: "This Dharma cannot be shown; its verbal expressions are quiescent.

Those who cling to the two collections—the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—or who are dogmatically attached to the idea of a single vehicle (Ekayāna), all fall into the dualistic views of identity and difference.
They have not realized original quiescence and are thus not practitioners of the Buddha-dharma.
The ninth section clarifies the questions regarding the translation and the concluding record of the *Mahākaruṇā-bhikṣuṇī-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*. It states:

"It is said that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Large Version) and the *Svalpā* (Small Version) were first expounded, and from among them, the *Prasphutaprabhāsa* (Light Praise) and the *Mārgacaryā* (Practice of the Path) were later expounded.
How is this to be understood? Answer: This is also not the case. The *Mārgacaryā* is merely another name for the *Svalpā*. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Prasphutaprabhāsa* is listed first.
At the end of the *Praise of the Radiance* (*Prabhāsa-praśaṃsā*), it lists: "The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* (*Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*), the *Radiance Praise*.

Thus we know that the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* is simply another name for the *Mārgāloka* (or *Dàoxíng*). In the preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines*, Master Tanyǒu states: "This sūtra consists of thirty chapters; because they are unified by the Way (*mārga*), it is titled the *Mārgāloka*.
Therefore, we know that the *Mārgāloka* is indeed the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines*. During the Wei dynasty, there was the śramaṇa Zhú Shìxíng.

Daozun followed the *Xiaopin* (Shorter Version) because he knew its textual meaning was incomplete; thus, in the sixth year of the Ganlu era, he traveled toward the kingdom of Yutian to seek out a copy of the scripture.

There he encountered the *Dapin* (Larger Version), yet because the eminent monks of that country believed only in the Hīnayāna, when Zhu Shixing was about to return, those monks addressed the King of Yutian, saying: "The Daoist practitioners of the land of Han abandon the Buddha’s orthodox teaching."
He was carrying the Brahmanical scriptures with the intention of returning to his own country to propagate them;

however, the King would not grant him permission, and thus the King obstructed and refused his request. At that time, Zhu Shixing addressed the King, saying: "I have come from afar at this moment, regardless of my own life, solely for the sake of these scriptures.
If Your Majesty will not permit it, I must ask that you grant me one wish. He then made a solemn vow, saying: [text continues].
"If this sutra has a karmic affinity with the land of Han, then as it is now cast into the fire, the flames shall be extinguished.
Having made this vow, he threw it into the charcoal fire; the fire was spontaneously extinguished and the sutra did not burn.

At that time, the great virtuous monks of that country and all the people conceived a heart of faith and accepted this sutra, recognizing its great merit and being unable to stop [its spread]. Zhu Shixing... [continued].

When the time for its transmission had not yet arrived, it was translated into twenty or nineteen fascicles during the early Jin dynasty; later, Master Kumārajīva translated it into twenty-seven fascicles.
When he wished to depart from Shache City, the auspicious signs that appeared were most magnificent.
The tenth [section] provides an exegesis based on the text, which serves as the introduction to the subsequent fascicle; it is so called because it is extracted from the *Śāstra*.

Although it does not follow the original text word-for-word, it relies extensively upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da lun). Furthermore, since its meaning is inherited from an authentic source, there should be no doubt about this.
Commentary on the Meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll One;
Commentary on the Meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Three. Composed by Hu Jizang.
Chapter Three, Part One:
On Cultivating Practice (*Śikṣā-prasthāna*). The opening of the treatise states that there is nothing its scope does not encompass and nothing its intent does not reveal.

Furthermore, the subsequent chapters arise because one wishes to discuss and analyze the meaning established above; thus, while the preceding section opened the treatise, this section analyzes that very thesis. This intent applies universally to the whole.
Regarding the instruction on "practicing in accordance" (*anuyoga*), there are two meanings. First, the Buddha has previously shown the characteristics of *prajñā*;

now, because it is clarified that the Bodhisattva practices in accordance with *prajñā*, they are able to attain correspondence with *prajñā*. However, if the Bodhisattva practices *prajñā* through skillful means (*upāya*), they correspond with it;
if they practice without skillful means, they cannot attain correspondence with *prajñā*. Question: What constitutes having [skillful means]?
Regarding the answer concerning skillful means (*upāya*) and the absence of skillful means: if, at first glance, there is practice and that which is to be practiced, one cannot attain correspondence;

it is because there is no practice and nothing to be practiced that one attains correspondence. Next, if there is practice and yet no practice, this is not corresponding; only when there is neither practice nor non-practice is it corresponding.
Furthermore, if one holds the dual views of "practice and non-practice" or "neither practice nor non-practice," these two are dualities, and where there is duality, there is no [correspondence].

Second, it is that neither "non-duality" nor "not non-duality" is what is appropriate; rather, it is their mutual non-applicability that constitutes correspondence. Furthermore, regarding the practice of what is appropriate and inappropriate:

both practicing what is appropriate and practicing what is inappropriate are equally non-applicable; this very non-applicability of both appropriateness and inappropriateness is what constitutes correspondence. As for the arrival of the "Chapter on Practicing What is Appropriate":

since the preceding section has already demonstrated the characteristics of *prajñā*, this section now causes the bodhisattva to practice *prajñā* so that they may attain correspondence with *prajñā*. Had these characteristics not been shown previously, [this would not be possible].
Question: If the characteristic of *prajñā* (wisdom) is that there is nothing to be practiced, then one cannot be in accord with *prajñā*.
You previously stated that the Buddha acts as he speaks, and thus instructs the Bodhisattva to act as he speaks; since this also constitutes practicing in such a manner, one thereby attains accord.

What further practice should there be for accord? Answer: It is indeed so; however, it is only with respect to the two kinds of emptiness—emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) and emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—that [this practice is established].

The gate of explaining the practice of *prajñā* follows the gate of explaining the application of practice; after the gate of explaining the application of *prajñā*, one practices what was previously practiced, and as one practices what was previously practiced, one also practices what was practiced later. This is simply the manifestation of equanimity. Question: What is the difference between the explanation in the gate of explaining the application of practice and the explanation in the preceding gate?

Answer: They differ both horizontally and vertically. As for the horizontal difference: above, the two types of emptiness—the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)—were explained briefly.

The practice of the two emptinesses—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of persons (*pudgala*)—is now explained in detail. Regarding the distinction between "practice" (*xi*) and "establishment" (*shu*): above, practice was clarified solely from the perspective of the gate of emptiness;

here, practice is clarified by means of the gate that refutes the four positions (*catuskoṭi*). Therefore, it is said below that "there is practice, but there is no non-practice," and so forth; this constitutes the difference. Question:
Why was the previous section concerned only with the gate of emptiness, while the present section employs the gate that refutes the four positions? Answer: [As follows:]... (text continues)

Since these all first open the fundamental tenet of Prajñāpāramitā, they provisionally refute the existence of persons and dharmas; subsequently, for the sake of ultimate realization, they fully refute the four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the "Chapter on Practice and Response" (*Xiying pin*): it derives its name from the principle following the chapter’s conclusion, while "Offering the Alms Bowl" (*Fengbo*) derives its name from the event at the beginning of the chapter.
Furthermore, "Practice and Response" is explained extensively as the cause for responding, while "Offering the Alms Bowl" symbolizes the Bodhisattva.
Practicing *prajñāpāramitā* necessarily accomplishes the work of a Buddha; since this matter is so great, it is named from the very beginning.

It is also said that at the stage of the *sāṃbhogakāya* (Zhao ti), one practices for thirty mental states (*triṃśac-citta*) but does not respond [to them], whereas at the eighth ground (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one responds but does not practice.

From the first ground up to the seventh ground, one both practices and responds. As for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), they neither respond nor practice. Question Ten: The similarities of the thirty mental states.
Cultivation is also a corresponding response. If one were to depart from the eighth stage because it is effortless (*anābhoga*), then while there is a response, there would be no cultivation;

yet in the eighth stage, the response is spontaneous and cultivation is likewise spontaneous and effortless. Now, in contrast to this, four permutations are established: 1. Cultivation without response:

This refers to cultivation that has attainment but does not correspond with non-attainment Prajñā. 2. Response without cultivation: This refers to [the state of] Prajñā... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the extant portion.)

If one explains that which is neither cause nor effect as being the "cause," then this reverts to the ten stages (*bhūmi*); in that case, it would be a response (*pratirūpa*) rather than cultivation (*abhyāsa*).

If it is taken as the "effect," then it would be the Buddha’s response rather than cultivation. From the moment of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), practicing with non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is itself non-attainment;

it is a response to those who follow the stream of inversion, and thus it is neither a non-response nor a non-cultivation. Furthermore, the aforementioned explanation of the Dharma clarifies both the dharma of birth and the dharma of non-birth.

Now, by raising this analogy, I clarify that both phenomena (*dharma*) and sentient beings (*sattva*) are empty, showing that the myriad transformations are merely such. Do you believe in the sixteen *puruṣas*?

If so, then the present case of phenomena and sentient beings is likewise. Furthermore, according to the treatise, the former primarily clarifies the emptiness of phenomena, while the latter primarily clarifies the emptiness of sentient beings.
Why is it that although the former clarifies the emptiness of both sentient beings and phenomena, the contemplation still persists?
The subject perceives the contemplation of emptiness; now the contemplating subject is stilled. Above, it clarifies that conditions are exhausted;

below, it clarifies that contemplation is exhausted by conditions. Above, the object is exhausted; now, the subject is exhausted. Thus, when the object is exhausted, there is no "number" (conceptualization) within; when the subject is exhausted, there is no "mind" within.
When both internal and external are simultaneously darkened (unified), conditions and wisdom are both quiescent. The text consists of three parts; this is the first: the exhortation.

Contemplating the two kinds of emptiness regarding arising phenomena constitutes the first "elevation"; this is the third [of the three elevations]. When thought reaches what has been heard, one immediately possesses the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);

because of this contemplation, when one practices, one then possesses the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). This encompasses the causes and fruits of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as all persons.
Prajñā is the emptiness of the five aggregates and of mundane and supramundane phenomena.

In the passage beginning with "As I [have practiced]," the second point—comparing myself to all disciples—is presented because they hear of the sixteen-fold emptiness of self and know the sixteen unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*).

By citing what they lack, one contrasts it with what they possess; through practice, they come to have what was previously absent, and by attaining what was previously present, they no longer practice for the sake of what is absent.

Since there is nothing further to be attained, what could possibly be lacking? Thus, both views are simultaneously stilled. Furthermore, because the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is easily realized, the text cites that which is easily attained.

How much more so regarding the difficulty of emptiness: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [the community] divided into two factions. One faction believed in the emptiness of persons but did not believe in the emptiness of dharmas;
the other believed in both types of emptiness. There was no one who did not believe in the emptiness of persons, as this is easy to attain; therefore, it is raised [as a point of consensus].

As for people today, they also demonstrate that the sixteen [emptinesses] are non-existent, while the aggregates, bases, and elements are existent as conventional truth; thus, what is clarified here is that they are equal in this regard.

If one says that the sixteen [factors] are falsely imputed as a real self, then the Buddha-way is also practiced through the false imputation of a Buddha-self. Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and so forth:

to give rise to the notion of a self within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is called "the self. To act as a sovereign lord over the various collective phenomena is called "the sentient being" (*sattva*).

To achieve the faculty of life is called "the life-possessor" (*jīva*). When a father gives birth to a son, it is called "the progenitor" (*janaka*). When [the child] drinks milk, it is called "the nurtured" (*poṣa*).
Because they are nurtured by the causes and conditions of food and clothing at mealtime, they are called "nourished.

Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are composed of these various numerical factors, they are called "numerical collections" (*saṃkhyā*). Because a practitioner is able to initiate various activities, they are called a "person" (*pudgala*).

Because the faculties such as hands and feet have functions to perform, they are called "action," "agent," and "power. Because they can cause others [to act], they are called "the one who causes action" (*prayojaka*).
That which initiates good and evil karma in future lives is called the "initiator"; that which causes others to initiate such karma is the "instigator.

That which experiences suffering and pleasure in future lives is called the "experiencer"; that which causes others to experience suffering and pleasure is the "instigator of experience. The eye is called the "seer," while the other five sense-faculties transcend the two vehicles.
Furthermore, this is explained from the perspective of the two gates of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*) as the *prajñā* (wisdom) of the higher [vehicle].
Because it is the Dharma, that which emerges is known through the five sensory consciousnesses; this next point combines the illustration with its meaning.

When a Bodhisattva is thus able to practice such that both object and contemplation are quiescent, their path transcends that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Furthermore, above, the *prajñāpāramitā* was explained by way of the two gates of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons;
because of this Dharma, one now emerges from the two vehicles. Now, those who aspire to the Way should, with faith and practice, ascend toward the emptiness of persons.

The Dharma is taught through the two gates of emptiness; here, the Prajñā is now being explained. What is the difference between the emptiness of the practice of the Two Vehicles and the emptiness of the practice of the Bodhisattva?
The emptiness practiced by the Two Vehicles involves something to be attained (*upalabdha*), whereas the emptiness practiced by the Bodhisattva is non-attainment (*anupalabdha*).
Thirdly, above it was clarified that the Bodhisattva’s skillful means and true wisdom do not perceive persons or dharmas; now, the Bodhisattva’s true wisdom is clarified.
The previous statement—that one practices the ten thousand practices through skillful means to deliver sentient beings—indicates that skillful means are taken as the reality;

thus, although one performs the ten thousand practices, there is nothing performed, and although one delivers sentient beings, there are no beings delivered. The present passage indicates that reality itself is named "skillful means";

thus, although there is nothing performed, there is nothing not performed, and although there are no beings delivered, there are none who are not delivered. Only when both forms of emptiness (the emptiness of self and phenomena) are fully elucidated is the teaching complete.

The Prajñā-pāramitā path merely surpasses that of the two vehicles; others say that the Bodhisattva’s practice of existence is superior to the two vehicles’ practice of emptiness, yet this is not the case in the present scripture.
It clarifies only that the Bodhisattva’s "emptiness of the unobtainable" is therefore superior to the two vehicles, rather than speaking of the gate of existence (*yu-mén*).
Furthermore, if Prajñā were the common teaching for the two vehicles, then the two kinds of emptiness regarding dharmas and persons would simply constitute the [teaching] of the three vehicles.
In what sense is it said to be superior?

Others say that while [the śrāvakas] attain emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they do not attain existence (*bhāva*). Now, the Master clarifies that the scriptural text is divided into two types of emptiness: first, attainable emptiness; second, unattainable emptiness (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
Since the bodhisattva now practices unattainable emptiness, he transcends the two vehicles (*yāna*). Furthermore, there are two [reasons for this].
First, it is praised that the Bodhisattva’s practice is superior to that of the Two Vehicles because of the external causes of the skillful means of the emptiness of non-apprehensibility;
second, it is praised that the Bodhisattva’s assembly of practices is superior to that of the Two Vehicles because they are fully perfected. The first section has two parts:

first, the main exposition clarifying that the Bodhisattva’s practice is superior to the Two Vehicles due to the functional application of the skillful means of the emptiness of non-apprehensibility; second, the use of analogies for comparative evaluation. The first [of these] has three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.

As for "emptiness of the unobtainable according to the text," this is the emptiness of non-apprehension. Since the Buddha has previously taught the two kinds of emptiness—of arising and of phenomena—the Bodhisattva here, possessing sharp faculties, realizes the emptiness of both arising and phenomena; yet, because he does not cling to either, it is called "not abiding in the emptiness of arising and phenomena.
Thus, there is no apprehension. As stated above, by not abiding in any phenomena, one abides in Prajñā through non-abiding.

Because they abide [in suchness], they are able to deliver sentient beings through non-abiding; yet in reality, sentient beings have never been delivered, for it is precisely because there is no delivering that there is delivering.
Furthermore, as the Mahāyāna Sūtras state: "The followers of the Two Vehicles see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness;

they do not practice the Middle Way and do not see the Buddha-nature. Bodhisattvas, however, see emptiness, and by means of non-emptiness—neither as empty nor as not empty—they realize the Middle Way of Prajñā."

Since these alternative names do not reveal the Middle Way Buddha-nature, one does not perceive Prajñā; thus, regarding the dharmas of suffering and pleasure, one forms the conception of them as the Middle Way and as Prajñā.
For example, beneath the Jambū tree, there is a second section for weighing superiority and inferiority; according to the treatise, this constitutes two parts, the first being a general comparison.
Regarding the two distinctions of measurement—the specific and the general—there are three [categories] within the latter. First, Jambudvīpa; second, the trichiliocosm;
third, the ten directions. "Jambu" is the name of a tree; the continent is named after this tree as its designation.
Within the continent there is a Jambu forest, and because this tree therein is the longest, it serves as the name. Beneath the tree is a river with golden sand at its bottom, called the Jambu River.
The "small continent" (*kṣudradvīpa*) of Jambūdvīpa is also [included] within Jambūdvīpa itself.

First, one day [the teaching] descends; second, there is a separate classification based on the previous method of the public [teaching], which speaks of the general Śrāvakas and the general Bodhisattvas.
Next, regarding Jambūdvīpa, there is the specific Śrāvaka and the general wisdom; now, for the second [section], there is the specific wisdom and the general Śrāvaka. This is the explanation.
There is this underlying intent that does not contradict the literal text; now, based on this, it is divided into three parts: first, the formal logical analysis (*yukti*);
second, the question; and third, the answer. The question has three parts: first, a general clarification that because the wisdom of all sages is identical, it is shown to be non-different.

Regarding "the nature of non-arising is emptiness," this is the formal heading. It refers to the wisdom that illuminates the reality of emptiness as being non-different. There are two interpretations of this discussion: one says that wisdom is not non-existent.

It is called "emptiness of the nature of non-arising" because it arises as the emptiness of the nature of non-arising and illuminates the objective realm of the emptiness of the nature of non-arising.

Second, it is said that there are also seven wisdoms, which exist through the harmony of causes and conditions, and thus there is also the emptiness of the nature of non-arising. However, these seven matters are not different from one another:

first, the wisdom that illuminates the empty realm is not different; second, they equally correspond to the realm of non-arising and are not different; third, they equally transcend the realms and are not different.
1. The fourth [point] is that their abandonment of delusions is not different; 2. the fifth is that they equally attain the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, which is not different; 3.

the sixth is that they equally attain conditioned liberation (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*) and unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), which is not different; 4. the seventh is that they equally enter *nirvāṇa*, which is not different.

"If the dharmas do not contradict one another" refers to the second section, which sets forth their commonality to clarify that they are not different. "How is it, World-Honored One? refers to the third section, which addresses their differences. This is the question posed to the Buddha above.
Having completed the general and specific investigations that clarified the relative superiority and inferiority [of the vehicles], why does Śāriputra ask again now? The answer is twofold:

first, while the Buddha previously clarified superiority and inferiority through difficult challenges, it is now that the followers of the Two Vehicles clarify superiority and inferiority for themselves, thereby finally establishing the distinction between them.
Second, Śāriputra stated that the previous explanation showed the power of the Bodhisattvas' wisdom to surpass that of the Two Vehicles, a point about which there is no doubt.

What is it that Bodhisattvas possess which the two vehicles lack? It is that Bodhisattvas possess skillful means (*upāya*) capable of delivering sentient beings and extensively cultivate the ten thousand practices, whereas the two vehicles do not have these two.

Now, since we are merely inquiring about the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of wisdom, which is the same for both, there is no need for such tedious deliberation on their relative superiority or inferiority.

The Buddha’s response consists of two teachings and two analogies, forming four parts: first, clarifying the inferiority of the two vehicles compared to the Bodhisattvas; second, clarifying the superiority of the Bodhisattvas.

1. The first [analogy] of "riding upon" uses the metaphor of a firefly to illustrate the inferiority of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) compared to bodhisattvas. 2. The second [analogy] of "the rising sun" illustrates the superiority of bodhisattvas over the two vehicles. 3.

Regarding the Buddha’s answers to the three questions concerning the inferiority of the two vehicles compared to bodhisattvas, he here employs three successive counter-questions (*paripṛcchā*). First, he clarifies the two vehicles.
There is no practice for the task of delivering sentient beings. Second, it clarifies the absence of the thought of delivering sentient beings through practice.

Third, by extensively citing various virtuous deeds, it demonstrates that the two vehicles lack such thought. The reason for this cross-examination is to cause Śāriputra himself to state in his own words that he cannot equal a Bodhisattva.
Since the preceding text was not different from [the Bodhisattva’s] mastery, it is now examined for the sake of establishing their identity.
In the first question, two phrases raise the Middle Way wisdom within the causal stage as the subject of inquiry.

Because the Two Vehicles cannot, by means of this wisdom of the path, deliver sentient beings and practice the myriad practices—being obstructed by emptiness and existence—it is impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.

A Bodhisattva, however, can deliver sentient beings through the wisdom of the path; because they are unobstructed regarding emptiness and existence, they possess a wisdom that is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence. Thus, one knows that its essence is also [the Middle Way].

The same applies to the second [point]. Regarding the fruit, it is asked by way of contrast: "Does the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) deliver all sentient beings? [The answer is: "Even the two vehicles do not possess this.
Furthermore, there are five ways of delivering: first, delivering by means of the Great Vehicle; second, those delivered by the Great Vehicle cannot be delivered by the two vehicles;
third, those delivered by the two vehicles cannot be delivered by the vehicle of gods and humans; fourth, [the same applies to] the fourth [category].
The Vehicle of Humans cannot benefit others through present fruits, nor can it benefit them through the five types of present happiness;

because it lacks the benefit of a compassionate heart, it ultimately does not abandon sentient beings—a quality which the Two Vehicles do not possess. Others may say that while the causes practiced differ, the place where the fruit is attained is not different;

or that while the causes practiced are the same, the fruits attained differ; or that while the practice of emptiness is the same, the practice of existence differs. Now, I clarify that these views are all [erroneous].
Others say that Śāriputra raised the wisdom of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) as his question, while the Buddha gave the answer by means of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*).

If this were so, the question and answer would not correspond to one another. Now it is clarified that Śāriputra raised a question regarding ultimate wisdom, and the Buddha likewise answered by means of ultimate wisdom;
this demonstrates that while those of the Two Vehicles abide in ultimate reality and cannot save sentient beings, Bodhisattvas abide in ultimate wisdom and are able to save sentient beings.
If one uses only the wisdom of ultimate emptiness to deliver sentient beings, why is this so? Because the two wisdoms are non-dual, and their two objects are likewise non-dual;
thus, the object of form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the object of form. Through non-dual wisdom, one constantly cultivates the myriad practices to deliver sentient beings.
Cultivating these myriad practices is itself the true mark (*dharmatā*), and the true mark does not conflict with delivering sentient beings. If they were dual...

If one rides upon the vehicle [of the Bodhisattva] yet cannot use the wisdom of reality (*bhūtaprajñā*) to deliver sentient beings, then emptiness and existence are indeed dualistic; this constitutes a view of grasping and rejecting, or arising and ceasing.

Because the Bodhisattva views emptiness and existence as non-dual, it is a view that is without grasping or rejecting, and without arising or ceasing. Question: The text states that because one uses the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) to know all phenomena and deliver all sentient beings, it is superior;
it does not say "by means of the wisdom of reality. Why is this so? Answer: [The former refers to the ultimate fruit, while the latter refers to the specific method of realization.]
This alone constitutes the ultimate realization of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) through absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). If one does not believe this, one might ask:
"The preceding text stated that the Bodhisattva surpasses the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) by means of the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*); what further need is there to say this?
One should know that the Bodhisattva is able to form such a thought. Below, the second section clarifies how the Bodhisattva surpasses the two vehicles. [The following] two...
The two doubts can be clarified through analogy. To cite the analogy of the firefly illustrates the inferior nature of the two vehicles mentioned above:

1. The fireflies of the ten directions cannot equal the light of one sun; this serves as a general refutation of the former. 2. The sun’s illumination is superior to the fireflies of the ten directions, which have shone for kalpas;

this serves as a specific refutation of the former. 3. Fireflies lack the power to illuminate the affairs of the world; this illustrates the absence of supreme matters. 4. Fireflies lack... [text ends]

The analogy of the light illuminating the world illustrates that the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are without thought. Fifth, before the sun has risen there is illumination, but once the sun has risen there is no longer such illumination;
likewise, before the Bodhisattva has appeared, the two vehicles merely transform sentient beings, whereas when the Sun-like Buddha arrives, he purifies the Buddha-way.

Second, it is explained that because the Bodhisattva’s multitudes are fully endowed with practice, they surpass the Two Vehicles (dvi-yāna). This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the superiority of their merit;

second, clarifying the superiority of their field (*kṣetra*) as well as their functional efficacy. Because they can serve as the cause for the Two Vehicles, the previous question is followed by the answer.
Some say that "those who have long since [come]" refers to Śāriputra, a Śrāvaka, asking about the purification of the Buddha-way. What is this one? It is the fulfillment of the Buddha's [purpose].

Although there is no benefit for oneself once one has turned toward the Dharma of humans, [the questioner] asks for three reasons: first, to benefit others; second, to repay the Buddha's kindness through the two types of retribution;

and third, because while they have already mastered the Śrāvaka-dharma, they have not yet mastered the Bodhisattva-dharma. Although it was stated above in general terms that the Bodhisattva is superior to the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), it is not yet known how he transcends the stages of the two vehicles to enter the rank of a Bodhisattva and further purify the Buddha-way. [The disciple] asks the Master within the mountain retreat.
Regarding the statement "superiority upon arising," although it was said that [the bodhisattva] is superior, it was not known at what stage this superiority occurs. The Buddha replied:

"As for those who belong to the Śrāvaka lineage, they are equal in merit to the sixth bhūmi and become superior only at the seventh bhūmi; as for those who do not belong to the Śrāvaka lineage, they are equal in merit to the sixth resolve and become superior only at the seventh resolve.
However, in the present text, neither of these cases applies; rather, from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), one is already superior.
Question: Since superiority itself constitutes a fault, and since the two vehicles already enter the stage of a bodhisattva, why is there further questioning and answering?
Previously, the superiority was explained in general; now, the specific method by which the two vehicles surpass [their own level] and enter the stage of a bodhisattva is being set forth.

The Buddha’s answer specifically clarifies how to surpass the two vehicles and enter the stage of a bodhisattva by means of the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), and how to purify the buddha-fields. Thus, it proceeds by means of the three [gates].
Regarding the "clarity of the gates of liberation," it is said that if those of the Two Vehicles enter the three gates of liberation without skillful means, they will abide in *nirvāṇa*.
This is because the three liberations are the gates to the city of *nirvāṇa*. Because Bodhisattvas possess skillful means, they know that emptiness is existence;

although it is empty, it exists, and thus they do not cling to emptiness. Although it exists, it is empty, and thus they do not cling to existence. Being free from clinging, [they do not abide in *nirvāṇa*].

Because it is empty, the view of annihilation ceases; because one does not cling to existence, the view of permanence ceases. This is called skillful means (*upāya*), and only then can one enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva observes and knows that the Four Noble Truths practiced by those of the Two Vehicles are views of arising and ceasing:
suffering and its origin are the marks of arising, while the path is the mark of cessation. Knowing that this is a path of arising and ceasing and not the true Way, [the bodhisattva transcends it].
Entering the contemplation of the Single Truth, one contemplates that which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure.

Because it does not arise, it is not suffering or its origin; because it does not cease, it is not cessation or the path; because it is not defiled, there is no precept; because it is not pure, there is no liberation.

Thus, having transcended the contemplation of the Four Truths, one enters the contemplation of the Single Reality. By transcending the stage of the Two Vehicles, one enters the Bodhisattva stage; this is what is meant by entering the Bodhisattva stage.
Because one can transform sentient beings and bring about a Buddha-land, one attains the Buddha-way; because one brings about a pure Buddha-land, one attains the Buddha-way;

because one purifies all evils of the three karmas through great purity, the Buddha-way is pure; furthermore, the purity of the Buddha-way consists in viewing the characteristics of offenses as identical to Bodhi.
From "The Buddha himself abides in what stage to act as a field of merit" (Section Two), this clarifies the superiority of the field of merit through two questions and answers.
Upon hearing that Bodhisattvas possess supreme qualities, Śāriputra conceived a deep sense of reverence for them;

yet he did not know at what stage a Bodhisattva must be to serve as a field for the two vehicles. He reasoned that since a Bodhisattva’s afflictions (*kleśa*) are not yet exhausted, they cannot function as a field—how then could they be superior?

In the Buddha’s response to the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), there are three points. First, it clarifies that because [the bodhisattva] possesses all merits in their entirety, they serve as a field for the two vehicles.
Second, it clarifies that the bodhisattva externally possesses the merit of benefiting others, thereby serving as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Third, it directly answers the question:

since a bodhisattva is superior to the two vehicles from the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), they are thus a field; this is the meaning of this particular analogy. Why is this so?
Therefore, because of the second virtue of benefiting others, he is capable of serving as a field; herein, both worldly and supramundane merits are fully elucidated.
However, the designations for the "agent" and the "act" each have their basis: the agent exists by virtue of *prajñā*, and the act exists by virtue of the Bodhisattva.

Thus, one understands that among the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), not a single thing is worth adopting—just as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that shaving the head and donning robes are all like [the state of] non-purity, and as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* describes them as being neither pure nor impure.

Question: It is incorrect to say that begging for food and preaching the Dharma are [the domain of] the Two Vehicles; rather, even the five precepts and ten wholesome acts of worldly people must arise from the Bodhisattvas.
Answer: The Two Vehicles themselves must arise from the Bodhisattvas. How could what is now preached by the Two Vehicles not be due to the Bodhisattvas?
The Two Vehicles always depend upon the Bodhisattvas; it is because the Two Vehicles are able to preach the ten wholesome acts and so forth.

Question: Is it not because Bodhisattvas exist? [Objection: Now, even at times when there are no Bodhisattvas, there are still devas, humans, the ten wholesome paths of action, the five precepts, and so forth; how can these all be said to depend upon Bodhisattvas? Answer: There are two reasons. First, regarding the twenty-one precepts, they were established as skillful means for pure Bodhisattvas to act as human kings or celestial kings, or to appear as householders or renunciants, or even as followers of external paths; therefore, the ten [wholesome paths] are taught. Second, [the precepts] are taught because they serve as the foundation for the arising of the Buddhas of the three times. For this reason, it is said that the ten wholesome paths of action and the five precepts all arise from the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the ten wholesome paths of action are the root of the eighty-four thousand dharmas, and the eighty-four thousand dharmas are the root of the Buddhas of the three times. Therefore, the Buddhas of the three times all arise from the Bodhisattvas. It is like the case of the four great elements: although they are not present in a single atom, they are present throughout the entire world-realm. Thus, the ten wholesome paths of action and the five precepts are likewise present throughout the world-realm, even though they do not exist within a single atom. Therefore, it is said that they all arise from the Bodhisattvas. Moreover, the ten wholesome paths of action and the five precepts are the roots of the Buddhas of the three times. Just as the four great elements are the roots of all sentient beings, so too are the ten wholesome paths of action and the five precepts the roots of the Buddhas of the three times. Therefore, it is said that they all arise from the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the ten wholesome paths of action and the five precepts are the roots of the Buddhas of the three times. Regarding the two aspects of the five precepts of goodness: if Bodhisattvas were unable to transform sentient beings— whether by transforming ten through one or a hundred through one—

and if they did not preach the ten wholesome actions and the five precepts, then within the six realms of existence there would be only three types of sensation, and among those sensations, there would be only the sensation of suffering.

Having finished offering the white cloth to the Buddha, the second question and answer follows. [The opponent] asks: "If the field is for the sake of cultivation, yet the Bodhisattva’s afflictions (*kleśa*) are not yet exhausted, then how can the field be pure?
How, then, can the grace of giving be brought to completion? The Buddha answers with two points: first, as the field; second, as the donor. Regarding the field:
from the very moment of the initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*), it is fundamentally pure. As for its ultimate purity, it is because from the initial resolve...
Having realized that afflictions do not arise, one vows to deliver all sentient beings and seeks all Buddha-dharmas;

thus, one can repay the kindness of the donor. The Master further said: "If afflictions were exhausted at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, it would be impossible [for them to exist].

If they were completely severed, one would already be a Buddha. Since they are not yet exhausted, how can one say that they are fundamentally pure from the beginning? This is explained here for this specific reason."

The refutation of the initial view means that because [beings] were initially impure and later became pure, this now clarifies that they are fundamentally pure from the beginning, thereby dispelling the initial misconception.
Next, regarding the donor, this also explains the causes and conditions for pure giving; since one is able to act as a donor, how could one not digest the offerings?
He asks the Buddha: "How should one practice? Below, first, the opening of the school clarifies the characteristics of practicing *prajñā*. Now...

Second, showing the method for practicing Prajñāpāramitā: Although the characteristics of Prajñā were shown above, because Prajñā is extremely profound and subtle, there is fear that practitioners may frequently err or fail;
therefore, the complete method for study and practice is now further shown. However, these two gates possess both the meanings of "union" and "separation.
Regarding "union," the master [states] that the aforementioned demonstration of the practice of Prajñā consists of two gates, the first of which is...
This is the second section, which correctly demonstrates the characteristics of *prajñā* through the practice of the two bodhisattvas.

Because they transcend the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and enter the rank of bodhisattva, there are now two gates: first, the correct elucidation of training in and responding to *prajñā*;

second, the elucidation of how the bodhisattva, being in accord with *prajñā*, attains the fruit-roots of immeasurable merit. Regarding the term "detachment" (*li*), it refers to the two gates of *prajñā* previously explained, the first of which was the correct [practice].
Regarding the two explanations of the "Gate of Exposition" and the two praises of the "Gate of Praise," the present case is likewise twofold. As for the two explanations:

the *Píngbō pǐn* (Chapter on Receiving the Bowl) explains *prajñā* in terms of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena to clarify the emptiness that is the object of observation; the beginning of the *Záxí yìng pǐn* (Chapter on Miscellaneous Practice and Response) explains *prajñā* in terms of the two emptinesses to clarify the emptiness that is the subject of observation.
Regarding the two praises: the first praises the sublime and lofty wisdom-virtue of the Bodhisattva.
Because of the external application of skillful means (*upāya*), it surpasses the Two Vehicles.
Second, this praises the Bodhisattva assembly for being fully endowed with practice and entering the Bodhisattva stage. Now, regarding the four gates:

first, the primary exposition demonstrates the training and application of Prajñā; second, by citing the retribution of the fruit, it praises [the Bodhisattvas] and clarifies that such praise is due to their training and application.
Regarding the second cycle, at its beginning, the practice and application are further explained; the second part clarifies the praise for attaining the fruit.

Previously, there were two explanations followed by two praises in succession; now, the praises and explanations are interwoven. This is because skillful means employ many different approaches to lead beings to awakening, as these are not limited to a single method.
Within the first cycle of practice and application, there are two parts: first the question, then the answer. The question has two sections.
First, because from the time he first practiced Prajñāpāramitā until now, Śāriputra has praised the merits of Prajñāpāramitā in every sutra;
and because Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable, and because practitioners desire to study it, Śāriputra asks these questions.
Second, Śāriputra knows that Prajñāpāramitā is extremely profound, like an illusion or a transformation; fearing that bodhisattvas might err in their practice, he asks these questions.
In response: The Master had not yet lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, but he opened with two types of questions—single and double—and one type of abandonment (*tyāga*).

Should it be considered appropriate or inappropriate? If it were appropriate, there would be no need to further discuss the two types of abandonment; if it were inappropriate, why did he speak of them? The answer is:

If it were appropriate at that time, then by means of a single abandonment, both would be appropriate; if it were inappropriate, then both would be inappropriate. Since the actual record shows that even a single abandonment was appropriate, [the former must be the case].

When practicing emptiness, how could one perceive emptiness as distinct from existence? Therefore, this is also appropriate. However, since the preceding discourse was insufficient and feared that sentient beings might give rise to [dualistic] views, both [extremes] were set aside.
Now, let us establish seven kinds of clear wisdom: first, the cessation of conditions; second, the cessation of the practice of contemplation;

third, the pure practice of both conditions and contemplation; fourth, the cessation of the practice of results; fifth, the practice of gratitude; sixth, the cessation of the practice of conduct; and seventh, the cessation of the practice of purpose.
Because there is no perception of a Tathāgata regarding the realms of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, one cannot correspond to Prajñāpāramitā;

therefore, at the outset, one is instructed to purify all objects in order to still the habitual tendencies of conditions. Although these objects are thus purified, one still maintains that there is a mind capable of observation.

Consequently, the second stage clarifies the purification of the habitual tendencies of observation by means of stilling the observation, because one remains attached to the purity of the observation. Thus, one perceives the conditions; yet if those conditions are empty, then one observes.

If that which is not empty cannot be made empty through the contemplation of non-emptiness, and if one contemplates this as empty while the object remains non-empty, then who could make that non-empty object empty?
Therefore, the third stage must clarify that both object and contemplation cease together: when the object is exhausted, contemplation is exhausted;

when contemplation is exhausted, the object is purified. Since it is neither cognition nor contemplation, it is clarified that only when both object and contemplation are pure does one truly possess contemplation.
Furthermore, because such purified practice accords with *samyak-saṃbodhi*, the fourth stage is the "resultant purification through the contemplation of the conditions of practice";
thus, both cause and effect are empty. Seeing that both cause and effect are empty and taking this as true practice constitutes the fifth stage.

Since cause and effect are already empty, the sixth and seventh stages clarify that practice is not a substantial purity; the intent for these two stages will be explained in the text at the beginning of the Path.
The section on the "Gates of Cessation from Conditions" follows the scriptural text and addresses its difficulties.
