The eye is the skillful means for transforming others; because it is difficult and profound, it is the third, the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and the fourth, the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).

Based on the six consciousnesses, these are categorized as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: the eye sees, the ear hears, and the mental consciousness knows; the remaining three [consciousnesses] are termed "sensing" (*jñāna*).

Because their functions differ across these three phases, they are able to know worldly affairs first and subsequently know supramundane affairs, and they can also attain the three karmas. [One] sees forms and hears sounds.

Regarding the contemplation of the Dharma through hearing, one attains the Path and further penetrates the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for the other three [faculties], they only take the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) as their object.
One knows worldly phenomena because fragrance, taste, and touch are exclusively indeterminate matter (*rūpa*), whereas sound and mental objects (*dharma*) pertain to all three natures.

However, at this stage, there is no conceptualization (*vikalpa*) because it is non-conceptual. If the Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*) performs Buddha-work by means of fragrance, how could that fragrance not be indeterminate?
He further said: "The Buddha-eye only knows conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); the four eyes know the mundane, for mundane phenomena are manifold.

With the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus), one sees the Real; the Real is non-dual. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The wisdom-eye is conversely called the Buddha-eye; how could it see only the mundane?
Now, all five eyes see together, yet they do not see seeing, because there is nothing seen. Thus, they do not see at all, as it is said: "The five [eyes]..."
The eye does not fail to perceive the Bodhisattvas and others; the five eyes both illuminate the conventional and illuminate the ultimate, fully illuminating both the ultimate and the conventional.

The wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) has no phenomenon it does not see—how could it not illuminate the conventional? The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Always in samādhi, one constantly perceives all phenomena as non-dual.
Is this not the divine eye (divya-cakṣus) perceiving the ultimate? Furthermore, since the divine eye is not without that which it sees, it is the wisdom of the ultimate.
The eye sees by not seeing; therefore, it illuminates the world.
In the third section, the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are said to encompass all dharmas.

Furthermore, it is stated that "Prajñā encompasses all," which first clarifies that the six [perfections] encompass [all], and subsequently clarifies that it is precisely Prajñā that encompasses all. Now, Prajñā encompasses all wholesome dharmas.
How can it be said that this is merely the wisdom of emptiness?
The sixth bodhisattva clarifies that one who possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) is like the great ocean from which emerge various kinds of jewels:

some for neutralizing poison, some for curing disease, some for warding off demons, and some for producing instruments of pleasure. Within the ocean of *prajñā*, there likewise exist various kinds of real bodhisattvas.
The skillful means of the three evil realms open the three gates of goodness, purify the five eyes, and perfect the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*);
in combination, these constitute only Prajñāpāramitā. "Opening" refers to various types of persons, while "combining" refers to the single Prajñāpāramitā. "Opening" also refers to various dharmas.

The *Śāstra on Numbers* clarifies that the five supernormal powers are shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whereas the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) belongs exclusively to the sages. The *Śāstra* further states that [the former] is obtained as a karmic retribution.

Regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) attained through cultivation without obstruction: they both exist and do not exist. As for the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), one attains them immediately upon entering meditative concentration;
however, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is obstructed by the afflictions (*kleśa*). The treatise explains that each of the five supernormal powers has its own specific obstruction.

Furthermore, it clarifies that because the concentrations of knowing the minds of others and recollecting past lives function internally, they are wholesome (*kuśala*); whereas because the concentrations of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) function externally, they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the supernormal power of *ṛddhi*: if it is produced within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through the transformation of the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), it is wholesome;

if it is produced outside of concentration by transforming small things into large and so forth, it is neutral (*avyākṛta*). According to the Sautrāntikas, the five supernormal powers are produced from the four fundamental dhyānas and arise in the six stages;
according to the Abhidharmikas, they arise in the three dhyānas of the realm of form, while the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) arises in the seven stages based on concentration.
The "supernormal powers" (abhijñā) refer to the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments;

it should also be understood that the five supernormal powers herein are not only shared with ordinary beings, but are also not shared with those of the two vehicles. As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "What was previously unattained is now attained.

Here, it is clarified that all six supernormal powers are *prajñā* (wisdom), though they differ in their combination and separation; when combined and discussed as a whole, they are simply a single *prajñā*.
Because there are six functions, there are the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Through the transformative function of *prajñā*, it is like the fulfillment of wishes:

when there is nothing seen, that is the divine eye; when there is no hearing yet nothing is not heard, that is the divine ear; when there is no knowing yet nothing is not known, that is the knowledge of others' minds and past lives;
and when afflictions are ultimately exhausted, it is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Because *prajñā* is unobstructed, it is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*).
Because it is wondrous and unfathomable, it is called "divine" (*shen*). Furthermore, regarding the three [sections]:

first, the general indication of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); second, the detailed explanation; and third, the concluding explanation. Within the six [supernormal powers], each consists of an indication, an explanation, and a conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation of the liberation of the Three Vehicles; second, the distinction from the Two Vehicles. The first is as stated in the text.
Because their intrinsic nature is empty, [the text] below distinguishes this from the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

One fears that the supernatural powers of non-Buddhists arise because they habitually cultivate the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and perform such deeds, thereby giving rise to arrogance and dualistic attachment to the phenomena of supernatural power; this constitutes the two views of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-dṛṣṭi*).
The Bodhisattva is not like this. The preceding section clarified that there is nothing he does not do; however, because it is truly nothing done, he does not perceive his own body.

Furthermore, as for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because they purify the person, phenomena, and the mind, they constitute the penetration of *prajñā*. To exclude the two vehicles, [it is said] "for the sake of *sarvajñatā*.
Although Bodhisattvas have nothing to do, they act without anything to do; seeking the Buddha-way to deliver sentient beings, this is indeed the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The two vehicles, having nothing to do, merely contemplate emptiness and signlessness, and do not seek the Buddha-way to deliver [sentient beings].

Sentient beings also eliminate [the notion of self] for the sake of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). By eliminating grasping and eliminating their [false] severance, once they see that the Bodhisattva ultimately has nothing to do, they say there is no attainment;
thus it is said that by having "nothing to do," one attains *sarvajñā*. If there were something to be done, one would not attain it.
Furthermore, by eliminating and destroying the permanence of ordinary people, there is a Way that can be practiced. Thus...
If one attains *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) with the ear having something for which it acts, then that [attainment] is not achieved; furthermore, one must eliminate it.

One must break down the notion of a "person" who possesses a path by which to act, for this is ultimately the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). If there is an act performed for the sake of *sarvajñatā*, this too must be eliminated.
Next, regarding the Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) while abiding within *dāna*, the second section—concerning the six perfections—is divided into six parts.
This has four intentions: first, to clarify the six persons by means of the six perfections; second, to explain them in sequence; third, to clarify the attainment of contemplation;

and fourth, to distinguish the fruit from that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Because one practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) while abiding in *dāna*, *dāna* possesses *prajñā* and *prajñā* possesses *dāna*; therefore, it is able [to function].

Because the path of *prajñā* (wisdom) is opened and perfected, it is called "pure. Ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is itself *prajñā*. When one does not give rise to a mind of stinginess, that is *dāna* (generosity).
Because of ultimate emptiness, the mind of stinginess does not arise; thus, it is precisely because of *prajñā* that *dāna* is accomplished. Question:

If the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are treated separately, there should be six distinct individuals. Why, then, are they all attributed to *prajñā*? Answer: It is said that all of them abide in the practice of *prajñā*.
Sixth, it therefore belongs to Prajñā (Wisdom). Since the current text states that one "dwells in the practice of Prajñā," all preceding sections should likewise be understood as dwelling in Prajñā.

Because they dwell in the practice of Prajñā, there are nineteen types of persons in the section on Dhyāna (Meditation), and so on down to those who dwell in the practices of Śīla (Precepts) and Kṣānti (Patience);

thus, the various persons associated with Śīla and Kṣānti differ accordingly. Regarding the passage "no coming and no going," the second [section] explains that because of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), stinginess does not arise.
Because the mind has no coming or going, it is ultimately empty and does not give rise to a stingy mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattva attains the accomplishment of contemplation through the third eye, whereby he no longer perceives either giving or non-giving; although there are the two views of existence and non-existence, even up to Prajñāpāramitā, it is likewise so.
This is the internal benefit. Next, the explanation of not discriminating between disparagement and honor constitutes the external benefit. Above.
It clarifies that the Bodhisattva, seeing neither giving nor non-giving, transcends the two views of existence and non-existence and thereby attains internal benefit.
Now it clarifies that because external conditions come to destroy his mind, yet his mind remains unmoved, he attains further benefit.

Śāriputra, when a Bodhisattva attains such merit—as in the fourth section below, which distinguishes the fruit from that of the Two Vehicles—the distinction from the Two Vehicles is as follows: the Two Vehicles also... [text fragment] ...are also.
He is able to praise or disparage others without experiencing sorrow or joy—this is what is meant by the "arhat’s merit of being without sorrow or joy.
Fearing that [beings] might abandon him, as if they were his own beloved children, he again employs skillful means to deliver them; the Bodhisattva acts in this very way.

Thus, unlike those of the Two Vehicles who do not give rise to anger, he further generates compassionate skillful means; this is precisely how he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-land.
Since the substance [of the teaching] is thus, the text is likewise.
Regarding the second major section, which clarifies the formation of the two practices, this passage comes about to explain the nearness and distance [of the practice].
Within the ocean of Prajñāpāramitā, the words of countless Bodhisattvas could not be fully exhausted even if one were to speak for an eon.
A brief general demonstration of the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s universal practice: All Bodhisattvas must maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
having thus attained equanimity, they correctly contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*). This is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Because the principle of birth and death is equal, one attains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which is the attainment of the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*). When both the subject of contemplation and the object of contemplation are empty, this is the state where both mind and its objects are empty.
Because there is nothing upon which to rely, external conditions cannot destroy it. As for "the distant," it means that the two practices of merit and wisdom are perfected within all beings;
that is, the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni) are established as merit, whereby one brings sentient beings to maturity within the state of equality.
Furthermore, by generating a mind of equality toward all sentient beings, one realizes that all sentient beings are equal in relation to all phenomena.
"Birth and so forth" refers to the dharmas themselves.
The second major section below, which clarifies the merit of the fruition—beginning with "being protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present"—is as follows:
being remembered by the Buddhas and so forth is the fruit of merit; subsequently attaining the realization of unsurpassed Bodhi is the fruit of wisdom. This applies to all.
In truth, both are attained; indeed, both are attained. The former is the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*), while the latter is the fruit of cultivation (*niṣyandaphala*).

By practicing *prajñā*, one attains this dharma-fruit as the fruit of retribution; by cultivating the contemplation of *prajñā*, one attains the realization of the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment], and thus it is the fruit of cultivation.
Furthermore, the former refers to the fruit as taught by the Buddha when he preached *prajñā*; within that teaching, the latter indicates the actual attainment at that time.
Having realized the fruit, they were also remembered by the Buddha. Next, the "fruit-eye" never again perceives unwholesome forms; the subsequent fruit is precisely the "fruit of fulfilling wishes.
Regarding the three hundred bhikṣus at the time of the second stage of the fruit of practice, the assembly gained benefit in three ways:
first, the three hundred bhikṣus; next, the sixty thousand devaputras; and finally, the ten thousand people who had previously erred. One interpretation states there are twelve [categories].
The period when the precepts were first established and the *pārājika* rules were proclaimed was twelve years ago. A second interpretation states:
Suppose a bhikṣu has a "pure gift" (*śuddhadeya*) robe that is an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), and he intends to accept it as such.

Now, having set aside this extra robe, if he goes to another place and, knowing it belongs to him, develops the thought of accepting it back, will he necessarily incur the offense of "storing overnight"? [The answer is] no. Thirdly, this refers to a bhikṣu who has many acquaintances.
One can accomplish this immediately without waiting for a night to pass; thus one knows that there is no transgression of the four [grave offenses].

It is understood that this person cultivates the ultimate truth of non-arising (*anutpāda-paramārtha*) and that the establishment of precepts is a conventional expedient (*upāya*). Because they seek to realize non-arising and deliver sentient beings, even if they appear to slight the Buddha’s teachings, they do not transgress the precepts.
If one is lax regarding the precepts, it is not called "laxity" in this context; what is called "laxity" here refers only to minor precepts.

If it is broken, one should break it; if one acts with laxity, one should be lax accordingly, as stated in the Great Sūtra. Furthermore, there may be causes and conditions under which one is permitted to break the precepts. Question:
Among the three robes, if one discards one robe, this constitutes the perfection of *dāna* (generosity). Since one is now lacking a robe, should one not incur an offense against the precepts?
One interpretation states: The three [robes] are originally the Dharma of the Śrāvakas; now, having removed the Śrāvaka mind, one awakens to the Bodhisattva path.
The Way is that by which one discards the robes of the śrāvakas and ascends to Buddhahood.

It is called the "Great Sign" (mahānimitta) because it is named after the sign of attaining liberation manifested by raising an object with the hand; thus, attaining the signs of Buddhahood constitutes the Great Sign.

Because the sixty thousand devaputras and three hundred bhikṣus were spiritual friends from past lives, they spoke together. The Buddha prophesied that these bhikṣus would be born in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Because he longed to see the Buddha-lands of the ten directions due to his previous aspirations for those lands, and because he made a vow to be born there, a third person attained awakening.
Taking the present as the causal condition, it next clarifies the primary cause of error: because he saw the adornments of the Pure Land, he made a vow and practiced;
thus he is named the Buddha Adorned King (Zhuāngyánwáng Fó).
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Scroll Three (and Four) Compiled by Hu Jizang (Jiaozang) of the Northern Zhou Dynasty.
Chapter Five: Praising the Deliverance.
This concludes the section where the Buddha, in response to Śāriputra, briefly expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā* for those of superior faculties, and the assembly attained realization.

Now, in this third section, all the holy ones, having heard the teaching, rejoice and comprehend it; they praise and extol it, and by attesting to their attainment of Buddhahood, it is called "Praising the Deliverance."

It is not said that one praises *prajñā*, yet now one praises *prajñā*. Because each *pāramitā* penetrates the six [perfections], and because the text specifically praises the *pāramitā*, it says "converging with the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
While there may be *prajñā* where there is not necessarily *pāramitā*, that which is *pāramitā* must be *prajñā*. This is according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and...
□□□□□□□□ Pāramitā: It is now clarified that what the bodhisattva practices is necessarily a pāramitā.
In foreign lands it is called *pāragā*, which here is translated as "crossing to the other shore."

This chapter is divided into two parts: first, the praise; second, the description of the praise. The first part has two sections: first, clarifying that those who offer the praise are worthy persons;
second, clarifying the praise offered by these persons. Question: Why are the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and upāsakas listed here? Answer:

It is because the author now wishes to demonstrate that what the Buddha has spoken is the true Dharma by showing that the assembly of noble ones collectively praises it. Within this, there are three pairs; first, the exposition of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the two teachings of the Hīnayāna, among the five thousand [monks], there were over a thousand Sthaviras;
yet [the text] specifically cites four individuals to clarify that these four [exemplify] how one immediately attains present happiness for others.
Furthermore, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were preeminent in meditative concentration and wisdom, Subhūti practiced emptiness, and Mahākātyāyana possessed [great] conduct.
Furthermore, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were especially close to the Buddha’s countenance; they received his teachings and remained to uphold the Buddha-dharma after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Moreover, they shared seats with the Buddha when he bestowed robes upon them—these were individuals of virtue numbering over a thousand.
Those listed here among the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and lay followers are the persons who personally witnessed and verified this sūtra.
How is this known? A question in the *Śāstra* asks: "The Arhat has already accomplished what was to be done; for what reason is Prajñāpāramitā praised? The answer states:
"People know that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of an Arhat have been exhausted. Although the wisdom of a Bodhisattva is superior, his afflictions are not yet exhausted;
therefore, he reveres the Arhat, which is why [Prajñāpāramitā] is praised. Second, because this Arhat possesses a heart of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) and manifests transformative teachings."
Citing this as proof, it says: "Prajñāpāramitā is the true Dharma; it can give birth to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the requisites for happiness in the world.
Although the Buddha praised it all at once, that was not yet the ultimate, definitive teaching.
Therefore, now, with the second assembly of sages praising it together, it is established as the true Dharma of *kṣānti* (patience). Question: If that is so, why did he previously say...?
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who fill the ten directions, do not [possess] the wisdom that answers the *Sūrya-prajñā* (Sun-like Wisdom);
it is neither great nor small, neither great nor small in its skillful means, neither superior nor inferior, neither superior nor inferior in its spatial dimensions. Śāriputra is *prajñā*;
Śāriputra’s *prajñā* is neither great nor small, neither great nor small in its skillful means; Śāriputra is also neither great nor small, neither great nor small in his skillful means.

Since you are not [simply] "small" or "great," how could the skillful means of the small and great, or the superior and inferior skillful means, be said to be definitively inferior or definitively superior?
Therefore, while it was previously clarified that what is not inferior is used as if it were inferior, here it is clarified that what is proven to be non-superior is used as if it were superior.
Thus, one must not interpret the inferior as merely inferior; rather, it is understood as being superior.

Having addressed the Buddha, [the text] proceeds to the second section, "The Proper Praise," which is divided into two parts. First is the praise of the person; the Buddha explains this through both the meaning of the person and the meaning of the Dharma.
[Regarding the former,] one should explain *prajñā* by way of the Dharma-gate, while the rebirth [in Sukhāvatī] is explained by way of the person-gate.
Now, to receive and understand these two praises, there is the praise of the parable. Within the praise of the Dharma, it is further divided into two parts; first is the proper [explanation].
The praise of Prajñā-pāramitā concludes with two exhortations to practice; the explanation of Prajñā-pāramitā concludes with an exhortation to study.

Now, within this section on "Receiving and Understanding," there is likewise both a testimony to the praise of Prajñā-pāramitā and an exhortation to study. Regarding the two matters testified by the Buddha, Śāriputra enters to receive the bowl;

this is the weighing and praising of the efficacy of Prajñā-pāramitā, which exhorts study. From the opening of the primary teaching of Prajñā-pāramitā until the bowl is now returned, it serves as the "Receiving and Understanding."
Regarding these two, within the formal praise there are two parts: first, the praise of the merit of *prajñā*; second, the explanation of that praise.

Regarding the praise of the merit of *prajñā*, there are three sections: first, the praise from the perspective of both emptiness and existence; second, the praise from the perspective of existence and emptiness; third, the combined praise from the perspectives of both existence-emptiness and emptiness-existence.
Within the initial formal exposition, first is the gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which then contains the meaning of both existence and emptiness. Next...
In the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the meanings of emptiness and existence are clarified through the synthesis of the three;

because the two practices [of cessation and contemplation] correspond to the meaning, one returns to realize the aforementioned three gates. Thus, each and every point is identical in its response to the preceding discourse.

As for citing various Arhats who, being solitary and remote, separately offered distinct praises, these do not constitute authoritative proof. When comparing these perspectives, they are all fundamentally incompatible and cannot be reconciled.
Each and every characteristic reaches its fulfillment. [The following] eight phrases praise the Prajñāpāramitā for its merit in accomplishing the Great Task:
1. "Mahā" (Great): Because the Buddha-way is the greatest and the Prajñā can reach it, it is called "Great.
Because it is the foremost among all wisdoms, it is called "Venerable" (*vara*). Furthermore, because it is revered by the Buddhas of the ten directions, it is called "Venerable. It is correct.
Because it surpasses the five perfections, it is called "foremost. Because the five perfections cannot equal it, it is said to be "superior.

Just as the five sense faculties cannot equal the mental faculty (*manas*), which is able to benefit both oneself and others, it is therefore "sublime. Because it is the foremost of all things, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
Because there is no dharma that is its equal, it is called "unequaled. Since the unequaled Buddhas are born from Prajñā, it is called "unequaled."

[The preceding] is equal to... [omitted]. Praising the *prajñā* as ultimately pure and free from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of existence and non-existence, the void (*ākāśa*) is used as a metaphor. The following four [sections] praise [the *prajñā*] as being ultimately pure;
all conceptual proliferations cannot destroy it. The final four [sections on] emptiness clarify the *prajñā*.
Therefore, ultimate purity consists in illuminating the exhaustion of existence and non-existence to thoroughly penetrate the true mark (*dharmatā*).
By means of the four emptinesses, all emptinesses are subsumed: the myriad marks are the emptiness of self-characteristics; the original nature of all phenomena is the emptiness of intrinsic nature;

because the characteristic of emptiness itself is empty, the myriad dharmas are empty, which is the emptiness of all dharmas; and because this very emptiness is also empty, it is the emptiness of non-existence and existence. This is to be free from existence.
It is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Regarding all merits, the third section below combines the discussion of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence to praise *prajñā*.

Because it is ultimately free from both existence and non-existence, it clarifies that it reflects the true reality (*dharmatā*) and fully accomplishes the myriad phenomena (*dharma*), serving as the primordial source for all practices.
The first sentence praises *prajñā* as encompassing all practices in their entirety, like the rising sun; [it is] through *prajñā* that one can accomplish the multitude [of virtues].
If practice were not rooted in Prajñā, then all practices would not be accomplished;
because it is by means of Prajñā that all practices are perfected, it is said that Prajñā is the "root of all merits.
Regarding the phrase "indestructible," this is a praise of Prajñā, stating that no one in any world can destroy it. This is the second explanation of the praise.
Praising the efficacy [of practice]: because all Bodhisattvas are born from Prajñā, he praises Prajñā. Previously, it was clarified that Bodhisattvas practicing Prajñā obtain benefits;

this means that by virtue of their practice, the qualities of fruition are established. Next, he praises the Buddhas of the three periods of time, for it is due to Prajñā that the qualities of fruition are established through the cause of practice. Thus, the meaning of the text is clear. The "Incomparable Array" (Asamasama-vyūha).
"Revolutionary" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the mind of ignorance; because this giving is peerless, it is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
Furthermore, the Buddhas possess peerless conduct, and by performing this giving, one attains equality with the Buddhas. The subsequent visualization and practice are as stated in the text.
Following the World-Honored One’s second eulogy of persons—having praised the Arhats and now praising the Bodhisattvas—a thought arose [in the assembly]:
"Because the Path of Bodhi possesses wisdom, one knows how to pay homage to Bodhisattvas; that which is known in the three evil realms is [the domain] of the Bodhisattvas."
The Buddha told the assembly of disciples: "Because [the words] below are not false, the Buddha recounts the testimonies of the previous holy ones;
the Buddha speaks to cause the Buddha to seal the sayings of the holy ones. This recounting is for the most part the result of wholesome roots from past lives.

Above, there was praise for both person and dharma; now, however, we only recount the praise of the person. Since the meaning of the praise of the person above was brief, we now recount it with extensive praise.
Furthermore, previously there was praise for the existence of cause and effect by virtue of *prajñā*, whereas now there is praise for their mutual manifestation by virtue of the Bodhisattva.
First is the formal exposition; second, the two "Why is this so? sections provide the explanation for the praise. Regarding the explanation of the praise, there are two parts:

first, the explanation of why all mundane and supramundane fruits—both the primary and secondary (dependent and principal)—arise from *prajñā*; second, the explanation of how they arise because of the Bodhisattva himself.
Furthermore, because they cause sentient beings to practice various deeds, sentient beings obtain mundane and supramundane fruits;
one should know that these all exist because of the Bodhisattvas. Question: All worldly requisites for happiness arise from what? Answer: From the power and merit of giving. Answer:

They arise because the Bodhisattvas teach sentient beings three matters: first, giving; second, precepts; and third, the mind of goodness. When one practices these matters with a superior grade of conduct, the requisites for happiness are thereby obtained.
Those of middle capacity who practice these three things will naturally obtain wealth, honor, and the requisites of pleasure among human beings.
Those of inferior capacity who practice these three things must exert effort; such [attainment] belongs to Bodhisattvas. If it were not for the Bodhisattvas, it would be like hungry ghosts:
though they search everywhere for food, because they lack these three things, they seek in vain and find nothing. Even in a bright kalpa, they would not obtain it even by seeking.

Therefore, one should know that seeking [rewards] and thereby attaining [merit] constitutes the inferior grade of giving and morality. Question: If these exist by virtue of the Bodhisattva, why must sentient beings practice this giving and morality? Answer:
It is necessary for sentient beings to receive the Bodhisattva’s instruction before they can practice giving and morality;
otherwise, they would not understand how to practice them. Question: Sentient beings delight in giving and morality, yet they give rise to sinful karma; should the Bodhisattva not [intervene]?

Question: If a bodhisattva does not teach the practice of vows and does not attain goodness, they will not obtain happiness; if they do not obtain happiness, they cannot avoid giving rise to transgressions. Answer:
The original teaching states that goodness does not cause transgressions to arise. These transgressions arise from the sentient beings themselves.

It is like a person who digs a well but does not cause the traveler to fall into it; yet a blind person [falls in]. Thus, one must know that when pleasure arises, transgressions will inevitably follow.
For what reason does he cause [them] to arise? He answers well: even if there were no Bodhisattvas, they would likewise give rise to offenses...
[text missing]. ...Some explain that the Buddha spoke this *Prajñāpāramitā* in five chapters and a half to Śāriputra;
this chapter concludes what was previously taught, so that it may not be in vain for those who believe and accept it to emerge.
Regarding the mark of the tongue (*jihvā-vyañjana*): it is said now that this is not so; since the mark of the tongue was already manifested above, it should not be further verified here.

The commentary states: "This chapter concludes what preceded and gives rise to what follows. Concluding the preceding, it clarifies that what was spoken is not false; giving rise to what follows, it clarifies the further gathering of the assembly.
It cannot be [as previously stated]; since it was already clarified above, it should not be further verified here. Furthermore, the treatise (*śāstra*) does not [support this].
Now, in examining this, it is also the second [section] concerning its arising. Herein, the intention of the teaching is clarified:
because the profound and subtle nature of Prajñā cannot be fully elucidated all at once, what was previously explained in brief is now explained extensively.

Furthermore, since those of middling capacity had not yet attained realization within the preceding section, it is explained again; moreover, as there are differences in how realization is received, some attain realization upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching.
There are those who, having heard Śāriputra’s discourse, [observe that] what was previously taught for the assembly gathered before is now being taught for the assembly gathered later.

Although it was previously explained according to a single gate, it is now further divided into two sections. The first section consists of one chapter, which serves as the introduction to the exposition;
the second consists of twenty chapters, which correctly elucidate the exposition itself. Furthermore, the manifestation of the tongue-mark and the emission of light [are presented].

There are five reasons for this: first, to show that there is a mutual understanding between [the Buddha] and Subhūti; second, to demonstrate that Subhūti’s exposition of Prajñāpāramitā is not in vain;
third, because others might doubt the teaching—how could a Śrāvaka understand the Dharma of a Bodhisattva?

Fourth, because whereas previously the superior had taught the inferior, now it is a person of the Small Vehicle who speaks as a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages and so forth, and thus the matter is not to be treated lightly; fifth, for these reasons, he now extends his tongue.

The three signs—his physical appearance being exemplary, his speech being free from error, and his words never being false—are manifested for the sake of future generations so that they may manifest the *prajñāpāramitā* and cause Bodhisattvas to believe and accept it.
Fourth, the manifestation of the tongue-sign clarifies that this is the fruit of *prajñā*; desiring to obtain such a fruit, one must study the cause of *prajñā*.
From his heart he emits light and manifests transformations, whereby the devas and humans of the ten directions attain awakening.
O Śāriputra, you should know that the teaching of Prajñā has many gateways; both form and sound are, in truth, never truly form or sound. This chapter consists of five parts:
first, the manifestation of the tongue-mark and the emission of light; second, the gathering of the assembly; third, the reappearance of auspicious omens due to offerings;
fourth, the realization of the Way by the multitude; and fifth, the Buddha’s joy and bestowing of predictions upon them. The first is as explained in the text, which states:

Because the Prajñāpāramitā was not taught in a single assembly, the Buddha again manifested the mark of the tongue. There are two groups among the assembly: first, the gathering of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions;

second, the gathering of the celestial hosts. Regarding the gathering of the Bodhisattvas, there are five parts: 1) beholding the auspicious omen and raising questions; 2) the Buddhas of the ten directions providing explanations;
3) the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions intending to come; 4) the Buddhas of the ten directions granting permission; and 5) arriving with offerings. As it says:

The second section of the text is easily understood from its context. This third part, beginning with "These Bodhisattvas," explains that through the weight of their offerings, auspicious omens appear to symbolize that the causes of the myriad practices are identical for awakening.
Furthermore, this symbolizes that although the multitude differs, they all equally awaken to the single patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, within the assembly of Śākyamuni, the fourth part describes how the assembly awakens to the marks and radiance.
Upon awakening, one immediately sees the Buddhas of the ten directions and hears the Dharma they preach;

furthermore, one sees the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions coming, and subsequently, upon reappearing, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This is the fifth Buddha’s prediction (and so forth).

Just as one awakens to the Way by seeing flowers through their causes, they are all called "Accumulations of Flowers" (*Puṣpakūṭa*); because they awaken to enlightenment through flowers, they may be termed "Flower-Enlightenment."
Chapter Seven: The Three Kinds of Designation (Trijñapti).
From here below, twenty chapters correctly elucidate Subhūti’s exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā. Regarding this, the people of the North divide it into two parts:

the first chapter is the actual teaching; the second part, from the chapter on the beginner up to the chapter on Non-arising (*anutpāda*), consists of nineteen chapters that receive and propagate the teaching.
Regarding the three [sections]: first, the Buddha commands; second, the request to preach the Dharma; third, the Buddha reveals the discourse on the gate of existence (*yǒumén*).

This can be further divided into four parts: first, the discourse on the gate of existence through twelve chapters; second, the discourse on the gate of non-existence through the "Chapter on Non-Existence" (*wúpin*);
third, the conclusion of the first [section] through the "Chapter on Non-Arising" (*wúshēng*); and fourth, the [conclusion of the] gate of non-arising. Now, [I shall explain] this...

Regarding this same teaching, Master Chi Gong says it is divided into four parts: first, the exposition of right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*); second, the demonstration that his preaching can be spoken; third, [text missing];
and fourth, the realization and understanding of the assembly at that time. Now, this is also not the same as the intention of the *Chan* (Dhyāna) teachings.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on the Arising of the Tongue-Mark," clarifies the exposition of *prajñā*. If that is so, then from the perspective of the exposition of right livelihood, it constitutes a different assembly at a different time.
Now, the opening of the discourse on destiny is divided into three parts: first, the "Chapter on the Hidden Characteristics of the Tongue" explains the causal origination of destiny;
second, from the "Chapter on the Three Kinds of Falsity" onwards, it correctly explains destiny; third, the "Chapter on Śubhavyūha Receiving Destiny" explains the Prajñāpāramitā.

Because this accords with the Buddha’s mind above and adapts to the capacities of sentient beings below, without contradicting the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, the Tathāgata praises it, encourages those who doubt, and speaks in contrast to [wrong views].
At that time, those present attained the Way; this constitutes the sections of the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination.
However, since these are combined into a single gate, these specific names are not employed here.
Regarding the exposition on right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), there are three parts: first, the brief explanation of one aspect of livelihood as the life of a bodhisattva;

second, the request for the Buddha’s seal of approval; and third, the Buddha’s detailed narration of those words to fulfill that purpose. Following this, there is the extensive praise of livelihood, which consists of three sections:
first, the naming of the title; second, the doubt of the assembly at that time; and third, the resolution of that doubt to establish the meaning of the Buddha’s livelihood.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Three Fictions" (Sañjñā-prakaraṇa), there are five interpretations (*yùe*). [Omitted]. Now, in clarifying the three fictions, this is the opening of the fundamental tenet of Prajñāpāramitā.

While the characteristics [of phenomena] may be constant, it is only by clearly perceiving emptiness that one attains the Way and severs delusions; seeing existence does not achieve this. Now, if one perceives emptiness, one severs delusions, whereas perceiving existence does not sever them.
One should have titled this the "Chapter on Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-prakaraṇa); why then is it titled the "Chapter on the Three Fictions"? Since the fundamental tenet is now being expounded...
The three provisional [teachings] cause people to awaken to the Way and sever delusions. Why is it that one cannot see the existence of what severs delusions?

Is it that one severs delusions by seeing emptiness as empty, or does one sever delusions by seeing emptiness as not empty? If one severs delusions by seeing emptiness as empty, one does not now see the existence of this severing of delusions.
If one sees existence as existing, then since there is no severing [of delusions], how can there be a severing?
[Question: By what means are the afflictions severed? If none of them are severed, how is it that one attains the Way? [Answer: Because one perceives emptiness as truly existent.
Since the eighteen kinds of emptiness are for severing the afflictions, one attains the Way by severing ignorance. [Question: In your school, the seven categories transcend the four propositions;
are they not therefore non-existent? [Answer: Now we say they are even more non-existent, because non-existence itself transcends the four propositions.

Furthermore, your ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is without cause and effect, while conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) possesses cause and effect; this is certain. It is impossible for the present conventional truth to lack cause and effect.
[If you claim it does,] how can that which is truly existent be non-existent? That which is originally true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*) becomes a false emptiness (*tuccha-śūnyatā*). Why is this so?
Because one clarifies emptiness by means of existence, yet because that existence is itself false, it is a false emptiness; it is fundamentally a provisional construct.
Existence constitutes reality; why is this so? It is because there is this conventional existence (*prajñapti-sat*). Therefore, in relation to this, the two truths must necessarily exist.
Conventional existence is false, while true existence is empty. Because conventional existence is not [ultimately] existent, it is empty;

yet because it is not non-existent, it is truly empty. Because it is conventionally existent, it is empty; because it is not non-empty, emptiness is itself existence. Thus, it is both empty and existent.
One master said: "Emptiness is not emptiness; therefore, it is the emptiness of the non-empty color.

Because color is not color, it is the emptiness of the non-colored color. Now, regarding the three provisionalities (*tri-prajñapti*): because they are provisionally existent, provisionally non-existent, and not non-existent;

because one attains awakening through them; and because one cuts off afflictions and attains the Way through them—this first section clarifies the three provisionalities. Question: For what reason was Subhūti commanded to speak?
Answer: Previously, when [the Buddha] spoke of emptiness to Śāriputra, he already mentioned his immeasurable disciples;

because they were addressed in sequence, he did not summon others such as Maudgalyāyana to answer. There are two meanings: first, Subhūti practices the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) and possesses compassion, which clarifies that this is a Bodhisattva questioning matters concerning Bodhisattvas—this praises his possession of practice. Second, Prajñā is neither empty nor... [text fragment].
Amogha... Śubhākaragupta composes this "Explanation of the Name of Emptiness. Śubhākaragupta understands emptiness and is able to skillfully expound upon it;
this title may be understood as a praise for the aspiration regarding emptiness. Question: For what reason does the Buddha not explain this himself? Answer: There are also two reasons.

First, when sentient beings behold the physical marks of the Buddha’s body—such as the tongue of the King of Mount Sumeru which covers the great trichiliocosm—they stand in awe of the Buddha’s majestic power.

There are two reasons why those who are respectful do not dare to pose questions: first, because they are hesitant; second, because when they do pose a question, they are able to limit themselves by directing it to another person to explain.
Why, then, does he not direct a Bodhisattva to explain? The answer lies in six points: First, even the diminished qualities of a Bodhisattva are still vast.

Second, because their afflictions (*kleśa*) are not yet exhausted, their physical appearance and demeanor do not equal those of the Śrāvakas. Third, the three faculties, the conditions, and the analogies reside in Subhūti.
Fourth, it demonstrates that *prajñā* resides within the bodhisattva, thereby revealing the characteristic of doubt. Fifth, there are two types of *prajñā*:

the common and the uncommon; this present instance concerns the common *prajñā*. Because it cites the Small Vehicle, [it is said that] if a bodhisattva proclaims the Great Way, this is itself the constant essence and cannot be cited from the Small Mind to explain the Great. First, regarding the Small Mind:
Regarding those in the second assembly who harbored doubts, it was said that the Śrāvakas lack the capacity and thus should not preach the Dharma for Bodhisattvas;

furthermore, Prajñāpāramitā belongs neither to the Buddha nor to the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), but belongs solely to the Bodhisattvas, and is therefore the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.

Moreover, because the previous exhortation urged Bodhisattvas to study Prajñā, it is known that this is not the Dharma of the [Śrāvakas], and thus they should not preach it. This further clarifies the four propositions.

Because the methods of preaching the Dharma differ, there are four permutations: first, commanding a Bodhisattva to preach for a Bodhisattva, as in the *Avataṃsaka*, where it causes great beings to preach the Great Dharma;
second, commanding a Śrāvaka to preach such a sūtra as this, desiring to lead those of small capacity into the Great [Vehicle];
third, commanding a Śrāvaka to preach the Dharma for Śrāvakas, as exemplified by Śāriputra within this very sūtra.

It is said that the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaches the Dharma for the sake of the four types of livelihood, while the Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma for the sake of the Śrāvakas in order to lead them [to enlightenment], as in the case of Vimalakīrti.
Third, regarding the resolution of doubts: it is commonly said that those who transmit the lamp take one lamp and light a thousand lamps; this is the Buddha-lamp.
When Śubhūti understood that the Buddha was the lamp, those who dared to doubt him as being merely a disciple of the Buddha were answered thus:

it is clear that whatever Dharma all disciples of the Buddha preach, they do so by relying upon the Buddha’s power; how could it be through the power of a single person such as myself? Furthermore, he demonstrated the standard for preaching the Dharma:
all disciples of the Buddha, whether before the Buddha’s command, in the presence of the Buddha, or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [preach]... [not without the Buddha’s mandate].

Whatever is subsequently spoken is all the fruit of the Buddha’s power; yet one might fear that it is not the Buddha’s own command, for one asks before the Buddha and does not achieve the fruit of the Buddha’s power.
However, when the Buddha teaches the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the foremost among them is this:

the explanation that concludes the meaning of the Buddha’s power—that because all phenomena lack a foremost characteristic, they respond to the Buddha’s power. If the Buddha’s teaching were to conclude [otherwise], it would be as the Buddha himself [taught].
When one speaks of the characteristics of what the Buddha taught, my own speech likewise does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma.

Those who study this Dharma and attain realization offer supreme praise to the Buddha’s teaching as being non-contradictory to reality. The Buddha is like a person who transmits words exactly as they were received. As for those who have realized it:
although the Tathāgata possesses eyes, if there is no lamp, he cannot see the path; likewise, even if one possesses the eye of wisdom, if there is no lamp... [the text is incomplete].
Seeing the Right Path, he is able to preach it for the sake of Bodhisattvas. In the *Jingde-pin* (Chapter on Attaining the Teaching), the Buddha says:

"The Buddha's teaching is a lamp; because I have realized the Buddha's teaching, I understand it. Thus, the Buddha says it is like a lamp. All Śrāvakas who truly lack power constantly say that the previous explanation resolves their doubts.
This doubt of the Bodhisattva is not limited to one person; it is said that no one else is able to preach the Dharma for the sake of a Bodhisattva.
The Śrāvakas also lack the power to preach the Dharma.

At that time, the second section begins with "The Venerable Āyuṣmat" (*Āyuṣmān*), which is the formal reception of the command to speak; it sets forth what has been realized and requests the Buddha’s seal of approval.
All of this is spoken according to his own understanding. However, since Subhūti does not yet understand the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha now [proceeds].
If it is said that [Subhūti] does not understand, why not say that ordinary beings do not understand?
However, because the Buddha has awakened to prajñā and Subhūti has likewise awakened to prajñā—sharing the same awakening as the Buddha—it is said that he speaks as the Buddha speaks.

Since what Subhūti understands is precisely what the Buddha understands, it is stated that "all is by the power of the Buddha. When the Dharma constitutes a person, and the Dharma is itself the person, how could there be any difference?
Subhūti is able to set forth what the Buddha has spoken. Others say that Subhūti is certainly small and not great; however, this is not so.
Since Subhūti is one whose essence is Prajñā, and since Prajñā possesses neither smallness nor greatness, how could Subhūti be definitively small or great?

Therefore, when he is in a state of greatness, he can manifest greatness; when he is in a state of smallness, he can manifest smallness. [Question: When the Buddha commanded Subhūti to speak, it was because he ought to do so.
Question: Since you have been commanded to speak, why do you say that you do not see a bodhisattva? Answer: It is because I do not contradict the command.

The Buddha has commanded me to speak on the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of a bodhisattva; however, I do not know who this bodhisattva is, nor do I know what constitutes the "seeking" [of enlightenment].
Both subject and object are unobtainable. This is as in the "Chapter on Receiving the Alms Bowl," where the fundamental principle is questioned.
It is clear that one ultimately does not see the dharma practiced by a bodhisattva, nor does one see practicing or not practicing.
When such prajñā sees the Buddha, this is the practice of the dharma of prajñā; if there were a dharma to be practiced, it would reach the point of non-practice.
At that time, the assembly thought that the Buddha was commanding Subhūti to explain prajñā for the sake of the bodhisattvas, and so they said to Subhūti:
The noble Prajñāpāramitā is that which is able to speak; the Bodhisattva is that which is spoken of. Because of these causes and conditions, it is called "preaching the Dharma.
Thus, life is pure. Such various views are called Prajñā. One does not see a Bodhisattva... [as] a person who can speak.
Since there is no person who can speak, there is no teaching to be spoken. Regarding such a person who is able to speak...
To say that ultimately nothing can be apprehended is itself called the teaching of *prajñā*. If all views are primordially pure and now purified, is this not indeed *prajñā*?
The general purport of this chapter takes the breaking of practice as its core thesis; since it refutes "teaching," it takes non-teaching as primary.
Because the preceding section clarified the absence of practice, that was the practice of *prajñā*; because this section clarifies the absence of teaching, it is therefore...
This explains that regarding Prajñā, Subhūti, if there is no speech within non-speech, this is truly awakening to non-speech;

now, in order to cause awakening to non-speech, he speaks with words that are not real words. Since Subhūti has not yet explained it, [the Buddha] requests him to do so, and only then does he clarify it.
If Subhūti has not yet explained Prajñā, how could the Buddha have already [done so]?
"Is it life? [The text here is fragmentary. This is a refutation of the view that the Dharma is pure;
to hold such a view regarding the purity of the Dharma is to accept the teaching of life. To now clarify the refutation and cleansing of such views is to teach the Prajñāpāramitā.
All practices are the practice of Prajñāpāramitā; because they are the perfection of wisdom, they are called the "sacred silence" (āryatūṣṇīmbhāva) of the teaching of Prajñā.
Therefore, it is called the "Noble Teaching of the Dharma. If the mind has anything upon which it acts, that is acting in perversion;

if the mouth has anything that it speaks, that is speaking in perversion. How, then, could one speak of *prajñā*? Subhūti asked: "Why do you not simply accept my request and speak directly, rather than posing these three questions?
The Buddha replied: "Subhūti wishes to personally state what he has realized and requests the Buddha’s seal of approval; therefore, I have provided that seal."
The formation of these three propositions clarifies that Śrīgupta’s realization was like the Buddha’s own realization;

it was only when he spoke thus that the great assembly finally believed him, and his turning of the teaching was only then completed. Question: Since the doubts have already been resolved above, why is it now necessary to provide a seal of confirmation? Answer:

Because this involves the Śrāvakas transforming those below by means of those above, the matter is not trivial; therefore, it must be firmly confirmed once more. Thus, [it is explained] in the following "Chapter on the Gathering and Dispersion."
□□□ says: "I do not see a Bodhisattva. Buddhism speaks of *prajñā* (wisdom), yet it does not say there is a Bodhisattva to be taught or *prajñā* to be expounded.
It is the very life-force that causes one to understand this; therefore, it is called "life" (*myō*). There are three questions:

First, that there is no Bodhisattva in principle—this is the reality-mark (*shisō*) of emptiness. Second, that even when sought through contemplative wisdom (*kanchi*), [it is not found]. Furthermore...
Seeing that this light arises from the objective realm of emptiness, one contemplates the light of emptiness; since both locations are non-existent, how can a bodhisattva provide salvation?

Since this light is non-existent in both locations, there are no words to be uttered. Subhūti himself states three propositions: first, within the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the three types of *prajñā*, there is no bodhisattva;

second, within the *prajñā* of true mark, there is no bodhisattva; third, within the contemplation of [the *prajñā* of] observation, there is no bodhisattva. Thus, in the contemplation of [the *prajñā* of] observation, there is no bodhisattva.
Illuminating Prajñā.

Third, regarding the teaching spoken: since the aforementioned sutra initially sought the person and the dharmas within the Buddha and found them unobtainable, it opens its fundamental tenet by stating, "One does not see the word 'Bodhisattva' nor the nature of a Bodhisattva. [If this is so,] why should I instruct you regarding a Bodhisattva?

Next, [the text] explains by itself that [the self] cannot be found, and I do not know which teaching this refers to. When the Buddha answers the three questions, they constitute three primary points; the first question is divided into two parts.

First, the Buddha extensively describes the speaker and the spoken in order to contemplate the word "Bodhisattva. Second, he poses two counter-questions to Subhūti to confirm the capacity for speaking.
Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, a brief refutation of the three types of provisional existence (*prajñapti*) to clarify the Bodhisattva.

The second section, "The Contemplation of the Non-apprehensibility of the Bodhisattva’s Name," extensively refutes the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*) to clarify that the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, thereby instructing the bodhisattva in the initial practice.

This section further consists of three parts: first, an exposition by means of the Dharma; second, an exposition by means of an analogy; and third, a conclusion by means of the three provisional designations.

The first of these [the Dharma exposition] contains two sub-sections: first, refuting the three provisional designations by borrowing names; and second, refuting [them] by borrowing the three provisional designations.
The name is now the first [type of] conventional designation (*prajñapti*), namely the "Dharma-conventional"; next, the Bodhisattva is the "appropriation-conventional" (*upādāna-prajñapti*);
and the Prajñā is the "name-conventional. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva and the Prajñā possess only names; these are conventional designations.

Because they are called "appropriation-conventional," and because the name of the Dharma is also a conventional designation, one borrows a name [to refer to them]. Since they are merely conventional designations, they have no substantial existence whatsoever.
Regarding "internal, external, and intermediate," this refers to the second [category], which borrows the three provisional designations and further removes even these names.

Master Zhaolun said: "If names cannot be applied to things, then things cannot fulfill the function of names; if things cannot correspond to names, then names cannot be realized as real. Thus, when names cannot be applied to things and things cannot fulfill the function of names, there is no name;
when things cannot correspond to names and names cannot be realized as real, there is no thing. Being neither name nor thing, they are established like the collection of form (*rūpa*).
Because it is based on two dharmas, it is called "fire. Now, if the name "fire" were within those two dharmas, then when one calls for fire, the fire [itself] should burn one's mouth.
If the name "fire" were outside those two dharmas, then when one calls for fire, water should come forth.

Furthermore, if the name "fire" is outside the fire, and likewise [the name] "water" is outside the water, then since the fire comes from outside the fire, why does the water not also come from outside the water? Moreover, both are equally external.
It should follow that both do not come; furthermore, there is the difficulty of the fire not coming and being cast [away].
Because there is no place to rest the fire between the two phenomena, it does not abide in the middle.

For example, as in my second [section] below, where the phenomena and the metaphors are explained in combination, eight metaphors are raised and seven are combined; now, these eight metaphors serve as...
Sixth: First, the person and the dharma are raised as one pair; next, the internal and external are raised as one pair; third, the past and present are raised as one pair.

Regarding "the person and the dharma," the unconditioned is raised as a metaphor for the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*); since that stage lacks the three provisional [categories], it likewise lacks a simile.
Following this, in the second section on the body, the dharma is raised as a metaphor, stating: "Because I am the expansive dharma, there is no dharma that should not exist. Next...

This is the citation of the Dharma. Next, regarding the pair of "internal" and "external": the *Śāstra* states that there are two types of bodhisattvas—those who practice seated meditation and those who do not.

To explain this, the internal body is cited as a metaphor for the bodhisattva who practices seated meditation, while external objects are cited as metaphors for the bodhisattva who does not practice seated meditation.
This is because the Buddha’s intention is simply to cure the diseases of the body here and now; therein lies self-benefit.
To speak for others is to cause them to find peace within themselves and to enable them to attain their own benefit.

To say directly that [things] exist according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) while they do not exist according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—as the people of the North say—that they do not exist because of the true nature (*lakṣaṇa*) and that there is no worldly fruit (*phala*)—what answer does this provide regarding self and other?
For example, taking the past as a basis, the third point cites the past and present as metaphors: the Buddhas of the past have already passed away, yet...
Just as it is with the metaphor of the "name-only" [of emptiness] regarding faith, so too for all phenomena; one may successively cite ten metaphors for them.

Since the past is non-existent, it can be said to have the name of emptiness; however, the present exists and ought not to be non-existent. Therefore, the ten metaphors are cited to show that all which is seen and heard is like those ten metaphors.
Thus, Subhūti, the third section below, titled "Lifting up the Three Provisions to Exhort through Discussion," states: "To break the 'name' (nāma) provision is to reach the 'vow' (saṃketa) provision;

to break the 'vow' provision is to reach the 'perception' (upādāna) provision; to break the 'perception' provision is to reach the 'dharmas' provision, which is the true reality (dharmatā) of all dharmas.
As for the sequential breaking [of these], one enters into the true reality. Regarding the commentary on the three provisions, there are two [interpretations], the first of which says:
The five aggregates (*skandha*) are the provisional designation of dharmas; the person (*pudgala*) formed by the five aggregates is the provisional designation of a person.

First, regarding dharmas having names, these are the provisional designation of names. Second, it is like how a coarse form is produced from a multitude of subtle atoms; this is the provisional designation of dharmas. Furthermore, from coarse form, further dharmas emerge:

for instance, because of the conjunction of form and touch, there is the name "great"; because of the conjunction of form and mind, there is the name "person. This is the provisional designation of a person. Beyond the locus of these names, there is furthermore...

Names are like the roots and branches of a tree; when there is a name for the tree itself, and when bamboo and wood are combined, there is a further name for that combination—this is what is called "provisionality" (*prajñapti*).
Herein, three types of provisionality are cited to exhort those who study as Bodhisattvas; these are not merely the three provisionalities previously mentioned.
Now it is clarified that all arising phenomena are analogous to the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*; this is the "provisionality of dharmas. As for the sages of the Three Vehicles and the six... [text fragment].
Sentient beings are conventionally designated as such; these names and dharmas of persons are likewise conventional.
This is the third [point]: conventional dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas; conventional feeling is neither feeling nor non-feeling; conventional names are neither names nor non-names.
One should encourage Bodhisattvas to train in this manner. Now, in this sutra, the preceding section refutes names, stating: "This name is neither internal nor external..."
Because it is intermediate, one says that there is no name for it; however, some might then say: "If there were no name 'Bodhisattva,' how could a Bodhisattva manifest?

Since a Bodhisattva is actually perceived, the name 'Bodhisattva' cannot be non-existent. Thus, the notion of a nominal designation (*prajñapti*) is refuted by the existence of the underlying substance (*dravya*).
If the substance itself has no name, how can there be a designation? Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no Bodhisattva, how could there be the five aggregates (*skandha*) that constitute him?"
Furthermore, it breaks through the provisional existence of dharmas to reach the true mark (*dharmatā*), where there is no person, no dharma, no thing, and no name.
It is said that from the beginning, one has received this ultimate Dharma and received this ultimate name.

Furthermore, Subhūti, one does not perceive the name "form" as permanent. This is because, in the second [section], it is extensively explained that the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) are unobtainable;

thus, there is no bodhisattva. Above, this was briefly clarified by showing that the three provisional designations are unobtainable, and therefore there is no bodhisattva. The question asks: "What is this?
The extensive answer above should be sought by examining the three locations—internal, external, and intermediate—to find that the name "bodhisattva" is unobtainable.
Therefore, this was a brief observation; now, expanding upon it, one seeks names in all places and finds them unobtainable.

One cannot speak of permanence or impermanence, nor even of arising and ceasing, because since names do not exist, things likewise do not exist. The above briefly clarified that the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) are unobtainable, which refutes "existence" (*bhāva*) alone;
here, by extensively clarifying that the three provisional designations are unobtainable, both [existence and non-existence] are shown to be transcended.

Because one is free from illness, it is said that one does not perceive permanence or impermanence, self or non-self; this is the practice of the Middle Way. Above, the refutation of illness was brief and incomplete, and thus the fruit was not attained;
now, because the refutation of illness is comprehensive and complete, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva attains the fruit.

Previously, the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) were discussed horizontally as being unobtainable; now, they are discussed vertically as being unobtainable. Question: Since the three provisional designations have already been refuted...

One should say that it is conventionally designated and unapprehendable. Why, then, does he speak of a "bodhisattva"? He answers by saying that because Subhūti does not perceive a bodhisattva, there is nothing to be taught.
The Buddha now directly answers this question by stating that there is no bodhisattva; in reality, this is the non-existence of all dharmas.
It is also the illumination of the non-existence of all unconditioned phenomena, clarifying that there is no bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva serves to clarify that non-existence.
All dharmas. Question:
For what reason was all naming refuted previously? Answer: Now, in order to turn the teaching to the great assembly, it is said that there is a teaching to be turned;
therefore, it is now clarified that names cannot be found when sought in any place—how then could there be a teaching to be turned? Thus it is known.

Such non-instruction is precisely the instruction for Bodhisattvas; regarding this, there are five points: first, causing the Bodhisattva to practice non-conceptual contemplation to destroy the name "Bodhisattva";

second, causing them to practice contemplation of the true mark to attain the wisdom of the true mark; third, the contemplation of non-reliance and non-attachment; fourth, the fruit of performing these contemplations;
and fifth, the concluding exhortation for Bodhisattvas to train. Of these, the first three [subdivisions] are: first, the actual attainment.
Because of non-conceptual contemplation, one does not differentiate whether names are permanent or impermanent. As for the passage beginning "For what reason," this is the second explanation:
that although conditioned nature (*saṃskṛtatva*) exists, it is not perceived; this is because the broad is subsumed within the concise, and thus permanence is not perceived.

Regarding why permanence is not perceived: it means that within the conditioned, one does not perceive the permanence or impermanence of names, and within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not perceive names.
Regarding the characters for "permanence" and "impermanence," one should not perceive them as being within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); how could one perceive the permanence of names therein?
When a Bodhisattva practices Prajñāpāramitā, they do not engage in such conceptual discrimination. This concludes the third section, which establishes non-discriminative contemplation.

Do not entertain the notion that there is discrimination in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and non-discrimination in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Furthermore, do not entertain the notion that there is discrimination in the practice based on conditions (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*) according to the *Dilun* school.
True cultivation is non-discrimination; do not now act like a person from the North. True reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is non-discrimination, while within the false there is discrimination.
Now it is correctly said that when a bodhisattva seeks all forms of discrimination, they are unobtainable.

Since discrimination has always consisted of the distinctions between the permanent and the impermanent, one now seeks this view of discrimination and finds non-discrimination. This is the dwelling of the bodhisattva.

In the section on the "Non-Destructible Dharma," the second part clarifies the practice of the contemplation of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Because it is that which is conceptualized by the Bodhisattva, it is the contemplation of reality.
If there is any conceptualization—namely, discrimination—it is false and delusive, and thus a contemplation of unreality.

This also has three parts: first, the practice of the contemplation of the true mark; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding "abiding in the non-destructible dharma": if one discriminates between permanence and impermanence...

Thus, it is neither permanent nor impermanent, yet it also functions as both permanent and impermanent; is this not the subversion of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by abiding in the contemplation of reality?
Within this cultivation of all things, one does not perceive a subject who cultivates, nor does one perceive the name of the object being cultivated—the essence of the contemplation itself.

Next, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is raised for explanation; finally, the provisional names of contemplative wisdom are concluded as in the text. One should know that these names are merely provisional.
The third section below concerns the contemplation of non-attachment (*asaṅga*). Because the contemplation of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) has been perfected, the mind is without attachment.
That which the mind does not attach to is not because it is [some fixed] thing; rather, it is because one correctly seeks all phenomena and finds them unobtainable that there is no attachment.
If something could be obtained through seeking, only then could it be called "attachment. Not only is there no attachment to all phenomena, but furthermore—
Because one does not grasp at the observation that all phenomena are unattainable, one is not attached to any phenomena;
thus, one understands purity and is also not attached to the observation of purity. Because it is ultimately pure, one does not know how it could be forcibly named "right observation.
This also has three parts: first, clarifying non-attachment; second, explaining the conclusion; third, observing as the text describes. Such practice increases the result.
The sixth *pāramitā*, Part Four: Attaining the Fruit, as in the text. Above, the brief explanation and this detailed exposition constitute the practice of causes;
this section begins with the attainment of the fruit. Above, the practice of causes was clarified as being without obtainment (*anupalambha*);

now, the state of non-obtainment is clarified. A Bodhisattva should know it thus: "Names are merely provisional designations. Below, Part Five: Concluding the Contemplation. It is necessary... [text ends].
