Chapter Thirteen: The Vajra Section; also titled the Mahāsattva Section, or alternatively the Mahāsattva Section.

From here below, the second part consists of four sections explaining the meaning of *mahāsattva*. According to the persons for whom this treatise is intended, there are four types who explain the *mahāsattva*;
that is, the four foremost [beings]. Because the Buddha is the head of those whose destiny is certain (*niyata*), he is the *mahā* (great).
The second, Śāriputra, is a mahāsattva because he has severed the view of nihilism;
the third, Subhūti, is a mahāsattva because his bodhicitta is peerless and not shared with the two vehicles;
the fourth, Pūrṇa, is a mahāsattva because he is adorned with great vows and sets out upon the Great Vehicle, riding in the Great Vehicle. If categorized by chapter, there should be four chapters.
The combinations and separations differ: first, one person constitutes one category; next, two people together constitute one category; next, one person constitutes two categories.
Furthermore, the first case is neither separated nor combined; the next is combined but not separated; the next is separated but not combined.
The Buddha himself taught one category because it is not the case that two people share one category; thus, being neither combined nor separated, they are established as two categories.
Therefore, they are not separate. Next, because the two individuals, Śāriputra and Subhūti, share one chapter together, this is a combination and thus not separate.
Next, because it is spoken by a single person, it is not a combination but a separation; since there are two people, it is said that they are separate and not combined.
If we follow the underlying meaning and divide them into three parts: first, praising his great resolve and profound wisdom as a Mahāsattva.
Second, praising his being without fault and not departing [from the path] as a mahāsattva; third, praising his being without objects and not practicing [them] as a mahāsattva.
First, eight aspects of mind explain the term mahāsattva; from the first mind being firm, it is named "vajra."
Regarding the second part, there are two questions and two answers. Since the Bodhisattva was questioned above, he is now questioned as "Mahā-mahā.

*Mahā* is what is called in foreign lands; it means "Great" (*sa*). Alternatively, it is named the "Sentient Being" (*sattva*). Among all sentient beings of the ten directions and the three periods of time, this sentient being is the greatest.
Furthermore, because this mind is that which delivers all and knows all phenomena, it is called the "Great Mind."
This also explains the "superior mind" and "wondrous mind" of ordinary beings and superior beings, respectively.

In the Buddha’s answer, this first section establishes the ultimate, with the "multitude" (sattva) as the primary subject; thus, they are "Mahāsattvas. Second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Within the headings, there is a dual establishment:
namely, that which surpasses the two [lower] categories and the two individuals who can surpass them. The explanation and the conclusion are likewise so. [Thus it was said to] the Buddha.
The following commentary is divided into two parts: first the question, and then the answer. Within the answer, there are three sections: first, the nine classes of beings through whom one passes;

second, the explanation of the "one who passes" (the Bodhisattva) who transcends the eight stages and reaches the ultimate end; and third, regarding sentient beings, [it explains that] those of the *mithyātva-niyata-rāśi* (wrongly fixed group) will inevitably enter the three evil destinies;

those of the *samyaktva-niyata-rāśi* (rightly fixed group) will inevitably attain *nirvāṇa*; and those of the *aniyata-rāśi* (unfixed group) also desire to take up this Bodhisattva path among the sentient beings of the rightly fixed group.
Furthermore, for those at the head [of this stage], he explains the remaining three aggregates; this Bodhisattva is thus the "Lord of the Path" (*mārgādhipati*). The *Śāstra* states:

"The person of the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*) is one who grows within the noble lineage (*āryagotra*) during the four roots of goodness. Regarding the numerical school (*Saṃkhyā-vādin*), they hold that falling back from "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) or "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) does not necessarily mean one has left the stage;

because these four roots of goodness do not involve falling back, they are termed "ultimately fixed" (*atyanta-niyata*). The numerical school further asserts that only "Patience" (*kṣānti*) is [ultimately fixed].

Regarding the statement that "those who retreat from the preceding stages all retreat," what is the intent behind saying that the *gotrabhūmi* (stage of the lineage) is identical to the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*)?

If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the chapter on non-retrogression (*aparihāṇi*) regarding the first four roots of goodness explains that there are those who retreat from the mind, those who retreat from the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), and those who retreat from the person;

however, this does not necessarily mean they are subject to retrogression. Since the treatise speaks of "non-retrogression" because there are those with sharp faculties who do not retreat, it is so stated.

The four fruits [of the path] consist of fifteen moments of mind. Because patience (*kṣānti*) is of the greatest efficacy, it is used extensively within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereas wisdom (*jñāna*) is used within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

thus, [the defilements] are severed by patience, and subsequently realized by wisdom. Regarding the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), the *Śāstra* explains that there are three types of distinctions, as they are fully cultivated:
first, the arousal of the thought through cultivation; second, the arousal of the thought named "attaining the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*); and third, as described here.

Regarding the statement that "one attains Buddhahood by generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*) within the Dharma," the "generating of the resolve" here must refer to the initial generation of the resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*), because there is also the "Non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*) as superior;
it simply takes the non-retrogressive initial resolve. Within this state, the mind is indestructible like a diamond (*vajra*).
Second, the clarification of "being able to transcend" explains the "foremost" [of the bodhisattvas]. Eight types of resolve are cited: first, the diamond resolve (*vajra-citta*); second...
1. The mind of great joy; 2. The unshakable mind; 3. The mind that seeks benefit and happiness; 4. The mind that delights in the Dharma, desires the Dharma, and rejoices in the Dharma;

5. The mind of the eighty emptinesses; 6. The mind that abides in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); 7. The mind that abides in the three samādhis. The first section [of this chapter] has three parts:

1. A general heading; 2. Questions; 3. Answers. Within the answers, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the ten minds to clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s practice for self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

Next, the transformation of others (*parārtha*) is explained through the first ten mental states, which are divided into two parts: the first five mental states are those of transforming others, and the subsequent five are those of one's own practice (*svārtha*).

In the first mental state, one does not calculate the duration of kalpas, but vows to deliver sentient beings. In the second, one does not abide in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), desiring to relinquish both internal and external benefits for the sake of benefiting others.

In the third, there are the contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth; these four combined [constitute the section on transforming others]. Although in the aforementioned [second state] one has practiced giving both internally and externally, one has not yet attained liberation.
Because of old age, sickness, and death, one next attains liberation through the Three Vehicles. Previously, one was granted worldly happiness;
now, one is granted the supramundane wealth of the present Dharma. Regarding the fifth mind, although seven practices are performed, in reality there is nothing to be delivered.

As for the first of the subsequent five minds, it speaks of the "mark of non-arising" because, by realizing non-arising, one knows that there is no deliverance to be effected, even while knowing non-arising.

Fearing that [others] might not understand, and because even those of the Two Vehicles possess some degree of knowledge, it is said that one should practice the six perfections with a mind of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Those of the Two Vehicles should know non-arising (*anutpāda*), yet they are unable to practice the six perfections through non-arising; for practicing the six perfections is itself non-arising.

This is because one fully understands the reasons for performing actions pertaining to both the mundane and supramundane realms. Thus, although one practices the six perfections, one does so by means of full knowledge. Furthermore, [one practices] by means of full knowledge.
Regarding the mundane and supramundane: ninth, knowing one characteristic through desire; tenth, the gate of knowing all characteristics through one. All gates are non-dual.

Next, there is a partial clarification of the practice for transforming others: there are bodhisattvas who, although maintaining equal mindfulness toward the six realms of existence, encounter those who have fallen into the three [evil] destinies;
because this situation is urgent and pressing, they may strike them and further transform their minds without regret. This mind is both vast and long-lasting. Second.

Although the nature of the mind and so forth are firm and stable, they have not yet reached definitive certainty, just as a bird, despite possessing great strength, is not necessarily able to rend [its prey].
To cite the Buddha’s explanation of the "Great Swift Mind": first, the unstained mind; for although the Buddha has attained equality toward all sentient beings, he does not harbor partial affection.
Second, the non-angry mind; because he has attained a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, he does not become angry.

Third, because one understands that causes and conditions are merely provisional designations, the mind does not grow weary. Fourth, because one regards all sentient beings as one's own infant, one does not give rise to the diamond-like [hardness] of aversion.
Fifth, one does not give rise to the mind of the two vehicles, meaning one does not abandon sentient beings but honors the noble path of the Buddha.

Next, regarding the immovability of the mind: previously, it was explained that the mind is unmoved by external adverse conditions; now, it is explained that internal cultivation of wisdom cannot [disturb it].

Furthermore, although one may have previously fallen [from the path], it is not necessarily the case that there is no movement, just as when pulling something out, there is still movement even if it does not emerge.
Next, the five kinds of the mind of benefit and peace are explained: first, regarding benefiting through the Mahāyāna, it is said to cause them to attain peace and happiness;

second, for those incapable of the Mahāyāna, one bestows the Three Vehicles; third, for those incapable of the Three Vehicles, one bestows the human and celestial vehicles; fourth, for those incapable... [text ends].
The phrase "gods and humans manifesting joy" means relying upon oneself and others. Fifth, regarding "being unable to experience joy," one benefits them with a mind of compassion.

Next, explaining the "mind that delights in the Dharma": only great beings (mahātman) can delight in the Great Dharma. Ordinary people and those of the two vehicles cannot endure delighting in this Great Dharma;
because they delight in the Great Dharma, they are called "great beings. Next, they abide in the eighteen kinds of emptiness.

Because he is empty of the ten views, he is called a "Great Man. The *Śāstra* says: "By abiding in the eighteen kinds of emptiness, one does not fall into the eighteen dharmas and thus does not give rise to sinful karma.
Next, the explanation of "abiding in the mind of the myriad practices" states: "By abiding in the myriad practices, afflictions are extinguished and one attains the cultivation of roots of goodness.
The eighth [section], the "Eight Hundred and Eight Samādhis," states: "The Buddha, having attained the bliss of samādhi, becomes weary of the world and increases the three types of wisdom."
The third and final section is as in the text. Chapter Fourteen:
The Chapter on Eloquence (*Pratibhāna-varga*). It is also titled "The Chapter on Severing Doubt" (*Vicikitsā-prahāṇa-varga*) and "The Chapter on Pūrṇa.

Regarding this chapter in the *Lun jing* (Treatise Sūtra), later generations anticipated the subsequent meaning; since there is a separate chapter concerning what Pūrṇa spoke, this [chapter] is presented in contrast to that.

In this chapter, both individuals are designated as "Delighters in Eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) because they both possess this quality; thus, the chapter is titled the "Chapter on Delight in Eloquence. This chapter subsequently divides into two sections:
the first person is established as a *mahāsattva* by being free from the three views, while the second clarifies that one becomes a *mahāsattva* through the severance of the three views.

Regarding the formal analysis of these sections, both are faultless in their respective ways; however, because [the second] does not depart from [the first], it constitutes the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*). This is why it is so named.

The "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa) is so called because they transcend all signs (*nimitta*) through the Great Exceeding (*mahā-viparyāsa*). This "Great Exceeding" refers to the path of transcending all cravings and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*);
thus it is called "Great. Because they can [endure] great suffering, it is called "Great"; because they sever [all bonds], it is called "Great.

Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha*) are not "Great Persons" and cannot sever this; only the Great Person can sever it. Within the transcendence of these faults, there are two parts. First:
The first person is called "Great" because he has severed all views; the second person is called a "Great Man" (mahāpuruṣa) because he has severed all cravings.
Furthermore, the first is "Great" because he has severed coarse afflictions (*kleśa*), while the second is "Great" because he has severed subtle defilements.

This sequence of first [severing the coarse] and then [the subtle] is the standard procedure for transforming sentient beings. Second, there is a person who had a karmic connection with Śāriputra from a previous life; regarding this, it is said:

Because he is a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa), he is thus able to attain faith and awakening. Third, regarding the desire to assist sentient beings: the Bodhisattva finds great joy in the arising of even a small *kalpa*.

As for the Buddha’s permission, it is because there is no gate of "self" (*ātman*); having severed this craving, Śāriputra knew that his teaching would benefit sentient beings, and thus the Buddha permitted him to speak.
Within the formal exposition, three views are clarified: beginning with the view of self and ending with the view of the Buddha, which constitute the instruction for others.
To perceive the marks of form and to perceive the teaching of the Dharma constitutes mundane and supramundane views.

To sever [the notions of] permanence and annihilation, or existence and non-existence, is right view. Because it pertains to the past, it is considered wrong view. However, this is truly difficult to sever.

To resolve to seek Buddhahood—where there is a Buddha to be sought—and to seek the severance of the view of existence and the view of non-existence; likewise, to think there are sentient beings who can be saved or cannot be saved—is what others call [wrong view].

From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it exists; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it does not exist. Possessing these two views, the Prajñā of the true and the conventional are inseparable:

the true is itself the conventional, and the conventional is itself the true. While this is the view, it is distinguished according to the division of the true and the conventional. This is the meaning:

seeing that the true and the conventional cannot be different, yet cannot be identical, one avoids the views of difference and identity. Thus, all that exists below [this realization] is characterized by attainment and externality.
Seeing that those who now wish to study Prajñāpāramitā are great beings, from the very first moment they resolve their minds, they have stilled such views as these.

There is never a distinction between the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti), nor is there a lack of distinction between them; yet, for the sake of provisionally teaching and transforming sentient beings, the ultimate and the conventional are established.

Thus, one opens up the practice of the ultimate and the conventional. While sentient beings speak of the two characteristics of the ultimate and the conventional—such as "form is emptiness" and so forth—this [teaching] binds together both their identity and their non-identity.

"Duality and non-duality are both means by which the Buddhas transform sentient beings; how could one claim that there are two truths, fall into such a view, and further produce interpretations of identity or difference?
Question: "If one wishes to sever this view of dharmas, is it because this view exists that it can be severed? Or is it because it does not exist that it can be severed?
If it does not exist, what is there to sever? If it does exist, how can it be severed? If one perceives existence, that perception itself is a [false] view. Answer: "Non-existence has never existed."
There are those who directly take emptiness as a sentient being; because they perceive this emptiness through the view of emptiness, there is nothing whatsoever to be found.

Therefore, it is merely a provisional designation that "it is exhausted"—what, then, is there to be exhausted? The subsequent meanings and the concluding passages are easy to understand. Next, Subhūti’s discourse on the Great Man also has five parts:
first, the request to speak; second, the promise to speak; third, the actual exposition; fourth, the two persons’ adjudication of the meaning of the doctrine; and fifth, the conclusion.
In this correct exposition, first three minds are indicated, followed by an explanation of the three fetters. Regarding the three minds: first, the arousal of the bodhicitta;
second, the desire to praise this mind as being equal to that of a Buddha, as the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The bodhicitta is itself the Buddha-mind";

third, the clear distinction that this mind of a Buddha is not shared with the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), whereas the two vehicles possess only the attainment of self-deliverance, while the Bodhisattva delivers others.
The mind that has no attainment saves both oneself and others. Why? This is the second explanation below: the three minds are all called the single mind of wisdom (*jñāna-citta*).

Because these three minds are not different from the Buddha-mind, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says, "The initial aspiration for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*) is itself the Buddha," and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states, "The initial aspiration and the ultimate [realization] are not two and do not differ. This is because there is no past [to be attained].

Being untainted (*anāsrava*) and having no basis (*anāśraya*), its attainment (*prāpti*) constitutes non-attachment; this is the praise and explanation of this mind. This mind is the attainment of non-basis, which is also omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and is unattached.
Previously, the three minds were praised as being the attainment of non-basis; now it is clarified that this attainment of non-basis is also unattached.
Previously, the three minds were explained as being unattached to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); subsequently, it is explained that [this mind] is also unattached.
These three minds are concluded here for these reasons. In the fifteenth chapter, "On Eloquence" (*Pratibhāna*), all three meanings are fully explained;
it is named after the capacity to speak. Regarding the three parts of this chapter: first, the request to speak; second, the granting of permission to speak; third, [the actual speaking].
Regarding the correct exposition, within the correct exposition there are two parts: first, the brief exposition; second, the extensive exposition. Question:
Do these two meanings possess a hierarchy of depth and shallowness, or not? Answer: They possess both meanings.

To say that there is no hierarchy of depth and shallowness is like a person who must have a weapon to break a vessel, or a person traveling a long distance who must have provisions. When a Bodhisattva breaks the four māras themselves, they also cause [others to do so].
Because sentient beings must shatter the four māras, they require the adornment of the myriad practices; this is the "subsequent adornment.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva seeks the Buddha-way and also causes sentient beings to seek the Way, they likewise require the adornment of the myriad practices; this is the "subsequent adornment" of sentient beings.
Although one thus adorns oneself, even with the designation of the Three Vehicles, one desires to approach the Buddha-way; yet the Buddha-way cannot be attained instantaneously.
The successive stages are called "setting out" (*prasthāna*) because they derive their name from the act of setting out.

Since there is necessarily a person who sets out and a dharma that is the vehicle for setting out—just as there is a person who rides a horse or a boat—there is the "Chapter on the Vehicle and the One Who Rides. A similar question is asked here; how does this differ from the previous one? Answer:

Here, we take the ten thousand practices (*sādhana*) from within Prajñāpāramitā. These ten thousand practices are precisely what constitutes the adornment; it is not Prajñā itself [that is the adornment].
The myriad practices cannot adorn [the path] because they involve the removal of something attained; therefore, the subsequent text states that there is no "Great Adornment.
Only when there is neither coming nor going is there true setting forth. Because one sets forth without grasping, and moves while remaining unmoved, there is the vehicle (yāna).
Thus, a single thought-moment possesses these three meanings; therefore, the present text brings together and takes up the Prajñāpāramitā.
This Mahāsattva, by taking up the Prajñā at the lower assembly, is truly a Mahāsattva; therefore, it is called "ornamentation" (*vyūha*).

Regarding "ornamentation," it refers to the absence of stages (*bhūmi*), yet there are stages as explained in the treatise: practicing the two kinds of emptiness—of beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) and of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—while not yet having attained [realization] is "great ornamentation";

attaining the emptiness of beings but not yet attaining the emptiness of phenomena is "setting out" (*prasthāna*); and attaining both the emptiness of beings and of phenomena is [the stage of] "departure" (*niryāṇa*).
Practicing the giving of the two emptinesses is the vehicle of vehicles. There are always three interpretations, as explained in the separate commentary.
Regarding the third section, the extensive explanation of the three meanings following Śāriputra’s question: first is the question, followed by the answer. The question states:
"If Bodhisattvas cultivate merit and wisdom as their provisions and destroy afflictions to become great beings, what of the Two Vehicles? The answer follows.
This Dharma should be called "The Great Man. In the response, there are two parts: first, explaining how the Bodhisattva attains the name of "Great Adornment";
second, explaining how they are praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions. Within the first part, there are three points of meaning in the answer:

first, it explains that because the Bodhisattva’s mind remedies arrogance and delivers sentient beings, he possesses great adornment and is thus named a "Great Man. Since the followers of the Two Vehicles lack this, they are not so named.
First, the Bodhisattva is called a "Great Person" (Mahāpuruṣa) because he himself possesses the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and causes sentient beings to likewise possess them;

the followers of the Two Vehicles lack this and are therefore not called Great Persons. Second, the Bodhisattva is called a Great Person because within a single practice he fully encompasses all practices;
the followers of the Two Vehicles lack this and are therefore not called Great Persons. The remaining two passages concerning the six perfections are easy to understand.

Regarding mutual inclusion, its function consists in the harmony of causes and conditions; it is like breaking a great army or besieging a city, where extensive conditions must necessarily exert combined force.
Second, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva practices unimpeded conduct because *prajñāpāramitā* is an unimpeded dharma;

thus, within a single practice, all six practices are complete. The practitioners of the Two Vehicles engage in obstructed conduct, possessing only a single practice. Why is this? When sentient beings hear...
The six [perfections] are not six; they are one. One hearing is one non-recognition; one is six. Therefore, it is clarified that one is six and six is one.
Although Prajñāpāramitā is generally one, it possesses the ten thousand practices; although there are these ten thousand practices, they are but one Prajñāpāramitā.
Within this, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) subsumes the other five perfections below it. All five are subsumed by giving because giving has superior, middling, and inferior degrees.

This is because from the lower [generosity] one gives rise to the middle, and from the middle one gives rise to the superior, up to the point where the arising of wealth is identical to the Dharma. The same should apply to the other five perfections;

however, since generosity (*dāna*) is at the beginning, it is said that this is the self-inclusion of its own stage. For example, as the Sāṃkhyas hold that the eye includes the eye, so too should generosity clarify the meaning of generosity itself.
Thus, generosity does not function as a mutual inclusion characterized by subject and object; nevertheless, the mutual inclusion of the six perfections is indeed possible.
There are five meanings of "mutual inclusion": first, mutual inclusion by way of stages, such as when the practice of *dāna* (generosity) and so forth on the first stage is included;

second, mutual inclusion by way of the characteristics of the practice, where it is simply called *dāna* or *kṣānti*, yet not called *dāna-śīla* and so forth—the same applies here; third, mutual inclusion by way of a single essence, such as when a single essence of *dāna* is endowed with the meaning of the six *pāramitās*;

fourth, inclusion by way of non-inclusion of dharmas, which refers to the essence itself; and fifth, inclusion by way of cessation, such as grasping the fault of stinginess alone and naming it *śīla*, while excluding the rest.

Second, regarding the four [aspects]: first, mutual inclusion through a single mind, which means that within a single kṣaṇa, essence and function are simultaneously complete, such as a single mind possessing the ten thousand practices;
fifth, mutual production and mutual inclusion, meaning that they arise through mutual causality, with preceding and succeeding moments producing one another.
Next, to explain the meaning of "arousing" (*utpāda*): first there is the question, followed by the answer, which establishes that a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) possesses three meanings.

It further takes up the aforementioned adornment of the ten thousand practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*), wherein the subject and object differ. When those of the Two Vehicles aspire toward the Great Vehicle, it is called "setting out for the Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna-samprasthita*).

This person is able to practice the ten thousand practices, and these are what is practiced; therefore, it is called "riding upon the Great Vehicle. However, we shall now further discuss this from the perspective of a different meaning.

Regarding "setting out" (*prasthāna*): although it was previously explained that all attain it through manifestation, here, with respect to depth and shallowness, because one further sets out toward the Mahāyāna, it is explained again by means of a different sense. According to the text, there are four meanings:
first, the five phrases of the Mahāyāna setting out are subsumed within dhyāna; second, the five are subsumed within the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) within dhyāna.

Attaining the threefold setting forth consists of: first, practicing the ten thousand practices with the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as the setting forth; second, taking the correct wisdom of the Middle Way as the setting forth. Regarding the first two, the first clarifies the dedication toward the Buddha-way as the setting forth. Regarding the four [perfections] shared with sentient beings—namely, dhyāna and the four immeasurables—to dedicate these toward the Buddha-way is called "setting forth" (*prasthāna*). Question:
Among the six perfections, why are they not explained starting from the beginning and ending at the end, but rather starting with dhyāna as the point of setting forth?

Answer: Within dhyāna, ethical discipline (*śīla*) arises from generosity (*dāna*), for it is essential for gathering in sentient beings; or, because wisdom (*prajñā*) is the root of all practices, ethical discipline emerges from it. Thus, dhyāna is established as the starting point.
Because this is the practice of the Bodhisattvas of the household, their precepts and diligence universally stimulate all deeds. However, there are currently two meanings:

first, although one has initiated the Mahāyāna with the intention of heading toward the Buddha-way, there may be obstacles and hindrances; therefore, it is now clarified that within *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) one generates loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

When the concentration of loving-kindness is established, its great power is such that even water or poison cannot cause fear. Second, within *dhyāna*, one develops the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to transform sentient beings.

In essence, one seeks the textual passages within the text itself. Next, regarding the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), it is explained that they subsume the five [virtues] as the means for setting out toward the Mahāyāna.

However, while dhyāna actually possesses all merits, such as the ten bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth, it is now specifically clarified because, in setting out toward the Mahāyāna, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the root of the Buddha-way.
Next, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) through all modes.
The third passage of the sutra states that one should practice with the *samyak-prajñā-citta* (perfect wisdom-mind), or it speaks of "cultivating all minds," or "practicing the bodhicitta.
Now, the bodhicitta is the true path; as the Buddha said, it consists of seeking the Buddha-way above and delivering sentient beings below.
Yet, in the present case, it is not so; seeing sentient beings who can be delivered, one is unable [to do so].
To save sentient beings while perceiving that the fruit of Buddhahood can be sought prevents one from attaining the Way of the Buddha;

only when one knows there are no sentient beings to be saved can one truly save them. To know there is no Buddha to be sought is the true seeking of a Buddha. This is the fourth stage: the practice of the Middle Way and Right Contemplation.

First comes the wisdom of the eighteen kinds of emptiness; next, one knows that the three periods of time are not three periods of time. Nevertheless, it is essential to exhaustively purify all attainment.

The four propositions regarding the three periods of time are ultimately unattainable; only then can one realize that there is no discourse on the three periods, for the three periods themselves lack the nature of being "three periods.

Question: Since the *Juyi pin* (Chapter on the Meaning of Propositions) was not yet complete, it was known that there were both mundane and supramundane realms; now, this [chapter] concerns the pure attainment of the mundane and the supramundane.
Chapter Sixteen: The Vehicle of Vehicles.

It is fitting to discuss the adornment of the myriad practices as the adornment of the Dharma-body. Because Bodhisattvas who practice correct contemplation are endowed with the myriad practices, these constitute the adornment of their aspiration and the locus of their beginning and end.
Now, to clarify the "Vehicle of Vehicles," it refers to being fully possessed of the vehicle of the person, the vehicle of the Dharma, and the vehicle of the teaching.
It is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*) because it is that which is mounted; furthermore, this name signifies the meaning of the "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*) who possesses self-correcting understanding.

The *Twelve Gates Commentary* explains this extensively through the interpretation of the person, stating: "Because it is what the Great Man mounts. Here, we clarify this through the interpretation of the dharma:
the Great Man is so named because he mounts the Great Dharma. Thus, this chapter presents the question: the person mounts the vehicle to transport the myriad practices.

Question: How does this differ from the adornment of the myriad practices (*samskāra*)? Answer: Previously, it was explained that one takes up the adornment of the myriad practices for the sake of the person;

now, it is clarified that one takes up the person to wield and govern the myriad practices. Previously, the person was established through the Dharma; here, the person is taken up to govern the Dharma.

If interpreted according to the sequential stages, it is as stated in the treatise. Following the question at the beginning of the chapter, the answer follows. The answer has three parts: first, clarifying the vehicle of vehicles; second, praising [the Buddha] for the sake of the ten directions.
Third, the general conclusion of the first two sections: First, it clarifies the vehicle and the causes of the vehicle; second, it clarifies the attainment of the fruit through the vehicle.

Within the first [section], there are three parts: first, it clarifies that the vehicle consists of merit and wisdom; second, because the present context emphasizes "wisdom," it specifically clarifies the vehicle of wisdom;

third, because it emphasizes "supernatural powers" (*abhijñā*), it specifically clarifies the attainment of the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). Below, the second part clarifies the attainment of the fruit; this is called [the conclusion].
The third section below concludes the text as it appears.
Chapter Seventeen, "The Adornment" (*Vyūha*).

This marks the second part of eight chapters praising the Dharma. While previously the person who practices the Dharma was praised before the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, here the person is praised.

Are the dharmas practiced different from the person who practices them? Are the dharmas different from the person? Therefore, person and dharma are not two. The previous praise was of the person, which is in fact a praise of the dharma;
the present praise is of the dharma, which is in fact a praise of the person. Though non-dual, they appear as two. Previously, the person who practices the dharma was praised as venerable;
now, the dharma practiced by that person is praised as great. These eight chapters form two sections; this first chapter serves as an introduction.

The first sentence of the chapter establishes certainty regarding the Buddha, clarifying that what he taught is not erroneous; this serves as the explanation for the salvation of the assembly at the time [of teaching].
Second, it restates the latter two schools to establish certainty regarding the Buddha. This section has two parts: first, the formal presentation of the first sentence;
second, although Subhūti had realized it, he sets forth his own understanding to initiate the realization of the assembly’s previous errors. Within the first part, there is the initial exhortation.

The first phrase is further divided into two questions: the first asks about the Dharma, and the second asks about the person; likewise, the first asks about the essence, and the second asks about the person;

and again, the first asks about the essence, and the second asks about its function, as in the text. The Buddha’s response to these questions is twofold: first, he answers the question regarding the Dharma, and second, he answers the question regarding the person.
The former also clarifies the causes for adornment and one's own practice, followed by the fruits of adornment and the benefit of others.

The answer to the first question follows the text; however, while Pūrṇa (Man-yuan) mentions only the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), this passage now extensively enumerates the ten thousand practices (*daśasahasra-caryā*).

The initial response follows the text in answering the question regarding the adornment of the fruit (*phala-vyūha*), which is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the adornment of the fruit itself, and second, clarifying the adornment of the Buddha-fruit.
In Pūrṇa’s text, the three meanings do not go beyond the attainment of practice; therefore, I shall here describe and confirm the adornment of the fruit through practice.
According to the Sūtra, there are four sections: first, it clarifies the manifestation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) but does not clarify the teaching of the Dharma;

second, it clarifies that the body of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) also manifests supernatural powers while fully practicing both material wealth and the Dharma; next, regarding the four *pāramitās*, it only clarifies the teaching of the Dharma and does not clarify the manifestation of the physical body;
finally, regarding the two *pāramitās* of skillful means (*upāya*) and dwelling [in the ultimate], it collectively manifests all bodies and teaches all Dharmas. This is based on the Śāstra.
To accomplish these four textual sections: first, assuming the body of a Buddha, he generally expounds the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to benefit those who have left the household life.

Second, through the two perfections of *dāna* (generosity) and *śīla* (ethical discipline), he attains wealth and nobility to become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); thus, by practicing both material and Dharma benefits, he delights those sentient beings who prefer the household life.
Third, through the [remaining] *pāramitās*, he assumes the bodies of a Brahmā king and a Bodhisattva to preach the Dharma for the sake of all beings.
Next, dwelling in the perfection of concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) and the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), he manifests bodies in the six realms of existence to teach all dharmas.
If one judges this according to the six perfections, the first [section] establishes the Buddha-body; it does not clarify the perfection of dwelling, because the Buddha-body is the fruit.

The next two sections dwell in the six perfections, and the fourth section dwells in the two perfections of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means. Thus, the fourth person fully practices the ten [perfections].

The statement that "deliverance consists solely of wisdom and skillful means" refers to the beginning and end of the latter four [perfections]. Skillful means is the beginning of these four, while wisdom is their end.
Regarding the practice of benefiting oneself and others: the former person merely transforms others to bring them to Buddhahood, as this is the fruit;
the latter person possesses both self-benefit and the transformation of others, as this is the cause. These two constitute the roots of the king: generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
First, the person is endowed with practice, wealth, and the gift of all dharmas; next, within the section on ethical discipline (*śīla*), only the gift of dharma is clarified;

next, in the section on the perfections (*pāramitā*), only the gift of dharma is clarified. Afterward, the distinct explanation of the dharmas is taught: for example, while dwelling in patience, one again explains patience.

The first two perfections involve both self-cultivation and the transformation of others in a general sense, whereas the latter four involve self-cultivation in a general sense and the transformation of others in a distinct sense. This may be sought according to the text. Question:

Regarding why the three preceding individuals spoke of the *mahāsattva* while Śāriputra alone was confirmed [as such], the answer is that Śāriputra is the Buddha’s interlocutor regarding phenomena (*dharma*), and thus there is no need for doubt;
Subhūti contemplates those [phenomena], and thus there is no need for confirmation. Furthermore, some divide the text into three parts:

the confirmation [of Subhūti] as the fulfillment of the son of the Fulfiller (Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra); among these three meanings, hearing one [point] answers the question concerning the adornment of the Dharma, thereby fulfilling the description.
I pray that among the three meanings, you will provide one answer to the question regarding the adornment of the Dharma, thereby completing the third [section];

and provide a second answer to the question regarding the adornment of the fruit, thereby completing the second [section], and a third [answer] to complete the first [section]. Regarding the second passage, "Abiding in Generosity" (*dāna*), the text is divided into four parts:
first, the Dharma; second, the analogy; third, the application; and fourth, the explanation starting from "For what reason? Within the explanation of the Dharma, there are two pairs. First:
The two fruits of the environment and the sentient beings refer to the transformation-purified land and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Just as King Vimalacitra [the "Lapis Lazuli King"] ultimately desired that things and appearances not obstruct one another so that they might be seen, the Bodhisattva likewise acts. Next, he practices the two kinds of giving: material wealth and the Dharma.

Regarding those who come with the analogy of an illusion, when Subhūti was present at the assembly, he heard that the transformed body acts as a Buddha-king to transform and deliver sentient beings; yet, because the Bodhisattva’s afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been exhausted, [he must continue to practice].
One should emerge from [the state of] self-conceit regarding one's own nobility; subsequently, because there is a substance that can be transformed, the analogy of an illusion is raised.
Although [the Buddha] acts, in reality there is nothing acted upon; therefore, there is no attachment. This may be understood by combining the explanations.

Furthermore, in the section "Abiding in Patience" (Kṣāntivihāra) and below, the third section concerns the four Buddhas, the Brahma Kings, and Bodhisattvas benefiting sentient beings. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Adornment (Mahāvyūha) is tenfold.
The fourth section below explains that the "all-bodies" (sarvakāya) preach the "all-teachings" (sarvadeśanā) according to the capacities of those to be converted;
this refers to the aforementioned skillful means (*upāya*) of the noble ones—whether they be renunciants, householders, kings, or celestial kings.

Since these have not yet manifested their bodies universally nor preached the Dharma universally, they are explained subsequently. The intent of the treatise is to clarify how the aforementioned Bodhisattvas, acting as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), fulfill the six *pāramitās*.
The Bodhisattva abides in the two pāramitās of skillful means and wisdom; dwelling in these two pāramitās, he teaches the six perfections to sentient beings.
Some explain that while previously he practiced the six perfections individually, now he dwells in them collectively.

Furthermore, he does not give rise to the thought that "there are so many people. Second, it clarifies that his vow is uninterrupted as a great adornment; although four [aspects] were previously established...

It may be feared that expedient means (*upāya*) do not necessarily encompass the universal salvation of the ten directions throughout the future limit; therefore, there is a subsequent passage [addressing this].
Although it answers the second question, from the initial question up to the manifestation of the four bodies, all serve to clarify the adornment of conduct (*caryā-vyūha*).

Now, it clarifies that these very [bodies] constitute the answer to the first question regarding the adornment of excellence (*viśeṣa-vyūha*), while the subsequent [passage] constitutes the answer to the second question regarding the adornment of pervasive penetration with causes (*hetu-vyūha*).
It cites four kinds of fruits of illumination to adorn those whose desires are not yet adorned. Furthermore, Pūrṇa cites adornment, which has three meanings:
first, a boundless vow of mind; second, saving oneself and others; and third, encompassing all practices through a single practice. These are condensed into two categories:
the first two constitute the vow, and the last one constitutes the practice. Now, as a seal of the Buddha, these two are described above.
This section summarizes his conduct and now seals its correctness. Question: What is the difference between Pūrṇa’s adornment and the Buddha’s illumination?
Answer: There is no difference; it is simply that this [text] now provides a seal and a summary. There are four meanings regarding the distinction between these two:

first, because the preceding section cited the Dharma to establish the person, it was called "Great Adornment" (mahā-vyūha) for the sake of the Great Man (mahā-puruṣa); whereas here, citing the person to establish the Dharma, there are various non-terms [for the adornments].

The Dharma is great. Regarding these two points: previously, the adornment of the cause was clarified while the result was briefly indicated; now, the result is explained in detail. Previously, only the six perfections were mentioned; now, all ten are fully elucidated.
Previously, the details were extensive; now, they are concise. This conciseness does not clarify the mutual inclusion [of the perfections].

He addressed the Buddha: "The absence of great adornment is itself the great adornment. This second section, concerning Subhūti’s mistaken self-assertion of having attained realization at the time of its inception, establishes the meaning of the aforementioned adornment.
Although he was mistaken, because he heard the Buddha’s seal of approval, one knows that Pūrṇa’s statement—that [Subhūti] had not realized it—was also refuted.
Above, it was clarified that "adornment like an illusion" refers to non-adornment.

When he manifested his majestic desire to inspire the assembly, it was as previously described: the Bodhisattva dwells in the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena while manifesting all bodies and delivering all teachings.
Although he manifests all bodies and delivers all teachings, in reality there is nothing manifested;
although he utters all teachings, in reality there is nothing uttered. At that time, the assembly said, "This is the Great Bodhisattva, the Holy Lord."
This capacity is not something that can be achieved through the practices of the lower realms; therefore, one quiets the mind and does not study them. This is why Subhūti said:

"The self-characteristics of all dharmas are empty—there is neither difficulty nor profundity. If you can realize that form is empty of the characteristic of form, then you will realize that adornment is empty of the characteristic of adornment.
If you can thus apply diligence without abandoning your original vow, then there is nothing further to be done.
Regarding "the adornment of great adornments," as previously clarified, for a Bodhisattva there is no such thing as a "meaning of words" (*pada-artha*).

Now it is clarified that, according to the Dharma-principle, there is neither adornment nor non-adornment. Throughout this one section of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, six instances clarify both persons and dharmas, and in all cases these words are taken as correct. That people today suddenly do not believe this and laugh upon hearing it—is this not the mark of an inferior person? The text has three parts; first, the direct [explanation]. *Note: The term "無句義句義" (wú jù yì jù yì) is a technical rendering of *apada-artha-pada*. The phrase "一部般若" refers to the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (or a specific recension thereof), specifically the section on the "Six Kinds of Non-attachment" (六無著). The commentary emphasizes that the negation of linguistic referents is the true meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā.*
This section consists of three parts: first, expressing what has been realized to inspire the sentiments of the assembly; second, describing the fulfillment of this meaning;

and third, Subhūti’s reiteration of the removal of the assembly’s doubts to clarify the attainment of benefit. The first part [of the third section] has three sub-points: first, designating that there is no adornment; second, designating that there is no non-adornment;

and third, citing the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) to explain the previously clarified emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Next, the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is explained. Regarding the phenomena of the mundane and supramundane, there are four categories.

As stated in the text, there is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Below, the conclusion follows the text’s description, which consists of three parts: first, the direct presentation of the emptiness of arising and phenomena;

second, the presentation of the two types of emptiness—of arising and of phenomena—through question and answer; and third, the explanation. Regarding the latter: *sarvajña* (omniscience) is the emptiness of phenomena, and sentient beings are the emptiness of persons.
Because there is no person, there is the emptiness of adornment; thus, there is no adornment. Yet it is said that this is not so.
Regarding "performing actions" (*kriyā-karaṇa*): when a bodhisattva adorns themselves with the ten thousand practices, this constitutes performing actions;

furthermore, transforming the body to act for a specific purpose constitutes acting as a person to transform sentient beings, leading them to practice and attain Buddhahood. Now it is clarified that even *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) is empty and possesses nothing;
all dharmas and sentient beings are likewise so. For one who acts as a Buddha for the sake of bodhisattvas, there is no action (*akriyā*).
"Desire is the adornment of non-adornment. Next, the question is asked as in the text. In the response, there are six constant shifts of meaning.

First, it correctly clarifies the two kinds of emptiness regarding the arising of phenomena (*dharma*). Second, it answers the previous point on "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Third, it first indicates the emptiness of the arising of phenomena; fourth, it explains the emptiness of phenomena;

fifth, it explains the emptiness of arising. These may be sought according to the text. Regarding the phrase "like an illusion or a dream," this is the second shift of meaning. It must be understood that [desire] is without real activity; how could it be otherwise?
If it is argued that there is no such thing as "acting" because illusions and dreams are ultimately empty, then one might ask: what is the function of citing the eighteen emptinesses?

Since the eighteen emptinesses destroy the notion of substantial existence and even the existence of illusions and transformations, they constitute a form of "action. Now, to clarify: if even emptiness itself does not exist, what could possibly act?

Fourthly, regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the myriad practices (*sādhana*): if dharmas exist, there must be action, just as there is with the foundations of mindfulness.
Since the overturning of inversions and so forth is itself an act of conditioning (*saṃskāra*), this passage now clarifies that the body is ultimately unattainable.
Where, then, could there be purity or impurity, inversion or non-inversion? Fifth, it is raised that, according to the Dharma-nature, the characteristics of phenomena are equal;

because the internal true nature (*tattva*) is suchness, the grasping of signs is dispelled and the four extremes are extinguished—this is the characteristic of the Buddha. Now it is clarified that the true nature of reality (*dharmatā-tattva*) is non-existent and devoid of deception.
If one asks whether the arising of wisdom means that wisdom can dispel the grasping of marks:

the sixth [point] explains that because the true wisdom of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can manifest the true realm of a Buddha and can separate it from the wisdom of ordinary beings, they manifest the arising of bodies and so forth for the sake of transforming sentient beings; thus, there is a reason for their activity.
As for the statement that the ultimate emptiness of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is ungraspable—how could there be any activity? At that time, Subhūti...
In the third section, "Subhūti Clarifies to the Buddha" and "Dispelling Doubts," the assembly says:
"If you yourself proclaim that the Dharma of ultimate non-action is profound and rare, then there would be no one who could escape birth, death, and the aggregates (skandhas). Is this not so?
They raise the interpretations of the Samkhya, the Mahāyāna, and the Hīnayāna as questions, saying: "Therefore, Subhūti said: 'All dharmas are neither bound nor liberated. How could there be..."
Regarding the passage "Is there purity or correctness in that which is sent forth? the text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the absence of bondage and liberation;

second, clarifying that because there is neither bondage nor liberation, one attains benefit. The first part [the absence of bondage and liberation] consists of two sections: first, because existence cannot be apprehended, there is liberation from bondage;

because bondage cannot be apprehended, there is no release. This was explained previously. The essential point is that phenomena (dharmas) are without bondage or liberation. First, this is stated directly; second, it is explained extensively regarding the three periods of time; third, it is addressed within the present moment itself.

When one thus universally investigates the nature of existence, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Regarding the *dānapāramitā* of non-bondage and non-liberation, secondly, there is no such attainment based on dependence;
because one does not attain by depending [on anything], after the attainment of non-dependence, one is fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas—this is the practice of practice.
If there were bondage and liberation, that would be the view of bondage and liberation. Now, for this *dāna*, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Because it is neither bound nor liberated, this is the giving (*dāna*) that is fundamentally without bondage or liberation.

However, this is explained from the perspective of the person (pudgala), wherein all things are not non-persons; it is explained from the perspective of phenomena (dharma), wherein all is one.

There is absolutely nothing that is not the Dharma. How is this known? The previous explanation of the meaning of "person" (pudgala) demonstrated that by undertaking the Great Vehicle through adornment, one is able to become a person;

thus, it clarified the meaning of "person. Now, since practice is shown to be concurrent with the Dharma, and because both person and Dharma are fully present within the *Mahā* [of Mahāyāna], it is called "Great" (*mahat*).
It is just as when the Mahāyāna is manifested as transformation—it is merely the Dharma—and likewise according to other interpretations of *nirvāṇa*.
However, it is only when one is now fully endowed with both the permanent and the impermanent, and neither the permanent nor the impermanent, that this is *nirvāṇa*.
When one is fully endowed with neither persons nor dharmas, and neither non-persons nor non-dharmas, that is truly the Mahāyāna.
If this is so, then if one knows that persons and dharmas are not two, they constitute the gate of persons and dharmas; if persons and dharmas are both dharmas, then persons are non-dual.
Because there are two [aspects], it is neither a person nor a dharma; it is the purity of dharmas, a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) for *prajñā*.
Thus, as in the case of Sudhana’s encounters with each spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), where each says, "This alone is the Dharma-gate," this single Dharma-gate is immeasurable because it is one;

There are five answers that respond to questions and doubts because they bring joy; thus there are both praises and confirmations. However, because those who have newly begun their study have not yet fully understood, it is necessary to reconcile them with the underlying principle.
According to the general interpretation, there are six questions: first, the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*); second, the function of the vehicle;
third, the beginning; fourth, the end; fifth, the intermediate abiding; and sixth, the person riding the vehicle. Now, this treatise explains the sutra as follows:

The *Zhenglun* (Treatise on the Correct), in the "Chapter on the Superiority of the Vehicle," states that Subhūti, having heard the answers to the five questions, offered five praises out of a joyful heart.

Regarding these five questions, there are two interpretations. The first interpretation holds that: (1) the first question concerns the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*), (2) the second concerns the function of the vehicle, (3) the third concerns the beginning, (4) the fourth concerns the end, and (5) the fifth concerns abiding in the interim. This is explained as such because it exhaustively inquires into the Dharma. However, the third interpretation holds that they are not equal.

The first question concerns the essence (body), the second the function (use), and the third the beginning and end; since the Buddha answers this beginning and end as a single response, we know this constitutes one gate.

The fourth question concerns abiding, and the fifth concerns the vehicle (yāna) and the person who rides it—the former four questions concern the dharmas, while the final question concerns the person.

Following this, there are five chapters which comprise both the dharmas that are studied (the object of the vehicle) and the person who is able to ride it. These are further divided into two parts, making five in total.

The first [of the five] and the last three are indeed the vehicle of the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*). Regarding the second question on "setting forth" (*prasthāna*), this is also "setting out toward" (*prasthiti*).

The Buddha’s answer to the five questions consists of five [sections], beginning from the first and extending through the extensive explanation of the vehicle. First, in answering the question regarding the essence (*svabhāva*) of the vehicle, he clarifies that there is nothing to be attained;
the myriad practices and myriad virtues are all the essence of the Mahāyāna. Second, in answering the question on setting forth, he explains the second [aspect of] setting forth.

If one proceeds toward the practice of non-attainment, one can then set forth for the first stage and proceed to the first stage—just as one who rides a horse proceeds toward an elephant, abandons the horse and mounts the elephant;
or as one who rides an elephant proceeds toward a dragon, abandons the elephant and mounts the dragon.

Third, from the beginning of the "Chapter on Departure" up until the point of departing from the triple world to abide within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), because of the immovable nature of the Dharma, [this] answers the question.

The third section concerns the question of the beginning and end; the fourth, from the "Chapter on Departure and Arrival," consists of the questions posed by Subhūti regarding where one arrives—namely, that it is because of the dharma of non-abiding and the dharma of immovability—which answers the question concerning the fourth dwelling place.

The fifth section, from the end of the "Chapter on Departure and Arrival" through the conclusion of Subhūti’s question, "Who will ride upon this vehicle and depart? provides the definitive answer to the fifth [topic], the vehicle.
The question concerns the person who rides [the vehicle].

At the end of the chapter, Subhūti asks, "Who is it that shall ride this vehicle? This is the answer to the question. Chapter Five provides the answer to the question regarding the rider of the vehicle.
It states, "There is no person who rides this vehicle and departs by means of it. Thus, two chapters provide the answer to one question. Two chapters provide the answer to one [question].

Question: This is an answer to three questions posed within a single chapter. Regarding the answer concerning the essence of the initial vehicle (*yāna*), there are two parts: first, a brief presentation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as the essence of the vehicle;
second, an extensive clarification of the six perfections as the essence of the vehicle, which specifically expands upon the two perfections of meditation (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The former briefly clarifies their essence, while the latter extensively clarifies their meaning; this constitutes the distinction between the extensive and the brief. Of these two parts, the first [section] restates the preceding question.

The total number of names is listed as two; separately, their names are set forth to explain their meanings. First, in explaining *dāna* (generosity), there are five phrases within the explanation of the name:
(1) corresponding to the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience); (2) relinquishing the internal and external; (3) sharing with all sentient beings;
(4) dedicating toward the Buddha-way; and (5) non-apprehension. First, regarding "corresponding to the Buddha-way": because one seeks the Buddha-way, one must correspond to it.

The mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) is a mind that has not yet realized its objective; therefore, within the second phrase, one gives both internal body and external objects to all beings with a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Thus, one obtains the fruit of giving and shares it with others. The internal and external objects previously mentioned were the causes for practice;
now, these are the causes for obtaining the fruit. One gives the fruit to sentient beings and also gives the fruit to sentient beings, seeking nothing else.

Because it is a response, one dedicates [merit] toward the Buddha-way; because it accords with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is likewise appropriate. Third, "presently having nothing to obtain" permeates these four matters;
although they are appropriate, there is nothing to which they are appropriate, and there is neither that which is to be abandoned nor that which abandons, and so forth. Question:

Regarding the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*, by abiding in the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*, one remedies the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśas*). How do the six perfections remedy the four corruptions?

Furthermore, for what reason is it said that there are six perfections? The Master of the Treatise answers: "Because there is the suffering of the hells within the realm of the six perfections; the suffering of being interrogated and tortured among humans;

the suffering of seeking the five desires among men; and the suffering at the time of death among the devas. The treatise concludes directly that giving (*dāna*) is the remedy for hungry ghosts (*preta*);

ethical discipline (*śīla*) should be for those in hell; patience (*kṣānti*) for animals (*tiryagyoni*); vigor (*vīrya*) for asuras; meditation (*dhyāna*) for humans; and wisdom (*prajñā*) for [the devas].

Question: Regarding the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* composed by Tianxian, under which of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are the bodhicitta, vows, and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed under diligence (*vīrya*), because the Buddha’s courageous diligence gives rise to the great vow and great compassion.
Question: As for the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*) and the attainment of wisdom (*jñāna*) mentioned later, to which [perfection] do they belong? Answer: Both belong to wisdom (*prajñā*).
The Treatise says: "Because wisdom is pure, its transformation is termed 'expedient means' (upāya). After the profound aspiration has been generated, it subsequently gains power;

this subsequent wisdom is decisively pure. Question: Since the Mahāyāna encompasses all practices while the Prajñāpāramitā encompasses only the six perfections—and since the six perfections separately open up Prajñā as one specific perfection—should the Mahāyāna likewise separately open up [the encompassing of all practices] as one specific practice? Personal Response: It should not.

Furthermore, regarding the Mahāyāna treatise, its general and specific aspects, its unity and multiplicity, and its six perfections—when one seeks to discuss these, they serve as answers to previously raised specific points.

From the section on the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) onwards, the second question extensively clarifies that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the Mahāyāna.

It explains the meaning of "dispersion" (*vikṣepa*) and "unobtainable emptiness" (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*): because it is free from dispersion, it is empty; because seeking it is unobtainable, it is empty. All other things are phenomena that are themselves empty.
In the second chapter, the "Vajra," it says that the eighteen dharmas of emptiness are named the "eighteen emptinesses.

Although the text states that the eighteen mental activities (*manopavicāra*) are designated as the eighteen emptinesses, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that the "great" refers to the emptiness of the object (*viṣaya-śūnyatā*), while the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that the "great" refers to the emptiness of wisdom (*jñāna-śūnyatā*).

Even the Hīnayāna explains that the eyes and so forth constitute internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), yet this merely empties the self; here, we fully encompass both persons and phenomena. The Hīnayāna also explains [this].
That the eye is empty is merely emptiness; now, because it is not merely emptiness, it is said to be "neither permanent nor ceasing.

It is not permanent because it refutes existence, and it does not cease because it is non-attached to emptiness. Regarding the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and furthermore the emptiness of the conditioned and the unconditioned, there is no further distinction.
This is because this emptiness exhaustively encompasses all phenomena; thus, there is no separate emptiness apart from this one.

The categories of "existence" (*bhāva*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) do not exhaustively encompass all phenomena, as in the case where birth is considered existence and cessation is considered non-existence.

Furthermore, regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is also "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), such as the emptiness of existence following non-existence and non-existence following existence.
Regarding these four types of emptiness, there are three meanings: first, they are taught briefly for the sake of those with sharp faculties who may practice them; second, they are easy to maintain.

There is also "existence" and "emptiness of existence": the five aggregates (skandhas) encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). There is "non-existence" and "emptiness of non-existence": these two [categories] exhaustively negate all phenomena.
Regarding "self-nature" and "emptiness of self-nature," the aforementioned two types of phenomena are its names. Within existence, there is the solidity of earth and so forth;
within non-existence, there is the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth. These two—existence and non-existence—are both empty of their own nature.
This clarifies that these two dharmas—existence and non-existence—are by their very nature empty from the beginning; they are not made empty by the operation of vision or wisdom.
Regarding the emptiness of other dharmas: just as the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) encompasses all dharmas exhaustively, there is no further dharma outside of this.
Yet, some might erroneously think that there is a dharma existing apart from the *dharmatā*; this too is empty. As it says below: "Even if there were something beyond *nirvāṇa*..."
The term "pan" (the suffix -tā/-tva) is also empty; the first two emptinesses subsume the seventeen emptinesses mentioned above.

Within these emptinesses, there are existent phenomena (*dharmas*) that belong to the category of existent phenomena, such as these. Furthermore, the first two emptinesses constitute the two types of emptiness—conditioned and unconditioned—within the eighteen emptinesses.

The third, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), belongs to the aforementioned emptiness of nature. The fourth is the negation of heterodox views and does not belong to the aforementioned eighteen.
The severance of the one hundred and eight [afflictions] through the samādhis is as explained in the treatise; it causes one to recite and understand liberation.

The text and phrases of the nineteenth chapter, "The Extensive Vehicle," are as follows; there is no difference between this commentary and those [other versions]. Taking oneself as the internal [self], and wife, children, and wealth as...

Regarding the external body: one's own living body is the internal body, while a corpse is the external body. Furthermore, that which perceives suffering and pleasure is the internal, while that which does not perceive them is the external.
Moreover, the five sense organs, such as the eyes, constitute the internal body, while the five objects, such as form, constitute the external body.
The reason for practicing these three contemplations is either for a single person or for three people; it is said that for three people, it extends to a hundred people.

There are those who are attached to their own bodies, wives, children, and so forth, yet not to others; there are also those who are attached only to their wives, children, and so forth, while regarding their own bodies as being composed of earth and other elements.
One should investigate that there are those who are attached to both. Attachment to the body is considered "external," while attachment to the mind is considered "internal.

Furthermore, sensation associated with the five consciousnesses is "external," while sensation associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is "internal. These constitute the one hundred and eight types of craving.

The remainder within is considered external; furthermore, the two types of suffering—bodily and mental—are internal. When the mind harbors expectations, such as the four hundred and four bodily diseases, these are sufferings arising from external conditions;
these, such as wicked people or insentient things like wind and rain, are called external sensations (*vedanā*).

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the internal mind, while the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) are the external mind. Furthermore, that which takes external objects as its condition is the internal mind; the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are internal.

The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are the internal mind; the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅga*) are the internal mind. The five hindrances are the external mind; the seven factors of enlightenment are the external mind.
Excluding feeling (*vedanā*), the remaining mental states are called "dharmas. Those that take internal dharmas as their object are internal dharmas;

those that take external dharmas—namely, mental factors (*caitta*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—as their objects are external dharmas. Furthermore, there are consciousnesses that take dharmas as their object, which constitute internal dharmas.

Excluding from among these the mental factors associated with feeling (*vedanā*), they constitute internal phenomena (*ādhyātmika-dharma*); the remaining formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are external phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*).

Among the seven categories, two are given their primary names: namely, the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) and the eightfold right path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*). The meaning of "right effort" is the arousal of the mind;
it is given its primary name because it is the practice of the path that leads toward the Dharma, whereas [the opposite] would fall into a wrong path, and thus it is called the "right path."

Because one also attains the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), one subsequently gains wisdom; yet if one exerts further diligence and exertion, wisdom becomes strong while concentration (*samādhi*) becomes weak.
If one attains "as one wishes" (*yatheṣṭa*), then concentration and wisdom are balanced and equal, corresponding to the practitioner's own mind; therefore it is called "as one wishes.

Because it is sufficient to attain the balance of concentration and wisdom, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished; thus, it causes the practitioner's intentions to be fulfilled. This is the fourth [explanation].
It is sufficient to say that because one contemplates these four with mental diligence based on this [foundation], one attains concentration; therefore, it is called "sufficient.
Regarding the accomplishment of the "abandoning practices" (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*): because one practices the conduct of abandoning desire, one attains concentration.

As for the previous question—asking how the diligent abandonment of the three evil births and the production of goodness differs from that of the Two Vehicles—the answer is that one must take up the preceding [teaching] of non-abiding and the non-arising of phenomena; thus, it is complete.

Although the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth now extinguish evil, one knows there is nothing to be extinguished; because there is nothing to be extinguished, they are called "extinguished" (*nirodha*).

It is the same for diligence (*vīrya*). Question: What is the difference between the three categories? Answer: When wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates, they are called the foundations of mindfulness; when diligence predominates, they are called the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*); and when concentration (*samādhi*) predominates, they are called the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
These twelve factors are called "faculties" (*indriya*) when they reside within the minds of those with dull faculties, and "powers" (*bala*) when they reside within those with sharp faculties.

The mind is called "power" (*bala*), and the growth of the faculties (*indriya*) is also called power. The nine signs (*navanimitta*) universally counteract lustful desire, while the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*) universally counteract the thirty signs.

Among these, one sign—the perception of impurity (*aśubhasaṃjñā*)—subsumes the nine signs. Furthermore, it is explained that the perception of impurity consists of the perception of the unattractiveness of all worldly things and the perception of the impurity of food;
thus, there are nine perceptions. Moreover, it is said that the nine signs are for the purpose of destroying the fetters (*saṃyojana*), whereas the ten perceptions are for [the same].

The nine marks (*navanimitta*) constitute the cause, and the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*) constitute the fruit. Furthermore, it is explained that there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority among them, as they equally serve to extinguish the three poisons (*triviṣa*).

By contemplating the nine marks as impure, one realizes impermanence; by realizing impermanence, one realizes suffering; and through this, one becomes detached from desire, thereby attaining cessation (*nirodha*). Moreover, the nine marks are the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

First, regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body, one opens it into three: mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of sensation, and mindfulness of phenomena. Regarding the foundations of mindfulness, one asks about the objects and the modes of inquiry.

The Section on the Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment consists of thirty-seven gates. Together with the six powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness, they total sixty. Regarding the preceding eighteen [factors]: the two absences of error in body and speech, the two modes of acting in accordance with wisdom, the absence of false notions regarding the aggregates (skandhas), and the absence of a mind not in samādhi—these constitute the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha). The remainder constitutes the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha). The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is as previously explained.
