The preceding section clarifies that "form does not know form" and so forth; these are external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*), meaning that the recipient and the material wealth are external phenomena.
Now, by not seeing the self, one does not see the giver; the giver is the emptiness of internal phenomena (*ādhyātmikadharma*).
The following thirteen types of emptiness explain this meaning. These thirteen emptinesses constitute the specific refutation of all phenomena, while the final five emptinesses are general.
This merely refutes all phenomena.

At that time, since the second [category], the "inferior and so forth," has already established the dharma as belonging to persons and because persons practice the dharma, there is no practice that is not accomplished;

thus it becomes threefold: first, the accomplishment of one's own practice; second, the accomplishment of the practice of transforming others; and third, the simultaneous accomplishment of these two practices, whereby the stage of a Bodhisattva is attained without further reliance.

Regarding the two initial sections of the "External Protection": first, it clarifies the Bodhisattva’s practice of unimpeded action; second, it clarifies the practice of relinquishing both the impeded and the unimpeded.
Within the exhortation, there are two parts: first, Subhūti clarifies the coarse practice of non-obstruction; second, the Buddha explains the subtle practice of obstruction and non-obstruction.
Regarding the first of these, a celestial lord previously asked because, as clarified above, there is nothing that can obstruct due to the power of skillful means.
Regarding this matter, within the *Subhūti-parivarta*, two aspects are established: first, the explanation of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), and second, the explanation of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, there are two types of matters: the dharmas and the merits; and two types of wisdom, each consisting of three. These are: first, obstruction regarding one’s own practice; second, obstruction regarding the transformation of others;

and third, obstruction regarding sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). The meaning of the text fully encompasses these points. As for why they are called "obstructions," Subhūti says that it is because of internal attachment to a self (*ātman*).

Because external dharmas are attached to, they constitute an obstruction. Furthermore, regarding the passage "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening," according to the *Śāstra*, this text belongs to the second section clarifying non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*).
Although the preceding section clarified one's own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*), the present section clarifies the non-obstruction of transforming others (*parārtha-vinaya*).

Having explained the non-obstruction of transforming others, the conclusion establishes that two benefits are obtained: first, one is free from error and delusion; second, one acts in accordance with what the Buddha has authorized.

Furthermore, regarding the second Buddha’s re-explanation of the subtle obstruction and non-obstruction, it is divided into four parts: first, the first Buddha explains obstruction and non-obstruction;
second, Subhūti attains realization and praises the Tathāgata, who then confirms his understanding; third, Subhūti asks further questions and the Tathāgata provides the explanation;
fourth, Subhūti again attains realization, praises the Tathāgata, and is confirmed by him. Regarding the first of these, it consists of the praise and the confirmation. Next...

Śāriputra listened and said: "This second verse of praise for its profundity—Subhūti joyfully spoke, saying, 'That which I understand is this profound Prajñā,' and he uttered these words desiring to pay homage.
The Buddha then recounted it: 'The Buddhas of the ten directions cannot grasp this Prajñā;
how then could you, Śrāvakas, have any Prajñā to obtain? Next, Subhūti, through this, realized that it was not merely..."
Prajñā is unapprehendable, and all dharmas are likewise unapprehendable. Next, the Buddha summarizes the middle section in three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
To clarify that all dharmas have a single nature means that the aforementioned Prajñā and the dharmas are both unapprehendable;
therefore, they are of one nature. "One nature" refers to ultimate purity (*atyanta-viśuddhi*). Next, it clarifies that if there were anything not ultimately [pure], there could be an end to it.
In the end, since there is no "not ultimate" because there is an "ultimate," there is no ultimate; thus, "no ultimate" and "not non-ultimate" are called the two natures (*dvitva*).
This single dharma-nature is itself the nature of being without nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); this is the second explanation of the aforementioned "non-dual nature.

Regarding "one dharma-nature," this reiterates the preceding "one nature. As for these two being "without nature," it is because even this one nature does not exist; therefore, it is called "not [dual]."
Second, that which is non-nature is itself nature; this is called the non-dual nature (*advaya-dharmatā*). It is neither arising nor acting;
it is thus from the very beginning, not brought about by non-wisdom (*ajñāna*). Thus, Subhūti—[this concludes] the third summary of the non-dual nature. Knowing this brings benefit.
[The passage] beginning with "He said to the Buddha" is the third section: praising the discourse as difficult to know and difficult to understand. The *Lun* (Treatise) says: Subhūti...
I previously thought that I had attained what the Buddha had not, and thus I knew that Prajñā is difficult to know and difficult to understand.
The Buddha replied: "It is not only you who find it difficult; all sentient beings are unable to realize it through direct awakening because the six consciousnesses cannot cognize Prajñā.
Fourth, regarding the difficulty of the inconceivable: it is because the teaching of the three periods of time is precisely for the purpose of explaining the absence of obstruction.
Question: Subhūti has already explained the obstructed and the unobstructed; why does the Buddha speak of them again? Answer:

The defilements of sentient beings' inversions cannot be washed away all at once. First, one washes away the coarse defilements—namely, the views that "I" and "the other" exist, and the perception of receiving material wealth.

These three matters are considered "obstructed," while the absence of these three is "unobstructed. Now, as for removing the subtle defilements, how could it be that seeing only these three constitutes an obstruction?
"Neither three nor non-three," and so forth, up to "neither non-three nor non-non-three"—if the mind follows what can be negated, it loses Prajñā;
therefore, this is called an obstruction. Second, Subhūti was a follower of the Hīnayāna;

fearing that he might not be able to properly discern whether the Bodhisattva path is the true path or not, the Buddha reiterated and confirmed his teaching, praised it, and spoke further on its behalf. Herein, it is discussed solely in terms of following [the negation].

The single gate of joyful dedication clarifies the distinction between the obstructed and the unobstructed; once this is clear, the remaining meanings will manifest of themselves. From "He addressed the Buddha regarding the profound...
onwards is the second section, which consists of the disciple’s understanding and praise, followed by the Tathāgata’s confirmation and completion. Regarding this, some say there are five praises:

first, profundity; second, worthiness of veneration; third, the unattainability [of its limit]; fourth, praise for the difficulty of understanding what is difficult to understand; and fifth, the inconceivable. Now...

This means that "unattainable" (*anupalabdha*) is not a separate eulogy. Some say that among these, the four eulogies below [the section on] "non-action" (*akṛtya*) constitute the first, while the fifth is the eulogy of the unconditioned non-action (*asaṃskṛta-akṛtya*).

Now, according to the judgment of the treatise, even if one were to further eulogize the Buddha’s unconditioned non-action as far as the following passage, it would still not constitute a true eulogy.
My view is that there are four eulogies: first, the extremely defiled; second, the worthy of veneration; third, the eulogy of the worthy; and fourth, the eulogy of the unsurpassed.
The "Explanation of the Four Inconceivables" corresponds to the four expositions. Regarding "profound": Subhūti knows that what the Buddha has spoken exceeds his own reach;
therefore, he calls it profound. Furthermore, if one directs the mind toward it, one loses Prajñā; thus, Prajñā is profound.
The Buddha’s exposition states that all subtle things do not enter into Prajñā; therefore, Subhūti enters into the wisdom of the profound Prajñā.
Because its power is ultimate, it is called inconceivable.
Chapter Forty-three: No-Action. Buddha Eleven:
Describing Subhūti’s Veneration and Praise. Prajñā is without arising and without action; Subhūti now [attests to this].
The title of this treatise on the Buddha is derived from its meaning of "non-action" (akṛta) and "non-arising" (anutpāda).
This constitutes the third section, consisting of Subhūti’s repeated questions and answers. Regarding the initial question, it is an expression of praise, asking:

"Since Prajñā is without arising and without action, how can one practice Prajñā so as to abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas? The Buddha replied: "Whether it be a person or a dharma, one does not seek the meaning of 'Buddha' [in such a manner]."
Since [the fruit] can be attained, there is no "acting"; how could there be evil to be abandoned or goodness to be attained? The intent of the second question is:
if there is no agent, how should one practice the cause of prajñā in order to attain prajñā? In the Buddha’s response, there are two parts: first, clarifying that non-acting entails having practice;
second, clarifying that non-acting entails having no practice. Within the section on non-acting yet having practice, there are three gates; first, non-practice in the horizontal sense.
Regarding all objects, one does not subsequently engage in any [fixed] contemplation, such as permanence or impermanence; these three do not proceed, for they are incomplete.

This is the practice of *prajñā*. Regarding its incompleteness, there are two interpretations. One says: ordinary beings give rise to the perversions of permanence and impermanence with respect to form (*rūpa*) in a complete manner;
now, by borrowing the "impermanence" of ordinary beings to refute this [notion of] permanence, impermanence is thus rendered incomplete.

Because one does not practice this impermanence, it is called "non-practice" and "incompleteness. Furthermore, having previously clarified impermanence to refute permanence, one now again refutes incompleteness;
this is precisely the refutation of impermanence, which constitutes a complete refutation. Question: Why does one not practice permanence or impermanence? Answer:
Because one knows that permanence and impermanence are non-dual, and one does not accept permanence or impermanence. Next, permanence is explained.

"Is it impermanent? Next, regarding the explanation of "not being complete," "insufficiency," and "fulfillment": the practices of the lower stages are fulfilled by the Bodhisattvas in the stage of 'one more birth' (ekajātipratibaddha).

To cause those incomplete practices of the lower stages not to be performed, and to perform the fulfillment-seal of the stage of 'one more birth'—likewise, this non-performance is itself the performance.
Second, explaining "non-performance": it is not merely that there is no such performance; rather, there is also... [the practice of] non-performance.
Furthermore, not practicing from the very beginning is the practice of a bodhisattva. Previously, taking impermanence, suffering, and non-self as ultimate was considered practice;
now it is clarified that because one does not practice with regard to permanence or impermanence, this is "unprecedented," and for this reason it is praised.

Moreover, since antiquity it has been said that practicing with something to be attained is practicing *prajñā-pāramitā*; yet now, suddenly hearing that practicing with nothing to be attained is practicing *prajñā-pāramitā*—this is likewise unprecedented.
If this is indeed so, it is yet another marvel. Some teachers say that when the number reaches eleven, it is complete;
they hold that having only the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is incomplete, whereas possessing fourteen is complete, while having only eleven is incomplete.
[The interlocutor] said to the Buddha, "It is a marvel! This is the fourth time he receives and praises [the teaching], and the Buddha reiterates it as in the text.
Furthermore, the second section below concerns the two gates of abandoning both obstruction and non-obstruction;

this is called "non-obstruction" because it clarifies that both the obstructed and the unobstructed are termed "obstructions," and only when there is neither obstruction nor non-obstruction does one begin to call it "non-obstruction."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha. [This concludes] the fourth section on receiving the teaching and expressing praise. Above, there were four praises:
the first three praised only the Prajñāpāramitā, while the last praised only the Buddha; now, this praise unites both the Prajñā taught and the person who teaches it.

This is divided into two parts: first, praising the Dharma; second, praising the person. Regarding the statement that "speaking and not speaking are not different from the Tathāgata," this is clarified in the "Chapter on Faith and Slander."

First, by means of faith and slander, both gain and loss are clarified; this is one. Second, within the context of faith, the presence or absence of gain is clarified, thereby distinguishing between the obstructed and the unobstructed;
this is two. Third, when neither the obstructed nor the unobstructed are operative, the three periods clarify that the teaching of the Tathāgata is no different from the four assemblies;
this is three. That is to say, because one is able to skillfully expound the *prajñā*, it is manifest; because one is not skillful in its exposition, it is hidden. Thus, for all who exist...

Because one can understand this principle of increase and decrease in such a manner, there is increase through understanding and decrease through non-understanding. Therefore, it is now clarified that whether [the teaching] is explained or not, and whether there is awakening or no awakening, the same applies.

Question: Regarding the meaning of others, they claim that the Buddha saves sentient beings, attaining the Way and leading them to Nirvana, thereby increasing [Nirvana] and decreasing [samsara], and so forth.
How do you respond to this? Answer: The Buddha constantly delivers beings, yet ignorance constantly returns to destroy [that deliverance]. (End of quote)
Question: Now, regarding the two—clarity and illumination—what do "inclining" and "filling" mean? Why are these four phrases applied specifically to all sentences and words?

It is said that within these four phrases, there is the movement between delusion and awakening: if one awakens, nirvana increases and birth-and-death decreases; if one is deluded, birth-and-death increases and nirvana decreases.
As for the second phrase, both birth-and-death and nirvana are full and complete; that is, birth-and-death is precisely nirvana, and nirvana is precisely birth-and-death.

There is nirvana, there is nirvana, and there is birth-and-death; all are filled. When the two rivers are diminished, neither birth-and-death nor nirvana can be apprehended—this is "non-duality," which is what is meant by "diminution.
These four phrases are all based on the conditions of birth-and-death and nirvana, yet in reality, it is not like this at all.
[The text] says to the Buddha: "All that the bodhisattvas do is praised as the second [type], praising the practice of *prāntakoṭika-vihāra* (the dwelling at the ultimate limit)."
"If a person... O Bhagavan, they should pay homage to all Bodhisattvas. This concludes the third section, which clarifies the accomplishment of the practice of transforming others.
Previously, the Bodhisattva’s own practice was praised; here, by speaking of "transforming Bodhisattvas," the praise shifts to the practice of transforming others.

Since it is stated herein that [the Bodhisattva] acts as a "great adornment for sentient beings" and so forth, this constitutes the practice of transforming others, following from their prior self-awakening.

Neither obstructed nor unobstructed, [the Bodhisattva] now causes sentient beings to attain this awakening; thus, sentient beings are neither of the nature of obstruction nor of the nature of non-obstruction, for they are empty.

The Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings who are empty, yet these are neither obstructed nor unobstructed; the Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings who are neither identical to nor distinct from obstruction.
Furthermore, in the initial passage, it clarifies Subhūti’s praise of the Bodhisattva’s practice of transforming others.
The formation of the subsequent single verse consists of the praise of the beginning, middle, and end—namely, the introductory praise, the intermediate praise, and the concluding praise.

First, regarding the introductory praise, there is one section where the World-Honored One praises [the teaching] in terms of benefiting sentient beings, meaning he causes sentient beings to attain worldly happiness and supramundane happiness.
Next, wishing to deliver sentient beings from birth, the World-Honored One praises the Bodhisattva’s ability to enable sentient beings to be liberated.

This is a praise [of the Buddha] because he has attained the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles from within the suffering of the three realms. Next, there is the praise regarding the meaning of the Three World-Honored Ones being able to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, as in the text.
"For what reason? begins the second section, which explains why they are called World-Honored Ones. "By these causes and conditions" begins the third section, which concludes the praise.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu... begins the second part: a single bhikṣu’s joyful reception and realization.

This clarifies that although the Bodhisattva truly has no one to deliver, they are able to deliver those in the six realms; although there is truly nothing practiced, they are able to perform the myriad practices.
Furthermore, within Prajñā, although there is nothing that exists, there is nothing that does not exist. The Śākya disciple asked: "By practicing what Dharma [is this achieved]?
The meaning of the Heavenly King’s question below is that because the Bodhisattva is able to perform such contemplative practice, sentient beings can be delivered and others can be transformed.

Regarding the statement that "the two preceding practices are accomplished, while non-practice results in neither attainment nor non-attainment," and that "these two practices, when accomplished, constitute the cultivation (*abhyāsa*) of what dharma?

The answer is: "Cultivating emptiness. This is the initial cultivation of the essentials. Next, one cultivates emptiness, just as in the beginning of the seventh turning of the *Saṃprayukta-skandha* (or *Saṃprayukta-paryāya*), one initially cultivates the seven kinds of emptiness.
Furthermore, within this context, the attainment of non-reliance is designated as "emptiness. What kind of Buddha is this?

I do not know what he is doing. The intent is to clarify that there is no protection. Furthermore, the Lord of Devas...

Seeing that the Bodhisattva exhorts the practice of profound and subtle deeds, [Subhūti] fears there may be obstacles for those with karmic affinity; thinking himself capable of protecting them, Subhūti replies instead that there is no one to protect. This meaning clarifies that once the two practices of the Bodhisattva—turning toward the profound and the subtle—are perfected, one perceives neither internal nor external reality or unreality. "Internal" refers to the Bodhisattva who is to be protected; "external" refers to the person who would be able to destroy [the practice]. Furthermore, since both are empty, there is nothing to be protected. Thus, it is said: "There is no dharma that can be protected. Not seeing that all phenomena are anything other than dream-like—realizing they are as empty as a dream—is why they are neither internal nor external, neither unreal nor non-empty;

this is the sublime practice of the Bodhisattva. Next, it clarifies that attaining right contemplation within the mind exhausts all fetters, and that praise cannot disturb this state, which is itself protection.
The commentary asks: "How does one know they are like a dream? The answer is: "Above, it was stated that the Bodhisattva has attained the dream."
Because of wisdom, there is no need for protection. Now it is asked: how can one know that [the world] is like a dream?
If a bodhisattva does not abide in reality but still acts within a dream, then they are a person who has fallen into perversion; would they not then require protection?
Regarding the "four matters of dreams," this clarifies that ordinary people perceive both the real and the unreal. To perceive the unreal refers to the matter of dreams. What are these four?
When ordinary people practice the dharma of dreams, they still say there are dreams; this is because they follow along with their dissolution.

Since this is both cause and dream, and effect and dream, it is said that one "recalls the dream" and discriminates between its good and evil, thereby giving rise to sorrow and joy. Thus, "recalling" refers to the function of recollection.

By means of this analogy of the dream, one attains the true wisdom that is like a dream; this is what is meant by "using" the dream. It is said: "I have attained [this] by means of this analogy of the dream."
To know that all phenomena are like dreams is called "my dream. Regarding the four actualities, to discriminate whether this is human form or non-human form is to be mindful of form;
to consider whether form is permanent or impermanent and so forth is to be mindful of it; and to give rise to pride because the mind arises due to form is to employ form.
Because one attains [the notion] of "I" through form, one says, "I am now. However, the Bodhisattva does not perceive such a mind.
Since the fourth [element] is likewise not seen as empty, one knows that all phenomena are neither real nor empty; only then can they be called a dream.
If it were as ordinary people perceive—seeing reality as real and emptiness as empty—then both would be real.

At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the third section follows, clarifying how initial faith, acceptance, and upholding the teaching are invariably beneficial. This is divided into three parts: first, exhorting faith;

second, accepting and upholding based on faith to be free from all afflictions; and third, personally upholding [the teaching] to be free from obstacles and afflictions, thereby transforming it for others.
If one explains it thus, one shall obtain inexhaustible merit. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the assembly’s gathering; second, clarifying the exhortation to faith.
Question: In other places it is simply said that "the assembly has gathered," yet here it says "by the Buddha’s spiritual power. Some explain this as follows:
previously, when the various devas heard the profoundly deep Dharma of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, their minds could not comprehend it, and they were about to abandon it.

Therefore, [the Buddha] secretly moved them to come so as to exhort the assembly at that time; how could they have abandoned it once they had gathered like clouds? Regarding this, there are two interpretations. One says: "It is still..."
This is because the celestial beings have been here for a long time; having departed, they come again. Another interpretation is that new celestial beings have arrived.
As for why the various devas make offerings: although the Prajñāpāramitā is excellent and profound, this chapter explains the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena with perfect clarity;
therefore, the devas rejoice and present their offerings.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings saw each of the thousand Buddhas appear and spoke a third time to encourage faith, clarifying that the path practiced by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time is no different from this; it is not merely Śākyamuni who alone makes this teaching. Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is to be trusted.
At that assembly, there were those who feared that because Śākyamuni appeared in a defiled land, the Prajñāpāramitā was merely a provisional means used to entice beings.
Because of this teaching, it is now clarified that although the Buddha-lands of the three periods and ten directions may be pure or defiled, the Way revealed therein is non-dual.

There is a commentary which states: because the members of the assembly found the principles and intent of what Subhūti had explained difficult to establish and were unable to believe them deeply, [Śāriputra] went there immediately.
This was a skillful means to allow them to hear and attain awakening. Furthermore, it is said that those who do not understand in the present will see Maitreya in the future.

Because one must awaken through the Buddha’s various teachings, it is now clarified that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time clarify the principle of non-duality; thus, it is said "there is also no duality.
If this [present teaching] is not understood, by what means could that [past or future teaching] be awakened to? It is the same for the past and the present. The text has two parts:

first, clarifying that the Way is identical throughout the ten directions; second, clarifying the identity of the three periods of time. Within the identity of the ten directions, there is the identity of the thousand Buddhas; here, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is being expounded.

First, they are identical in clarifying the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) as the characteristic; second, they are identical in name, for both are named *Prajñā*; third, they are identical in the number of chapters, being large or small;
fourth, it is said that their names, phrases, and sentences are identical to those in the *Avataṃsaka*; fifth, they are identical in the person who transmits the teaching;
and sixth, they are identical in the person who poses the questions and challenges.
At that time, the Buddha spoke [the second section], clarifying that the three periods of time are identical in two respects: first, clarifying the identity of the persons and the locations;
second, clarifying the identity of the teaching gates. Maitreya of the future will likewise preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* at this very mountain location.

However, as for the discussion of the "thousand Buddhas," this refers to the actual events of the Bhadrakalpa, as there are no such mountains for all of them. [Question: For what reason is it stated that the thousand Buddhas all [preach] at this mountain?
The *Madhyamāgama* states [that the Buddhas teach here] but does not say "the thousand Buddhas. This is because even the Buddhas outside the period of the thousand Buddhas teach within this mountain;

however, since the thousand Buddhas [specifically] endure until the end of the kalpa-conflagration, at which point this mountain no longer exists, it does not mention the Buddhas outside the thousand Buddhas. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that these Buddhas also preach the *Lotus Sūtra* within this mountain.
This is based on the inconceivable principle, whereas the present discussion does not take this into account, as is the case with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is the inconceivable discourse always held at Vulture Peak.

Subhūti asks: "What are the characteristics and what is the causal meaning? Below this, the second section clarifies that the teaching gates are identical. There are three questions and three answers; the three questions are as they appear in the text.
Regarding the three answers, they differ from those explained here; the lecturers of this region do not distinguish them, yet the people of the North say: "As for 'characteristics' (lakṣaṇa)..."

just as I, Śākyamuni, have explained the *Prajñāpāramitā* with such meaning from the beginning of the sūtra, so too will it be for future Buddhas. Furthermore, some explain that this is a comprehensive answer.

Question: Since this is precisely the mark of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)—being without dependence and without attainment—the text generally cites seven marks, namely:
neither permanent nor impermanent. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that the Buddhas sometimes say what is not the Path is the Path, and what is the Path is not the Path;
they constantly speak of the impermanent as permanent, and the permanent as impermanent. Why, then, do you now say that they all speak of that which is neither permanent nor impermanent?

Sentient beings constantly suffer from the maladies of grasping at annihilation or permanence and the dualism of acceptance and rejection; for this reason, all Buddhas always teach the Middle Way, which is free from the dharmas of annihilation and permanence.
Even if the words of the Great Sūtras speak of "permanence," they do so in order that sentient beings may awaken to the Middle Way of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
thus, the statement "the mind manifests the Way" is made. Some say that the principle of the True Truth (*satyadharma*) is eternally beyond the four propositions.
The four "cessations" (nirodha) are absolutely immutable; what is now commonly called the method of the four cessations is not identical to [the true] suchness (tathatā).
[The text] says: "He addressed the Buddha," which answers the second question regarding cause and effect. This Prajñā is the fruit, not the cause; it is not caused by the Buddha’s causal path.
It is said that Prajñā is not the fruit, yet it is the fruit of the Buddha. It is named "form" (rūpa), which is neither permanent nor impermanent. End.
Ultimate purity in *prajñā* is neither eternal nor impermanent; it is ultimate purity. Question: For what reason is this said? Answer: Because form (*rūpa*) is pure, *prajñā* is pure.

This is because all phenomena (*dharma*) are pure, and thus *prajñā* is pure. As stated in the "Chapter on the Equality of All Phenomena" (*Sarvadharma-samatā-parivarta*), because all phenomena are equal, *prajñā* is [that equality];
it is not that there is a *prajñā* apart from the equality of all phenomena. That which is called the equality of all phenomena is *prajñā*.
While various dharmas are distinct and all dharmas are fundamentally unequal, it is now clarified that all dharmas are originally equal;
therefore, Prajñā is equal.
The World-Honored One asked: "How is the dharma of form pure? This is the third question regarding its meaning. As for the meaning, it clarifies the locus of purity.

Regarding the phrase "for this reason": for what purpose is the purity of form and prajñā clarified? It is called "meaning" (*artha*) because it now provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of purity.
The *Śāstra* states that it is a "dharma-gate" (*dharmamukha*). Because there are various meanings, purity is likewise attained through various gates.
Among these four gates, first, by means of the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defiled, and non-pure nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one attains the understanding of pure clarity. Thus:
□ Regarding the sequence of the Dharma and the analogy: first, the five aggregates are raised as being pure because they are unstained;

here too there is a Dharma and an analogy. Next, space is raised as being pure because it can be described. Third, the section on the single analogy-gate clarifies purity: the first phrase clarifies purity because it can be described.
As for "the emergence of sound," this is due to the valley-space and the mouth-space acting as causes; thus, sound arises along with the great resonance. This is the metaphor.
Because Bodhisattvas abide in two matters: first, wisdom; second, eloquence. Prajñā-pāramitā constitutes the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma.
Second, the sound of the voice is also empty. The sound from the mouth is empty, just as the great sound emerging from a valley is empty;

since the sound from the mouth is also empty, ordinary people do not perceive these two as such, yet they claim the sound from the valley is no different from the sound [of the voice]. Now, by saying they are "not different," it clarifies this.
The second line [states that] the two sounds are like the "Great Sound" (mahā-ghoṣa) which is said to be pure; how could they not be pure?
The second phrase is pure because it is not intentional; as stated above regarding the Great Sound, it is pure because there is nothing to be spoken.
The third phrase, "space is unobtainable," means it cannot be characterized by existence or non-existence, according to the sixth chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. The fourth is single.
Regarding the explanation of the Dharma, this section provides a general clarification of all purities. The fourth [section] is the Dharma itself and not a simile;
whereas the preceding two are both Dharma and simile. Furthermore, while the first three clarify purity through specific meanings, the one [fourth] clarifies purity through a general meaning.

Nevertheless, since within the gates of the Dharma there is nothing that does not emerge from the categories of the general and the specific, as well as the Dharma and the simile, this explanation is provided; for this reason, it is also not [limited] therein.
Because this intention has emerged, it is the meaning of clarity and purity.
It will never suffer from eye disease. Regarding the second point, based on faith and upholding [the teaching], there is the question concerning the removal of obstacles to the Dharma:
"It is observed that some people explain the Prajñāpāramitā yet do not see any illnesses; how is this so? The answer consists of three points. First... [text fragment].
□ Because the world’s grave offenses are like a disease, one is cautioned not to commit them; even the power of *prajñā* cannot turn back such [karmic consequences], let alone other powers.
Second, if one acts exactly as taught in the *Prajñā*, there will be no manifold afflictions; yet sentient beings are unable to act according to the *Prajñā*.
Just as a disease is invariably cured when one takes medicine in accordance with the Dharma, so too [is it with the practice of *prajñā*].
First, although one wears the Dharma robes, the old illness does not subside; second, those who have lost the Dharma robes are not the medicine; third, they lack the power [of the medicine].
These three points indicate that what was heavy has become light. If one did not uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, one would have to undergo heavy retribution in the future;
now, by the power of the Prajñā, one undergoes only a small portion of this fruit in the present life and will not suffer it again in the future.
Countless hundreds of thousands of devas descend during this third period and turn [the Dharma] for others to speak, attaining infinite benefit.
This is divided into three parts: first, explaining how the speaker gains benefit; second, explaining how the listener gains benefit;

and third, illustrating the method of the Dharma through ten gates. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, Subhūti explains how the speaker gains benefit; second, the Buddha recounts it. Within the first of these, the explanation is clarified.
The deities arrive in succession; it is explained that he preaches the Dharma for them so they may obtain benefit and merit. Question:

Since there are already Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls in the heavens, why do they come? Answer: It is rumored that there are Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls in the heavens, but they have not been spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth.
Even if they did exist, when the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven fights with the asuras, they recite the Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding the existence [of the assembly]: there are two reasons why the Tuṣita Heaven exists [in this context]. First, because Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) preach the Dharma there, it exists.

Second, regarding those who have now come, there are two meanings: first, humans possess three things that surpass the devas—namely, the severance of desire, strong mindfulness and recollection, and diligence—and for this reason, they come among humans to hear the Prajñāpāramitā. Second, there are Bodhisattvas in the heavens who wish to cause humans to practice reverence.

Because of the *prajñā*, when one comes from afar, evil spirits depart at the time of arrival, and the malicious intent of those who harbor hatred is subdued; this is due to the power of the various masters.

The next phrase clarifies that by preaching the Dharma for the devas, one gains great merit: first, because the devas possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya`), and second, because their merit serves as a superior cause;
since the Dharma is preached for such [beings], the merit is vast.
The second part, the Buddha’s exegesis, is divided into two sections: first, the formal exegesis; second, the explanation of that exegesis.

Subhūti previously praised the merits of the present life—namely, the cultivation of freedom from all ailments and the attainment of benefits and blessings—and now the Buddha’s exegesis clarifies the merits of both lifetimes.

Regarding the section beginning with "For what reason," the second part, the explanation of the exegesis, is further divided into two: first, praising Prajñāpāramitā as being identical to a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi); second, praising Prajñāpāramitā [as being like a great physician].
If it is asked whether the *prajñā* wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) is identical to or different from [ordinary] wish-fulfilling jewels:

just as an ordinary wish-fulfilling jewel can eliminate all suffering and obtain all happiness, so too does the *prajñā* wish-fulfilling jewel enable one to eliminate the sufferings of both this life and future lives, and to obtain the happiness of both these two worlds as well as *nirvāṇa*.
Within *prajñā*, there is no dharma that can be apprehended. Next follows the second praise of *prajñā* as being neither arising nor ceasing.
The *maṇi* jewel is supreme, yet because this *maṇi* is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, one experiences joy upon obtaining it and suffering upon losing it.

Prajñā, however, is neither arising nor ceasing; it is free from gain and loss, and from suffering and joy. Furthermore, by obtaining a wish-fulfilling jewel, one exalts oneself and disparages others, which becomes a causal condition for committing offenses.
By attaining the wisdom of Prajñā, one realizes the non-duality of self and other, such that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal.
This is the opening of the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way. If a bodhisattva were thus ignorant, one would exhort that bodhisattva to practice according to the *prajñā*;
therefore, they obtain benefit. Of the two phrases, the first phrase concerns obtaining benefit through practice free from attachment;
likewise, if one is ignorant, knowing this, one does not speak of it. The devas now speak of *prajñā*, yet even here one does not become attached.
To know that there is nothing known is to be without power and without non-power; this is the second exhortation to practice neither grasping nor abandoning, whereby one attains benefit.
Because it is ultimately empty, one does not perceive power; because one can attain the Buddha-way through prajñā, one does not perceive power.
All that follows constitutes the mallet of the practice of neither grasping nor abandoning.
At that time, the various devaputras descended. This second section clarifies the benefits gained by the listeners and their subsequent praise, which is divided into two parts:
first, the devas gaining benefits and offering praise; second, Subhūti and the great assembly together offering praise. Regarding the first of these two, there are two sub-sections:
first, the devas joyfully making offerings and realizing the Way; second, the Buddha breaking the wheel of Dharma and preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*, beginning with its first four lines.
First, joy refers to mental action (*manas-karman*); second, making offerings refers to bodily action (*kāya-karman*); third, speaking words of praise refers to vocal action (*vāk-karman*);
fourth, the emergence of those who have attained or lost [the path] is the general explanation of the intent behind joy and making offerings.

Traditionally, it has been said that this is cited as proof for the teachings of the Second Period. Now I ask you: when you cite the various devas seeing [this], do you mean that the "Second Period" refers to the Second Turning of the Wheel?
Question: The Teacher [the Buddha] stated below that [the turning of the wheel] is neither one nor two; why does he not cite this as proof that it is neither at one time nor at two times? Answer:
The Buddha uses emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to dispel existence (*bhāva*), and therefore he does not cite it. Furthermore, the various devas use existence to dispel emptiness; thus, he cites it.
If one says that emptiness is for dispelling existence but does not dispel emptiness itself, then emptiness can indeed destroy existence, yet existence cannot destroy emptiness.

If emptiness and existence possess bliss, they cannot be mutually destructive, nor can they be mutually dispensed with. Furthermore, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (or *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*) refers to you as the "second period" and also speaks of "seeing the second turning";
how could this not be a contradiction? Moreover, within the *Dharmapada* (or *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*), the former small [teachings] are cited in contrast to the great;
how could this be the second period? Someone has explained it thus: hearing the One for the first time constitutes the First [Turning].
Within the "successive turnings," there are further two types of turnings; up to a hundred awakenings constitutes a hundred turnings. However, according to the treatise, this is not the case.

When the gods saw that in the past, at the first turning, eighty thousand devas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) while Cunda alone attained the first path, they considered it one turning.
Later, seeing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas attain the patience of non-arising, they [considered it] the second.
Second, regarding the turning [of the wheel]: Question—Formerly you turned the small wheel, and now you turn the great wheel; why are these two similar?

Answer—if one takes the perspective of the revealed teaching (*nītārtha*), where the former was small and the latter is great, then the small constitutes one turning and the great constitutes another turning.

However, according to the secret teaching (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*), the former was already the great [wheel]; therefore, immeasurable people have given rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, and even immeasurable people have attained [the fruit].

Because [the Buddha] attained the patience of birth (*utpatti-kṣānti*) as one on the stage of the "near-attainment" (*sāmyaktva-nyāma*), he turned the Great Wheel in the past and likewise turns the Great Wheel now; thus, they are similar.

Some explain that this period extends from the time of the request for the teaching until his initial realization of the Way. Regarding the falling of flowers and the three exclamations during the previous request for the teaching, these were instances of faith-based awakening (*śraddhā-vibodha*);
since he had not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), they are not listed in the text. Had he attained the patience of non-arising, it would have been long ago.
The enumeration of the stages is not clear because they had not yet been attained; now, for the first time, he has realized the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpāda*). The *Śāstra* says:

"The initial teaching is called the 'True Dharma' because it is the first turning of the characteristics of a single dharma. Up until the exhaustion of all dharmas, these are all called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Whatever the Tathāgata speaks with his own mouth is called the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. This statement should also be understood by analogy as referring to the beginning.

This is termed the "function of teaching": the initial teaching and the subsequent [teaching]. If both the initial and subsequent are called "teachings," then both the initial and subsequent are also called "Dharma-wheels.

Nevertheless, it is also permissible to provide an analogy; such an analogy may be drawn as follows: The Buddha’s destruction of the three propositions is the ultimate emptiness that eliminates the views of the various heavens regarding the "one turn" and "two turns";
his two functions—the non-existence of dharmas and the emptiness of existent dharmas—eliminate the views of "turning back" and "returning."

The arising of the world is explained as "transformation" (pravṛtti), and the cessation of the world is explained as "reversion" (nivṛtti). Since all phenomena are fundamentally empty, there is no transformation;

since this emptiness does not exist [as a substantial entity], there is no reversion. This single question-and-answer provides a comprehensive explanation that they are neither one nor two, neither transforming nor reverting;
it is understood because their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are empty. Thus, they cannot be refuted.

Next, Subhūti and the great assembly joyfully praised and extolled how the principle of Prajñā is ultimately pure and empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svabhāva-śūnya*), yet capable of causing one to attain the non-arising Bodhi.
Thus, it is not for the sake of creating a great dharma that they praise Prajñā as being able to attain the "unnameable" (*anabhilāpya*);
rather, they now praise its ability to attain the great fruit. The former [praise] refers to the present life, while the latter refers to future lives. Next—
The praise of the three gates of liberation regarding the absence of turning back or returning is as previously stated; this applies both to the present life and to future lives.
Next, the praise of the three gates of liberation regarding the absence of turning back or returning is as previously stated.
If one can thus explain the ten gates of the method for teaching the Prajñāpāramitā by means of the third illustration of illusion— namely: (1) speaking, (2) teaching, (3) proclaiming, (4) opening,
(5) demonstrating, (6) distinguishing, (7) revealing, (8) manifesting, (9) explaining, and (10) explaining in a simple manner—
whether by relying on the written text or orally transmitting the instruction, such a person praises the Prajñāpāramitā and causes others to receive and uphold it, and so forth.

The Imperial Edict on Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) means that through wisdom one realizes the state of those who have come before, and they attain awakening and understanding. "Opening" refers to the removal of doubt and delusion;
it is like a door being opened after having been closed. By breaking through the barriers of ignorance, one causes others to attain awakening.

When the gate of Prajñā is opened, one observes with the eye [of wisdom] such that things are no longer indistinct. If one points out what is right and wrong, what is gained and lost, one attains clear understanding and discernment.
As for this sutra: "Brief explanation" refers to that which is difficult to understand; "extensive analysis" refers to the correct awakening.

"Manifestation" means that the Buddha, for the sake of various sentient beings, speaks various [teachings] to gather those who seek [the truth], so as not to disparage them, but to cause them to practice and understand the Dharma.

"The speaker" explains the Buddha’s underlying intent by observing sentient beings to make them know the relative weight [of their capacities]. "Explanation" consists of various causes and conditions, origins and conclusions, and parables.
The explanation is made easy to understand because it renders the shallow and simple; thus, that which is profound is explained as shallow, and that which is difficult is made easily realized.
Furthermore, there is no speaker, yet the meaning of Prajñāpāramitā is fully established through this speaking. Although one may employ the ten gates of exposition, in reality there is no speaker.
The recipient of the Dharma has nothing received, and the one who attains realization has nothing realized—even merit is non-existent.
It is only because of such a person that one is able to purely expound the Prajñāpāramitā. If there is speaking or receiving, this is a teaching based on grasping (*upalambha*).

The four lines constitute the four stages: first, clarifying the expounding of the Dharma; second, receiving the Dharma; third, attaining realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*) as the fruit of proof;

and fourth, at the time of proof, the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*) which serves as the cause for merit, leading to entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder), and thus [grasping] ceases.
This is the cause of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Chapter Forty-four: Universal Praise.
Northern manuscripts state "Chapter Sixty-one," while others say it is the "Chapter on the *Pāramitās*. The text reads: "The Chapter on the *Pāramitās*. Now...
Established as the "Chapter on Universal Praise" (*Sarvastoṣaṇa-parivarta*). The reason this chapter exists is that it constitutes the fifth praise;

it is the final praise of the profound [teachings]. Regarding the practice of all practices, one reaches the other shore; therefore, they are all called *pāramitās*. This chapter consists of ninety phrases, divided into four sections:
first, praise through the teaching of the Dharma; second, praise through parables; third, praise by way of transcendence; and fourth, praise by way of attaining the gate.

Regarding the first seventeen phrases of the praise, some say that Subhūti praises those who have "crossed the shallow," while others say he now offers a praise of "universal pervasiveness" (*aparyanta*).
This meaning is like the three praises in the *Kusuma-vyūha* (Flower-Sprinkling) chapter, which treat both the "reception" (*pratigraha*) and the "immeasurable and boundless.

Below, the Master of the Treatise says: "The Buddha above praised from the perspective of the 'precious jewel' gate; Subhūti praised from the perspective of 'extensive explanation'; now [the praise] is extensive."

Because of praising *prajñā*, there are ninety phrases regarding "boundlessness. To praise *prajñā* as being boundless like the great ocean—these subsequent ninety phrases constitute the meaning of "boundlessness.
Furthermore, it is said that because all extremes, such as eternalism and nihilism, are completely severed, it is called "boundless.
The Buddha’s exposition also consists of ninety phrases; briefly explaining them in detail, they comprise four sets of four phrases. First, one must...
Subhūti once more praised the Buddha, citing [the teaching] as it is said:
"The perfection of coming from nowhere is eternally free from the meaning of coming; this is called 'pāramitā' (perfection). The Buddha said:
"'Non-existent' means that which is eternally free from going and coming; 'coming' is named pāramitā. Second, Subhūti [proceeds].

The conclusion praises the Buddha by returning to the root to describe it as follows: when there are no afflictions, the perfection (pāramitā) that eternally transcends afflictions is called a perfection.
The Buddha said: "A locus cannot be found; for the six sense faculties are the locus where afflictions arise, and thus they constitute the root.
Since even the root cannot be found, how much less so the branches? When both root and branches are eternally transcended, only then is it named 'perfection' (pāramitā). Thirdly, Subhūti...
Shallowly praising the Buddha and deeply describing him as being like a dream, the *Prajñāpāramitā* forever exhorts [the practitioner]...
as in the dream-like *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha’s profound depth is such that this dream cannot be apprehended; it forever exhorts one toward the crossing of emptiness.
Fourth, Subhūti praises the Buddha with the profound and describes him with the shallow, as when it says: "The *Prajñāpāramitā* has no further shore. The Buddha...
It is said that because there is no name and no body, the Buddha cites the "other shore" (pāra) to explain this; this is the exposition that establishes the meaning of "no other shore.
Since it is called the "other shore," one must understand what the other shore is; therefore, by citing the other shore, he establishes the meaning of "no other shore.

Fifth, Subhūti praises the Buddha with a single characteristic, and the Buddha answers with various [characteristics], as when he says: "The foundations of mindfulness are the *pāramitā* of the Buddha's four..."
That the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are unattainable is what is meant here; this brief statement of five aspects is still not exhaustive.

In the second line, Subhūti praises [the Dharma] from the perspective of *prajñā* (wisdom), exhorting that it is eternally unequalled. The Buddha cites all dharmas as being equal to *prajñā*, describing them according to the Dharma as being like the text itself.

In the third line, he praises from the perspective of detachment, meaning detachment from afflictions (*kleśa*); he cites ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) to show that it is not merely a detachment [from specific defilements].
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are also called "ultimate" because they are detached from all phenomena. Fourth is the "Gate of Non-Increase," which praises [the Bodhisattva] as follows:
although the Bodhisattva practices the aforementioned *pāramitās*, his mind has no attachment; because there are these two gates, others cannot destroy him, and thus it is called "indestructible.
Fifth is the "Gate of Forever Exhausting Both Banks," which praises the Buddha by describing him as being without name and without body.
Regarding this, some say: "The 'body of non-name' is refuted because it exists by virtue of the 'body of name.

Since the body of name does not exist, how could there be a body of non-name? Now, we say this is not so. Subhūti, in his profound praise of the Buddha, describes the "body of non-name" using shallow terms;
its name is "the other shore," as explained previously. Fifth, regarding the element of space and the inhalation and exhalation of breath...
One cannot apprehend inhalation and exhalation through the element of space; now, one realizes that inhalation and exhalation are like [empty] space, being non-existent.
(7) The seventh is the Ineffable Praise of the Buddha, which relies on the absence of vitarka and vicāra to describe awakening, for awakening is the source of speech.
(8) The eighth is the Nameless Praise: this refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); since *prajñā* is wisdom and "name" (*nāma*) is a designation, it is the Buddha.
Regarding the description of existence and non-existence, how could the four aggregates not be subsumed within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

The ninth [section] is the "Praise of Meritlessness," which uses the three seals (*tri-mudrā*) as the treasury of the Buddhas' Dharma across the three periods of time; gods and humans cannot alter this.
These are the three seals of Prajñā, which are also the two seals of non-abiding and non-attainment. When the Buddha replies that one "cannot rely" upon them, it means they cannot be brought forth.

Regarding "prostration" (*praṇāma*), that which cannot be fully extolled is perhaps said to mean that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) of the three periods of time are subject to exhaustion and cessation.

Now, seeking the exhaustion and cessation of the three periods of time means that while all conditioned phenomena of the three periods of time are subject to extinction, one cannot find such exhaustion and cessation within them.
Regarding "not making prostrations," there are two kinds of "making": first, a sentient being makes [actions] such as good or evil; second, there is no [such action].

Regarding the dharma of phenomena acting like fire burning or water rotting, those who do not respond with praise attain the eye of wisdom and do not see any sentient beings passing from this life to a future life.
Next, regarding "not losing" praise: "not losing" means not being in contradiction or failure;
it means causing all dharmas not to contradict or fail to realize their true nature (*dharmatā*).
In the second simile, "Like a dream," there are five phrases praising Subhūti. The first phrase praises him by means of the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*):
that which cannot be apprehended therein is the eternal cessation of both the unreal and the real. The remaining four phrases all praise Subhūti by means of the [metaphor].
Because the basis of the metaphor is empty, the metaphor itself is also empty. "Shadow" (*chāyā*) has the meaning of an "elephant" (*hastin*). This is because of the elephant...
Taking the mirror surface as real and the flame as unreal; taking wind, dust, sunlight, and moonlight as real and illusions as unreal;
and taking magical arts as real—whereas that which is real is the root, and if the root itself is empty, how much more so the branches?
Regarding "Stainless" (vimala) at the beginning of the third section: it is praised from the perspective of being free from faults because afflictions (*kleśa*) are fundamentally pure;

thus, it is "stainless. Because the three poisons cannot defile it, it is called "undefiled. The Buddha’s answer states that the locus [of these] is unattainable; since the locus where the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) produce afflictions—the place of their arising—does not exist, that which is produced also does not exist.
Next is the praise of mindfulness (*smṛti*); "mindfulness" refers to the removal through recollection, thought, and contemplation. Next is "non-existence" (*anupalambha*).

Regarding "unshakeable by praise," this means that for a Bodhisattva abiding in the *dharmatā*, no disputants can overcome them, no fetters (*saṃyojana*) can obscure them, and when impermanence arrives, their mind is not grieved; thus, they cannot be moved by these three conditions.

Next, regarding "unstained by praise," it means that they are not merely unstained by craving, but even all views based on grasping at attainments—which are all false understandings—cannot stain them.

Next, regarding "not giving rise to praise," Subhūti spoke of not giving rise to karma for future lives. The Buddha answered that those who lack conceptualization and discrimination (*vikalpa*) are free from it;

since the three poisons arise from conceptualization and discrimination, when the three poisons exist, there is karma, and karma is precisely the body. [Subhūti] answered according to the fundamental principle.

Next, regarding "quiescent detachment," this refers to the extinction of the fire of the three poisons. The Buddha answered that it is not merely the extinction of the fires of the three poisons, but also the one [fire].
The fact that the characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended is a brief praise that summarizes extensive matters.

Regarding the praise for being "without afflictions" (*niḥkleśa*), it refers specifically to the initial praise of the time when one attains non-arising (*anutpāda*), at which point afflictions are extinguished. When the Buddha answers based on the fundamental severance, he states that even the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) of the root is itself empty, let alone the afflictions.
Next, regarding the severance of the *pāramitās*, Subhūti speaks of severing contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), to which the Buddha provides an extensive answer.
Because [the marks] emerge from □□□□□□□□, they are severed. Next, regarding "not destroying" (abheda): not destroying conventional designations means that there is the true nature (dharmatā).
This is because they are inseparable; it is "not destroying" in the sense that the true characteristics of all phenomena are not destroyed. They truly possess these characteristics.
Regarding the "Impermanence Pāramitā," section four, the "Gate of Attainment": the Northern scholars divide this into three parts.

Now, as for the preceding [section], what is the intention behind its being an observation of cessation (*nirodha-vipaśyanā*)? For what reason is it not [an observation of] conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*)? The same objection applies to the subsequent [sections].

It is appropriate that Master Chi should summarize these according to the major categories and enumerations (as detailed in the commentary). Now, [this section] is divided into two: first, praising how conditioned activity is not established; second, praising the absence of fruit.
The perfection of impermanence that is not [characterized by] dissatisfaction is not the impermanence found through the Sāṃkhya school’s attainment of something;
this is the impermanence of nihilistic non-existence (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Because there is neither this shore nor the other shore, it is not a "perfection" (*pāramitā*).

What is now called its "impermanence" clarifies that there is no permanence; it does not mean that there is impermanence. Therefore, forever avoiding the two extremes is the meaning of "crossing over."
Furthermore, the Master previously stated that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is eternal, whereas he now states that the *pāramitās* are impermanent.

This means that the object of focus (*ālambana*) of the *pāramitās* is the *dharmatā*, which is eternal, while the subject that focuses upon it (*ālambaka*) is impermanent; this is explained from one perspective.
However, Prajñā possesses the functions of being both eternal and impermanent, as well as being neither eternal nor impermanent, and so forth. [This applies to] the *smṛtyupasthāna-pāramitā*.
The Buddha Maitreya replied: "Since body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*) are unattainable, how could there be the four [marks] such as suffering and impermanence?

To observe through such conditions until they are eternally stilled is the meaning of 'crossing over' (*tīrṇa*). This is precisely when the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) arise. Therefore, all masters hold that what is neither condition (*pratyaya*) nor observation (*vipaśyanā*) is called *pāramitā*.
Regarding the term 'perfection' (*pāramitā*), the treatise asks: 'Is it by citing the dharma of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) that one praises *prajñā*? "

If one asks how it is that Prajñā is praised, there are two aspects of Prajñā: first, when the five perfections (pañca-pāramitā) act in concert, they can sever or level all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
this is the Prajñā of wisdom. Second, because the Buddha’s deluded wisdom is unattainable, this is the Prajñā of constancy;
for this reason, the "constant Prajñā" is raised up as the object of praise. Thus, it is said that Prajñā is the answer. Prajñā...

Furthermore, these twenty thousand virtues should also be understood by analogy with this principle. If one praises the planting of *dāna* (giving) using the *dāna* of impermanence to praise the *dāna* of permanence—wherein the color [of the gift] is free from stinginess and constitutes the permanence of non-giving—this is likewise the two aspects of *prajñā*: essence and function.
From "The Ten Powers" (*daśabala*) downward is the second section, the Virtues of the Fruit. By practicing *prajñā*, the Bodhisattva assists in attaining the ten [powers] of a Bodhisattva.

Regarding the statement that "after the powers, one attains the ten powers," as for those who do not understand the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths), the treatise says: "The *mārgajñatā* is the beginning of practice.

This means that the Bodhisattva employs the beginning of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. [An objection is raised: "If this is now praising the fruit-virtues (*phalaguṇa*), how can the Bodhisattva’s *mārgajñatā* be the beginning of the Dharma? [The response is:
Because one realizes that what was previously attained through delusion was merely a semblance of fearlessness within the causal stage; thus, the *mārgajñatā* is indeed the beginning of the Dharma.

The meaning of the discourse from cause to fruit regarding the fearlessness of attaining the fruition later and the Buddha’s initial [attainment] is as follows: speaking according to reality is called the Tathāgata;

knowing according to reality is also called "speaking as it is. Regarding one's own lineage (*svagotra*), how could this world-cause further mean that one becomes a Buddha by means of one's own personal nature?
As for the *pāramitās* of the Buddha-dharma, because a bodhisattva practices *prajñā*, they are able to accumulate them.
The Buddha’s ten powers, fearlessnesses, four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and other such Buddha-dharmas transcend all phenomena;
these are the dharmas of the stage of fruition that surpass even the bodhisattvas.
*Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Seven.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Eight, composed by Hu Jizang.
Chapter Forty-five: On Hearing and Retaining.

Prior to following the Master of the Treatise, the three preceding cycles of exposition have been completed; now follows the fourth, the extensive exposition. This "extensive exposition" has two meanings:
first, because the meaning clarified in the previous three cycles was not yet exhaustive, it is now further elucidated, and thus this is an expansion upon those three cycles;
second, while the previous three cycles have already provided clarification, they did so only briefly, whereas here it is explained extensively. Regarding these four [cycles]:
The thirteen chapters are divided into two sections: the first twenty clarify *real wisdom* (prajñā), while the subsequent twenty-three clarify *expedient wisdom* (upāya).

It is also said that the first twenty chapters extensively explain the meaning of the correspondence and non-correspondence between superior practice and its non-practice, whereas the latter twenty chapters extensively explain the meaning of the capacity and incapacity of the universal efficacy of merit.
Furthermore, it is said that the first section clarifies the essence (*tattva*), while the second section clarifies [the function].

This work consists of twenty chapters: the first chapter is general, while the subsequent nineteen follow in sequence. Now, according to the treatise, the preceding five chapters praise the Dharma and explain *prajñā*;
the current half-chapter praises the person and praises the practice of *prajñā*. The "person" here refers to the one who explains *prajñā*.

Although the preceding sections praised the Dharma, it was not that there was no person; although this section praises the person, it is not that there is no Dharma. This is explained from the perspective of what predominates.

In the first part of this chapter, there are two sections: first, praising the person; second, exhorting to practice. Within the first section, there are three parts: first, clarifying the virtues of the person of clear faith; second, clarifying the losses of the person who lacks faith;

third, the Lord of Devas revering the Prajñāpāramitā to complete the praise of the person. The praise of the person begins with the praise of the practitioner of shallow capacity, followed by the praise of the practitioner of deep capacity.
The reason for praising the superior is that hearing the superior brings auspiciousness; this auspiciousness is expressed through a hundred phrases of praise.

Because the Buddha of Prajñā establishes his praise upon the profound principle, he speaks with joy, saying: "If there be one who hears this Dharma, they must have long cultivated the three multitudes.
An ancient said: "The 'Direct-to-the-Ear' chapter [means] that what passes through the ear must be due to having long cultivated roots of goodness.
This refers to praising those who hear and uphold it; how much more so for those who receive and maintain it—this is the second section.

There are nine individuals in total who are praised for being profound practitioners. The first seven are praised collectively for having received and upheld [the teaching], practicing according to what was taught.

The eighth is praised for being able to listen and receive it, practicing according to what was taught, and engaging in questions and answers. The praise for the tenth person begins with "Hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, they are not startled or terrified";
these ten all represent praises based on citing past causes. From the passage beginning "Śāriputra addressed the Buddha" onwards is the second section.
The disciple’s praise is a comprehensive praise of ten persons; it praises the virtues of two lifetimes by citing them as they appear, such as in the case of Vīra.
Why is this? Because the following section cites past causes to explain the praise of present virtues.
“World-Honored One, if one disparages faith,” etc. This second section clarifies that those who lack faith lose [their spiritual vision].

It is explained that because those who lacked eyes in previous lives were rebuked, it is proven that those who possess faith must necessarily have eyes. Question: Since they disparaged [the truth] in their previous lives, they should have followed along into the evil realms;
why then is it said that they obtain [eyes] again in this present life? Answer: This is discussed from the perspective of the beginning and the end. First...

If one slanders [the Dharma] in this life, one will receive both primary and secondary retributions. The primary retribution is that of Avīci Hell; the secondary retribution consists of other forms of animal existence and so forth.
After these two types of retribution are exhausted, the human body resumes once more. Having slandered it again, one undergoes suffering as before.

Therefore, the profound precepts must not be violated. A second interpretation states: because the karma of the previous life’s slander was not yet deep, the retribution has not yet been fully received; there remains residual merit.

Because their merit has ripened, they receive human bodies; thus they are "destroyed" [by the karmic retribution]. A third interpretation states: the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) necessarily take effect in the next life, whereas other offenses are not fixed;
they may take effect in the next life or in a subsequent life.
At that time, [the commentary] on the third section, "Revering Prajñāpāramitā," is divided into two parts concerning the personification of this reverence.
First, it describes Śāriputra’s disparagement to clarify that since he lacked the causal conditions for practice, his lack of faith is not to be wondered at.
Second, it reveres Prajñāpāramitā to form a praise, describing Śāriputra’s faithful understanding according to the text.

The Buddha spoke: Regarding the second section below, concerning the contemplation of cultivation, some interpret it as follows: from this point onward begins the fourth major section, the "Extensive Exposition" (*vistara-nirdeśa*).
From the beginning of this chapter up to the preceding five chapters was the "Praise of the Person" (*pudgala-stuti*), which praised the Dharma in contrast to those five chapters.

How do we know this is the "Extensive Exposition"? Because it further contemplates learning and further clarifies the practice of the meaning of *prajñā*; how does this differ from the contemplation and learning in the "Introductory Chapter" (*nidāna-parivarta*)?
Is this the meaning of practicing and cultivating? Although it has been explained extensively, there is no further praise for the assembly;

rather, because the gods have dull faculties and cannot be enlightened by a single word, it is repeated for their sake. It is like pointing at one's palm to bring about awakening. Within this, three sets of three are further opened:
the first set consists of (1) contemplation, (2) abiding, and (3) cultivation; the second set consists of (1) extensive matters and (2) the Buddha’s protection.
Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), after the accomplishment of merit, there are superior, middling, and inferior practitioners of the wisdom of the three knowledges (*traividyā-prajñā*).

Now, the preceding [section] differs from this; the present explanation proceeds from the second section, which has three parts: first, the beginner’s cultivation; second, the question on cultivation; and third, the answer. Within the first of these two [parts], there is (1) the description of accomplishment and (2) the actual contemplation. Question:

Since the *Sūtra on Exhorting Study* (the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*) in the introductory chapter already taught contemplation, why is it contemplated again here? Answer: It is because one wishes to describe...
This concludes the praise of the Lord of Devas. The Lord of Devas said: "To pay homage to Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to the Omniscient One. The Commentary explains:
Because Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to omniscience, this is paying homage to the Omniscient One. Since it gives birth to omniscience, it gives birth to all virtues;
therefore, those who wish to attain all [virtues] must study Prajñāpāramitā. Next, the Lord of Devas asked two questions regarding the cultivation of the Middle Way.

Regarding the inquiry into the "abiding" (*sthiti*) within the section on practice (*śikṣā*), as for the question of the difference between abiding and change: in the inquiry into practice, one should ask only about the practice of Prajñāpāramitā and not other practices;
the inquiry into the section on abiding is likewise. Now, the inquiry concerns the abiding of all formations (*sarva-saṃskāra*). As for the reason for inquiring into all practices:
since the Buddha has already stated that Prajñā gives birth to all formations, we now inquire into all of them. First.
Among the three responses, there are three parts: first, the response to the question; second, the praise of the person by means of the two bodies; third, Subhūti’s praise of the person.
Regarding the first, the response to the question clarifies that the person who practices the Dharma is one who takes up these segments as the Dharma they practice.
This response to the question has two parts: first, the direct answer; second, the reiterated explanation. The reiterated explanation answers the two questions collectively by means of non-abiding.
While it is said that "all dharmas are practiced for the sake of prajñā," one should also say that "one does not practice any dharma in order to abide in prajñā.
Furthermore, below this, the second [point] is that because this meaning is difficult to understand, the Master of the Treatise further explains the conditions of non-practice;
that is, "not practicing form" is what is meant by "practicing," clarifying that ultimate non-practice is precisely the sublime practice. One should also say "ultimate... [and so forth].
Ultimately, to have no dwelling place is precisely to dwell in *prajñā*. Question: For what reason does one not practice with regard to form (*rūpa*)? Answer:
Form is characterized by resistance, existence, impermanence, and so forth; these increase various views. Now, because one does not practice such views, it is called "practicing with regard to form.
Question: One should therefore be practicing *prajñā*; why is this called practicing with regard to form? Answer: It is precisely through this that one realizes form.
This is called practicing *prajñā*. Furthermore, it means that when a bodhisattva practices right speech and right action, guarding body and mouth, this is called practicing form (*rūpa*).

Attachment to this body and mouth is what is now being moved toward and abandoned. Because one has attained [the notion of] a wholesome body and mouth, those who hold such views—such as those who maintain precepts based on the attainment of something—are correctly refuted.
Therefore, it says "not practicing" such body and mouth and form; only then is it called practicing form. This is because...
Guarding body and speech, the *Śīlapariśuddhinirdeśa* establishes the beginning of the precepts; this is the Prajñā-precept.
At that time, Śāriputra—this is the second section where Śāriputra praises those who practice the Dharma. Within this praise, there are two parts: first, praising the Dharma practiced by people;
second, praising the person who practices it. The first of these two consists of: (1) the direct praise, and (2) the resolution of doubts. This is the direct praise.

There are three praises and three expositions; first is the praise of the profound. Upon hearing the Buddha’s reply to the Lord of Devas—that there is no dwelling and no practice, yet this is precisely the practice of Prajñā and the deep entry into the wisdom of emptiness—Śāriputra was filled with joy and addressed the Buddha, saying that Prajñā is profoundly deep.

Because it is deep, it is difficult to fathom; because it is difficult to fathom, it is immeasurable. These three praises manifest the characteristics of its arising. Such is the intended meaning of the Buddha.
It is merely that the nature of form and so forth is profound; do not believe that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are themselves profound. Why is this?

It is because for ordinary beings, the ultimate truth and the true mark are themselves profound, whereas form and so forth are shallow; thus, one turns their mind away from them. Furthermore, what ordinary beings call "profound" actually becomes shallow.
For instance, when it is said that the ultimate truth and the true mark transcend language and cut off the workings of the mind, in the end there remains this [notion of profundity].
Since principle (*li*) is something that can be apprehended, it is what is called "shallow";

as for the so-called "form" (*rūpa*), it is "shallow" only in the sense that one does not see its traces or location, and thus it cannot be apprehended, which conversely makes it "deep. "Universally" (*pu*) is a term used according to conditions;
how could there ever be such fixed characteristics of shallow or deep to be found?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “One cannot attain the profound. This is the second [section] explaining the removal of doubts. At that time, the assembly and Śāriputra harbored these doubts:
“Since the *prajñā* is so profound as to be difficult to fathom, how can a bodhisattva attain it?
