The first two employ these seven meanings, and the same applies to those that follow, though they are abbreviated below. As for the "immeasurable mind," it refers to the four immeasurable minds;

it is also called the "immeasurable mind" because it takes as its object the immeasurable dharmas of *nirvāṇa*. As for the "unobservable mind," it is that which practitioners of seated meditation [perceive] regarding the mind.
Because it is seen as a flaw within a pure pearl, it is now clarified that the mind cannot be seen;
one merely knows this "unseeable" mind. As for the statement below that "the five eyes do not see the mind": the two eyes of heaven and flesh see only form and do not see the mind;
the wisdom-eye sees nirvana and yet does not see the mind; the dharma-eye enters into the true reality (dharmatā) and does not see the mind; and the buddha-eye is likewise.

Furthermore, regarding the second general explanation of appearance and disappearance, contraction and extension: the four minds are explained as three by way of a heading, an explanation, and a conclusion.

The reason for this general explanation of these four minds is that they correspond to the eight superior minds calculated by the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), which are included within these fourteen [minds].
The four positions of permanence and impermanence constitute the first four extremes; adding the four of finitude and infinitude, as well as identity and difference, makes ten;

with the four such as "coming from" (the four regarding the Tathāgata), they total fourteen—these are the fourteen difficult questions (*caturdaśa-durvacana*). According to Master Chi, the initial pair of permanence and impermanence refers to views concerning the past;

finitude and infinitude refer to views concerning the present; identity and difference pertain to all three periods of time; and "coming from" and "not coming from" refer to views concerning the future.

Now, it is said that this interpretation is a great error; one does not recognize the Sūtras or the Mahā-śāstra, nor does one understand the meanings of the Madhyamaka-śāstra regarding the Great and Small Vehicles, the heterodox and the orthodox, and so forth.
Now, following the Master of the Treatise, these fourteen [views] are divided into two sections:
ten views collectively clarify the essence of views, while the subsequent four views specifically clarify the views of the future. The collective clarification of the essence of views is twofold.

First, the eight [types of] views; second, the view of the essence (*tattva*); third, the two views of identity and difference; fourth, the view of clarity (*prakāśa*); fifth, the view of equality (*samatā*). Question: How are these ten views the essence of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*)? Answer:
Because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive of the essence of the self (*ātman*) as being either permanent or impermanent, and so forth, up to being finite or infinite;

and because they conceive of the self and the body as being identical or different, these constitute the essence of "view. Question: Regarding the ten views, what is the essence of the "view of clarity"? [Third: The view of the essence.

Regarding the question, "In the world, what is this calculation regarding the ages? the Master replied: "The calculation concerns the self (*ātman*) across all three ages—past, present, and future—as being either eternal or non-eternal;
it does not refer to each age individually. Why? Because one calculates that the self in the past was eternal or non-eternal, and likewise for the future and the present.
The same applies to the finite and the infinite. [Question: "Does the essence of what is perceived not fall within the categories of eternal, non-eternal, finite, or infinite? [Answer: "It does not."

Why does [the text] further clarify "eternal" and "finite or infinite"? It is because being finite or infinite does not necessarily correspond to being eternal, and being eternal or infinite does not necessarily mean being non-eternal.
Their [heretical] calculation holds that the self (*ātman*) is one or two inches in size; this is "finite," yet they consider it "eternal.

The first four propositions calculate whether the substance of the self is eternal or non-eternal; the four views regarding "finite or infinite" calculate the size—whether large or small, broad or narrow—of the self. Thus they calculate.

Those who reckon the soul to be eternal maintain that the soul is one and the same throughout antiquity and the present; they practice giving and observe the precepts for the sake of supernatural transformations and the fruits of future lives.
Those who reckon it to be impermanent maintain that the soul perishes along with the body, practicing giving and observing the precepts merely for the sake of fame and profit in this present life.
Those who reckon it to be both eternal and impermanent maintain that there are two kinds of souls within a person: one coarse and one subtle; the subtle soul is eternal.
The coarse spirit appears to have activities; when the body dies, the coarse spirit immediately ceases. It is neither permanent nor impermanent.
If one views it as permanent, there would be no merit or demerit; if one views it as impermanent, it would decay and likewise lack merit or demerit.
Therefore, it cannot be said to be permanent, nor can it be said to be impermanent; yet, this spirit ultimately exists, as does the world.
Among these three kinds of worlds, this is the world of the five aggregates and the physical realm; it also possesses the four views such as that of a *puruṣa* (self). Question:

Since the *puruṣa* cannot be found through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and furthermore, since there is no *puruṣa*, the six kinds of worlds would likewise be unfindable through the four propositions, and thus there should be no worlds either.
Answer: The Master of the Treatise says: This is not analogous to the case where the four propositions regarding the *puruṣa* are unfindable. It clarifies [the distinction].
The Self (Ātman) is indeed not found within the four propositions of being eternal, non-eternal, both, or neither in relation to the world;
yet it is not that the world does not exist. As it is said, for one who is blind, a rope is not a snake, yet this does not mean the rope is destroyed.

Regarding the claim that the Self has limits (antavat), some explain that "limit" (anta) signifies "beginning" (ādi). For instance, atoms, primordial matter (prakṛti), or Maheśvara are called "limits" because they are the beginnings of all things. Furthermore...

The soul (*ātman*) resides within the body like a mustard seed, a jujube fruit, or a span-long man; thus, when the soul is small, it possesses form (*rūpa-dharma*), and therefore it has physical form.
That which is "boundless" (*ananta*) is like space (*ākāśa*); therefore, it is boundless.

Because it can endure for a long time and seek out suffering and pleasure, it is both bounded and boundless. Regarding these two interpretations, one says: the soul is boundless, while the realm (*deśa*) is bounded.

Therefore, it is said that there are two interpretations regarding both "finite" and "infinite": one interpretation holds that the *ātman* (spirit) is finite while the realm (*dhātu*) is infinite, as explained above.
As for those who do not hold it to be infinite, they perceive the two aforementioned faults and ultimately maintain that the *ātman* exists.

Regarding the four propositions concerning the realm, there are two interpretations of the proposition regarding the *ātman*: one interpretation states that it is finite above and below, but infinite in the eight directions.
Regarding "the zenith and nadir are boundless while the eight directions are both bounded and boundless": as for "boundless," it is argued that if there were boundaries, there would be a beginning;
having a beginning implies the absence of a cause, which would subvert the path to *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the land is boundless.

Regarding "both bounded and boundless," this refers collectively to the two preceding points: because the zenith and nadir are bounded while the eight directions are boundless, [the whole] is therefore boundless.
Because it is seen above as well, it is neither finite nor infinite. As for the claim that "the body is the self," upon analyzing this body and the self, neither can be apprehended;
therefore, one knows they are identical. Furthermore, since the experiencing of suffering and pleasure belongs entirely to the body, they are likewise identical.

As for the view that "the body and [the self] are different," applying this to the five sensory faculties, the attempt to apprehend them fails in the same way. This clarifies what the self is as perceived by ordinary people.

Because one perceives [the self], there is the view that the spirit (ātman) is distinct from the body. To claim that when the physical body perishes, the spirit perishes, or that the spirit is distinct from the body, or that the spirit perishes while the spirit is eternal—these are all extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The reason why the sixty-two views take annihilationism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*) as their basis is to demonstrate that their fundamental tenets deviate from the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). As for "going" and "not going," the Master [Nāgārjuna] refutes permanence and so forth.
This is stated generally because it concerns the essential matter of whether there is existence or non-existence in the present and future lives; it is explained specifically as follows:

"As one goes, so one comes to be born here; having gone, one reaches the next life, and the next life is likewise. Some say that what came from the previous life has no point of origin, and its cessation has no place to which it goes;
therefore, they say it is not like the body going away, for when the person ceases to exist, the spirit departs from the body.
Because the previous [position] was refuted by the same faults as "going" and "not going," it ultimately concludes that there is a "self" (ātman);

therefore, it is neither "going" nor "not going. Herein, the fourth of the four reckonings of the opponent’s views explains the faults of the third view—namely, "going like going" and "not going like going"—and concludes by clinging to the designations "non-action" and "neither going like going nor not going like going."
The two sets of two regarding "the self exists" constitute the views that "it is neither the Tathāgata nor not the Tathāgata"; these fourteen phrases, based on the five aggregates, total twenty-six.
The views of permanence and impermanence, based on the five aggregates, total twenty; the views of finitude and infinitude, based on the five aggregates, total twenty;
and the views of "the Tathāgata exists" and "the Tathāgata does not exist," also totaling twenty-six. The eleven [sets of] difference amount to sixty.

Regarding the two views: in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, both the "Examination of Nirvāṇa" and the "Examination of False Views" state that permanence and impermanence constitute the extremes of the past, while finitude and infinitude constitute the extremes of the future.
How does this differ from what is stated here? Answer: In the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, these are explained by distinguishing them according to the specific time periods.

Here, however, the extreme of permanence is presented both generally and specifically. Generally, it refers to the three time periods; specifically, it refers to whether [the world] goes on or does not go on.

To explain separately that the future possesses the meaning of the three times: just as "that which has gone" (gata) possesses the meaning of the three times by way of the future, so too "that which has gone" [from the future] and "that which is going" (gamyamāna) from the present to the subsequent world are called "that which has gone";

this statement encompasses the three times. The same applies to the following sentence. Question: Why does the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clarify [the nature of things] by way of the times? Answer: The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
To say, "I existed in the past" or "I did not exist in the past," constitutes the views of permanence and annihilation;

by this, one clarifies that if one holds the view that the present self existed fundamentally in the past, it is the view of permanence, whereas if one holds the view that the present self did not exist fundamentally in the past, it is the view of annihilation.

Thus, one establishes the views of annihilation and permanence based on the worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). Regarding the present self, one further engages in worldly discourse concerning finitude and infinitude. As for the future... [text ends].
If one holds the view of the infinite (*antānantika*) and does not posit a future, this is the view of finitude (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, regarding the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, how does this differ from the sūtras concerning whether there is a future limit or no future limit, and whether one goes or does not go? The answer is: "going" is the view of the infinite;
"not going" is the view of finitude. The same applies to both "going and not going," as well as "both finite and infinite. However—
Because the phrasing differs while the meaning is the same, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* merely speaks of "finite" and "infinite," without separately treating them like "gone" and "not gone.

Question: Since the Sūtra fully explains the eight propositions regarding permanence and the four propositions regarding "gone" and "not gone," why does the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* alone not further address "gone" and "not gone"?
Answer: This has already been explained previously; "gone" and "not gone" are [treated] just as [the other cases].

Since this [position] is already included within "finite" and "infinite," it need not be stated separately. Question: If that is so, since the Sūtra has already spoken of "finite" and "infinite," why does it further state "the Tathāgata exists after death" and "the Tathāgata does not exist after death"?

Answer: In the Sūtra, both the general and specific meanings are fully elucidated. Terms such as "eternal" and "finite" generally clarify the essence of the self (*ātman*) throughout the three periods of time.
"The Tathāgata exists after death" and "the Tathāgata does not exist after death" specifically clarify the future; these are intended to subsume [all possibilities] into one.
Because all [phenomena] are seen as neither emerging nor non-emerging, they are fully manifested.

Furthermore, from "The Buddha knows the suchness (tathatā) of form" onwards, the third section clearly demonstrates that both conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) are both the one suchness (eka-tathatā).
The reason this passage appears is that, having previously clarified the meaning of non-duality, it now opens up conventional truth and ultimate truth.
Since all meanings are the meaning of both-ness and non-duality, they are all the one suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, the arising of the aforementioned fourteen difficulties is due to ordinary people and non-Buddhists who do not recognize that all phenomena are the one suchness; thus, these fourteen false views arise.
The Buddha, however, understands that everything is the one suchness and that there are no fourteen views at all. As for all characteristics...
Regarding the meaning of the "suchness-character" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*): suchness is itself the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and its character is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

It is also said that it possesses the characteristics of both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing; this meaning is also present here. In the current text, the term "suchness-character" merely indicates the appearance or manifestation of suchness.

The first part of the second section, "Subhūti’s Statement," explains that all dharmas are realized as being identical to the nature of suchness (*tathatā*); because he has realized them as such, he is called the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he rejoices and extols the profundity of the *prajñā*, for it is through this that one is able to believe in it. The Buddha’s discourse follows the text accordingly.
Chapter Forty-nine: Inquiry into Characteristics.
From here below, the second section clarifies how the Buddha knows the grace of Prajñā and repays that grace. This chapter has three parts: first, it clarifies the characteristics of Prajñā;
second, it clarifies how the Buddha knows the grace of Prajñā and therefore repays it; third, it again clarifies how Prajñā can act as [the cause].
"Gratitude fulfilled" refers to the principle of repaying kindness.

This clarifies that within the characteristics of *prajñā*, there are questions and answers; because the subsequent questions are treated as a single unit, this section is titled "Chapter on the Characteristics of Questions.

The first four [sections] consist of: (1) the characteristics of the question, (2) the characteristics of the answer, (3) realization and understanding, and (4) the restatement and confirmation. These have already been clarified in various places above.

Regarding the question on the characteristics of *prajñā* now: as for the answer that they are identical, one interpretation states that this is because the assembly of devas gathered later had not yet heard [this teaching] and thus asked;

another interpretation states that although it is still the assembly of elders (*sthavira*), they ask because, while the preceding chapter clarified that *prajñā* can manifest the characteristics of the world, they do not yet know what those characteristics of *prajñā* specifically are.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for this: first, [the inquiry arises] from the various approaches discussed above.
The section on "Clarifying Prajñā" may discuss emptiness (*śūnyatā*), existence, or the karmic fruits of Prajñā;

it may clarify that the various devas—due to their dull faculties and inability to attain the fixed characteristics of Prajñā—are subject to praise or blame. Therefore, the intent of this inquiry is to clarify the characteristic of emptiness.

Thirdly, because Prajñā is profound and subtle, only a Buddha can exhaustively fathom its characteristics. Within the Buddha’s response, there are four parts; the first clarifies that Prajñā is non-existent.

First, it clarifies that both characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the meaning of what is taught through non-teaching (*anabhilāpya-abhilāpa*) are empty; second, it clarifies that both the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) and the meaning of what is taught through non-teaching are empty;
third, it clarifies that there is no luminosity, for luminosity cannot be conceptualized; fourth, it clarifies that there are no characteristics, for they are not produced by volitional activity.

The first point is as stated in the text. Regarding the conventional, the second point clarifies that there is no teaching through non-teaching. The devas then raised a doubt, saying: "If there are no characteristics, then there should be no teaching; therefore, the Buddha must surely exist."

Because they are characteristics, it is now clarified that since characteristics are non-existent, they cannot be described; yet, in accordance with worldly convention, one forcibly employs names and characteristics within that which is devoid of them to speak of "characteristics.
Herein, regarding the explanation of the two truths, there are four permutations concerning the two truths. Question:

When speaking of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), does one speak only of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) or also of the ultimate truth? Answer: One speaks [of both]. Regarding what can be spoken, one speaks [of both].
If one speaks, it is speaking of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); if one speaks of the unspeakable, it is speaking of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Question: Since the ultimate truth is unspeakable, how can it be spoken of? Answer: Others say it is "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

Now, it is explained that while the ultimate truth is what is spoken of, conventional truth is what is not spoken of; yet even this "not speaking" is itself the speaking of the ultimate. It is neither speaking nor non-speaking.
Because it is taught that what is spoken of according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) cannot be spoken of.

O Sons of Heaven, regarding these various marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the second section clarifies that this markless mark (*alakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is indestructible. The statement that humans and devas are themselves "marks" explains their indestructibility;
it clarifies that because humans and devas are ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnya*), they are the mark of Prajñāpāramitā, and thus [to destroy them] would be to destroy Prajñāpāramitā itself.

Those who cannot perceive false characteristics do so because they clearly understand that the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) are all non-existent; thus, there is nothing that can be characterized or refuted.
What is called "knowing the knower" means knowing that dharmas are clarified as being without objects and without persons; by clarifying these three, the four propositions do not exist.

Since that person is the very characteristic of *prajñā*, they cannot be characterized or refuted. Only those who are not the characteristic of *prajñā*—namely, gods and humans—can characterize and refute one another.
If this characteristic cannot be found when sought, how can there be a "non-existence" that seeks to destroy Prajñā?

Even if one were to later establish it as a non-characteristic, it still could not destroy the characteristic of Prajñā. It is like a blind man who does not see a wish-fulfilling jewel and says in his mouth, "It is not a jewel";
can the jewel truly be made non-existent by such words? This concludes the third section, clarifying that because Prajñā is unarisen, it cannot be destroyed; this is the refutation.
Explaining the meaning of "capable of being destroyed": Suppose someone asks about the characteristics of space (*ākāśa*).

To explain this, it is said that [space] is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), not with outflows (*sāsrava*), not without outflows (*anāsrava*), not non-existent, and so forth. If there were any characteristic, then it would be conditioned, unconditioned, with outflows, or without outflows.
It is precisely because there is not even a hair’s breadth of a characteristic that it is subject to these hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). Furthermore, if there were any characteristic, then...
"It can be made" is due to the fact that there are no marks; "it cannot be made" also explains the aforementioned "it cannot be made.

Regarding the statement that "whether a Buddha exists or not, the nature and marks are eternally abiding," a doubt arises: "If it cannot be made into a Buddha, then one should be unable to speak of Prajñā.
Since the Buddha now speaks of the marks of Prajñā for the sake of sentient beings, this is because the Buddha has produced the marks of Prajñā. To resolve this, it is said: "It exists."

The Buddha possesses no mark of "Buddha-nature" (buddhadhātu); since the Buddha is eternally abiding, how could he have created [it]? Third, the various devas attain realization; fourth, the Buddha’s exposition is as stated in the text.
From "Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas" onwards is the second section, which clarifies that because the Buddha knows the kindness of Prajñā, he repays that kindness.
Recognizing kindness is the most serious among unwholesome wrong views, whereas knowing gratitude is the supreme among worldly wholesome dharmas; therefore, one must repay kindness.
Furthermore, the gods may doubt that the Prajñāpāramitā lacks any mark of superiority and thus cannot be attained, wondering why it should be revered.

Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms; since he himself reveres the Prajñāpāramitā, how much more so should others? Third, there is the doubt that the Buddha’s mind is devoid of [conceptualization].
Question: For what reason is that which is clung to cherished and revered? Answer: It is not because there is clinging that Prajñāpāramitā is cherished and revered;

rather, it is because one deeply knows that Prajñāpāramitā can extinguish conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and can open the way for the Three Vehicles. Therefore, one cherishes and reveres all dharmas as being characterized by non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Regarding this passage, it harmonizes with other sūtras. In those other sūtras, the Buddha does not act; furthermore, the preceding text states that the Buddha knows both action and the agent.

Because these two [statements] appear contradictory, this section now clarifies them. Other sutras state that "one who does not create a person has no mark of a person," which is why it says "one who does not create a person.
This does not mean that one does not create a person because of being ungrateful;

rather, it means that other sutras clarify that the Buddha is naturally a person, whereas here it is said that the Buddha takes Prajñā as his teacher. To resolve this apparent contradiction, this treatise is now explained. Now, the treatise clarifies...
One should not provide an explanation in this manner, as was clarified above.

Furthermore, the Buddha attains all dharmas by means of *prajñā* and does not give rise to [dualistic] births; this third section further clarifies how *prajñā* bestows grace, thereby fulfilling the meaning of repaying that kindness.
Having already explained the "Mother of the World" chapter above, if this is so, then regarding the characteristics of the world and the present...
How does this differ from the previous response? It clarifies the "Manifesting" and "Revealing the Correct" aspects in contrast to the "Manifesting the Vehicle.

Regarding "Manifesting," it refers to the ninety-six non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) which do not manifest the fourteen principles such as permanence and impermanence; Prajñā does not manifest such meanings.

Regarding "Revealing the Correct Vehicle," it reveals that the five aggregates are neither arising nor ceasing, and that they are all one, just as in this present chapter; it merely clarifies and reveals the correct vehicle.

Therefore, from the subsequent form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), these dharmas are shown to begin with non-arising and end with solitary emptiness (*pratyekasūnyatā*).
The sequence of the text follows from cultivation: first, it clarifies the causes and conditions of the Buddha; if one attains the non-arising *prajñāpāramitā*, one can give birth to the Buddha.
Thus we know that if there is the birth of a Buddha, it is a "non-birth" that gives birth to the Buddha, and the Buddha abides in *prajñāpāramitā*, which is non-existence.
"Stop, stop! Subhūti," he said to the Buddha, "there is no one who knows. This praises the meaning of the Buddha’s vehicle of Prajñā: that among all phenomena there is no knower.
How could Prajñā alone have something known? The Buddha answered: "The former clarifies that because all persons and phenomena are unobtainable, there is nothing known;
therefore, there is nothing not known. Below, it clarifies not riding upon form; this clarifies non-existence.
Regarding that which is mounted upon and that which is not mounted: how can you say there is nothing that cannot be shown? If there is something shown, could it not be a non-showing?

Furthermore, as for the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the world, the meaning of "showing" was previously established; now, for the first time, the actual meaning of showing is clearly demonstrated.
From the five aggregates up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are all termed "the world" because they are known to be conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That which is called "knowledge of the world" (*loka-jñāna*) knows that all these things are empty; therefore, it is called the "supramundane ultimate truth" (*lokottara-paramārtha*).

Regarding the knowledge that the world is empty and the study of the emptiness of the world, people say that because beings are attached to phenomena (*dharma*), the *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught to show that the world is empty, yet this does not mean that all phenomena are actually empty.
Now, it is clarified that the Buddha truly knows that all phenomena are empty, and thus speaks of emptiness.
Regarding those who contemplate, awaken to, and discern emptiness: the Buddha did not hear from others externally that the world is empty.
Because he spoke of emptiness with his mouth while internally contemplating, reflecting, and investigating it with his mind, he taught it as emptiness.

Since the inconceivable and clear assemblies all take the manifestation of worldly emptiness as an understanding of emptiness itself, it is now clarified that the world is neither ever-empty nor non-empty.
Because it is [the nature of] permanence and impermanence and so forth, it is inconceivable. Because the Buddha is inconceivable, he is free from all views; this freedom is called "detachment.
Because he is detached from all views, he transcends language and severs the activities of the mind; therefore, he is called "nirvāṇa" (quiescence).
Because he is quiescent, there is ultimately nothing remaining; therefore, it is called "ultimate. This is the original suchness of the Tathāgata; it is not a negation.

Because of the Dharma, one clarifies that its nature is empty; because this emptiness of nature means that even the absence of dharmas is empty, next comes the emptiness of non-dharmas (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).

Since both the empty and the existent dharmas are empty, next comes the emptiness of existent dharmas (*bhāva-śūnyatā*). Because all eighteen kinds of emptiness are mutually dependent, they are called "empty.

This [emptiness of non-dharmas] is an existent dharma that can be emptied; it is called a "cause" (*hetu*) because it serves as a basis. Now, this [emptiness of emptiness] alone is without dependence, being neither empty nor not empty; therefore, it is called "empty."
Question: Emptiness does not depend on emptiness, nor does it depend on non-emptiness. When one asks about neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, there is purely emptiness;

this emptiness of emptiness is itself dependent upon emptiness. How can this be called "independent"? Answer: Fundamentally, there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, so what is there to depend upon?

This is no different from the "emptiness of non-existence and existence" (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). In the emptiness of non-existence and existence, there is likewise neither emptiness nor non-existence.

The emptiness of non-existent dharmas is empty of this non-existence; the emptiness of existent dharmas is empty of this existence. Now, because there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, there is nothing upon which to depend. Question:
If it is called "solely empty" (*ekākīśūnyatā*) because this emptiness and non-emptiness were originally absent, then how does this differ from "intrinsic emptiness" (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*)?

If intrinsic emptiness clarifies that the intrinsic nature is empty, what is the difference? Answer: Intrinsic emptiness refers to the fact that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty. Now, since there are no dharmas, [that nature] is non-existent.
Question: Is it not that all dharmas are empty? If one speaks only of "emptiness alone," is there nothing further that is non-existent? Answer:

In the chapter on "Emptiness Alone," emptiness has the meaning of being free from dependence; it transcends everything. The hundred negations cannot negate it, and the hundred affirmations cannot affirm it.
It is neither that which can be affirmed nor that which can be negated; it is neither affirmation nor negation. Even the hundred negations do not negate it.

I do not know on what basis one forcibly designates it as "empty," yet names it "solely empty" (*ekākī-śūnya*). It is called "solely" because it is devoid of all companions. Question: How is this known? The treatise states: "This sole emptiness is also called *nirvāṇa* and the *dharmatā*. Is it not that which transcends the hundred negations and surpasses the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)? Question: [If you say it is] dependent, does it depend on something else, or is it non-dependent? Since it is not self-sufficient, it must be non-dependent. [Response: It is non-dependent. Because it is non-dependent, it is not established by anything else. Because it is not established by anything else, it is the ultimate reality. Because it is the ultimate reality, it is the true nature of all phenomena. Because it is the true nature of all phenomena, it is the source of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Because it is the source of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is the foundation of all teachings. Because it is the foundation of all teachings, it is the refuge for all sentient beings. Because it is the refuge for all sentient beings, it is the great compassion of the Tathāgata. Because it is the great compassion of the Tathāgata, it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Because it is the unconditioned, it is eternal. Because it is eternal, it is quiescent. Because it is quiescent, it is blissful. Because it is blissful, it is the supreme liberation. Because it is the supreme liberation, it is the ultimate goal. Because it is the ultimate goal, it is the end of suffering. Because it is the end of suffering, it is the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Because it is the cessation of all conceptual proliferation, it is the realm of the Tathāgata. Because it is the realm of the Tathāgata, it is the sphere of the Buddhas. Because it is the sphere of the Buddhas, it is the object of the Buddhas' wisdom. Because it is the object of the Buddhas' wisdom, it is the truth of the Buddhas. Because it is the truth of the Buddhas, it is the Dharma. Because it is the Dharma, it is the Sangha. Because it is the Sangha, it is the path. Because it is the path, it is the practice. Because it is the practice, it is the result. Because it is the result, it is the fulfillment. Because it is the fulfillment, it is the perfection. Because it is the perfection, it is the completion. Because it is the completion, it is the ultimate. Because it is the ultimate, it is the end. Because it is the end, it is the cessation. Because it is the cessation, it is the peace. Because it is the peace, it is the coolness. Because it is the coolness, it is the liberation. Because it is the liberation, it is the nirvana. Because it is the nirvana, it is the sole emptiness. Because it is the sole emptiness, it is the non-dual. Because it is the non-dual, it is the suchness (*tathatā*). Because it is the suchness, it is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Because it is the reality-limit, it is the signless (*animitta*). Because it is the signless, it is the wishless (*apraṇihita*). Because it is the wishless, it is the unconditioned. Because it is the unconditioned, it is the eternal. Because it is the eternal, it is the quiescent. Because it is the quiescent, it is the blissful. Because it is the blissful, it is the supreme liberation. Because it is the supreme liberation, it is the ultimate goal. Because it is the ultimate goal, it is the end of suffering. The Third Section: A Petition to the Buddha Regarding the Arising of Great Matters. This section praises *prajñā* for its ability to accomplish great matters. Since *prajñā* can give birth to a Buddha, is it not indeed a great matter?

This section consists of three parts: first, a praise from the perspective of the fruit; second, a praise from the perspective of the cause; and third, a general praise from the perspective of both person and dharma.
Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, praising *prajñā* for its ability to attain the supreme fruit; second, resolving doubts; and third... [text continues].
Regarding the removal of doubt through the path of cultivation, Subhūti first offers five praises because he has heard the Buddha speak on the characteristics of *prajñā* and thus joyfully extols it.

The Buddha recounts these five praises; together they constitute the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*), for within this all causes and effects are fully explained, and thus the words are worthy of being received.
Second, the *prajñā* of contemplative insight (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*) contains and receives [all things] by virtue of *prajñā*.

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are only established through *prajñā*; they are not established without it, for their establishment depends upon *prajñā*. This constitutes the sixth section.
The three [aspects of] true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) are contained within the realization of true reality; thus, all conditioned phenomena finally achieve completion.

The "King" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s activities, while the "land" is a metaphor for the transformation of sentient beings. This land is the realm where sentient beings are transformed; it is the place where sentient beings are transformed. This is due to *prajñā*.
If one is only able to transform sentient beings, yet those sentient beings are not transformed by means of *prajñā*, then transformation is not accomplished.

The meaning of the sutra is that just as state affairs are entrusted to great ministers, so too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) entrusted to *prajñā* to bring them to fulfillment; this is based on [the practice of] one's own cultivation.

"Not grasping, not clinging" is the second section, which raises the point of non-grasping and non-clinging to explain the inclusion and acceptance [of all things], because through *prajñā* there is nothing to be apprehended.
It is by grasping at [the teachings] that one is able to accomplish all practices; if there were grasping and attachment, how could one accomplish all practices?
"Grasping" (upādāna) means to take up; "deep attachment" refers to clinging. [Subhūti] asked: "If it is because of cultivation, then it need not be categorized [as a fault].

The Buddha’s recitation and praise of the three verses constitutes the "Repeated Praise," each returning to its original place. Regarding the first part, there is first the praise of the Dharma and the praise of the person.

As for the praise of the Dharma: from the point of the characteristics of the inquiry onwards, the devas have posed questions, and the Buddha has extensively praised Prajñāpāramitā as being able to accomplish the merit of the fruit and able to accomplish one's own practice;
thus he praises them together. The passage beginning with "One who can believe in this Prajñā" is the first [of the two] praises of the person.

The initial passage is a profound praise of the fact that the wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) of the Great Thousand and Small Thousandfold worlds, as well as of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, cannot equal even a single day’s practice of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation based on Prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this so? The following section explains why they cannot equal it: "The two practices of faith and dharma... up to the wisdom and abandonment of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas—this is the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This meaning is difficult to comprehend; since it is already stated to be the Bodhisattva’s [patience], [how can it be compared to the lower stages?]
If there were no distinction between superior and inferior regarding patience (*kṣānti*), then if such a distinction existed, it would not be correct;

yet now it is said that it is correct, which is why the matter of superiority and inferiority is difficult to resolve. As for "it is correct": both Bodhisattvas and the followers of the Two Vehicles contemplate non-arising (*anutpāda*), and thus they possess the wisdom of non-arising and have severed their afflictions (*kleśa*). Because they equally contemplate non-arising, it is said that it is correct.
Regarding the distinction between superior and inferior: the Bodhisattva’s non-arising is true wisdom (*prajñā*) and is also endowed with skillful means (*upāya*).
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles contemplate non-arising and possess only true wisdom, lacking skillful means; therefore, their wisdom is inferior.

Since they lack skillful means, they cannot transform into the state of the Two Vehicles, nor can they perfect true wisdom. Because the Bodhisattva possesses both skillful means and true wisdom, this very [wisdom] is itself true skillful means.

Therefore, although both the Bodhisattva and the two vehicles possess the name "existence," they differ in substance and wisdom. Furthermore, while the two vehicles contemplate non-arising, they lack great compassion;
the Bodhisattva, though contemplating non-arising, possesses compassion. While the two vehicles contemplate non-arising, they do not extensively cultivate the myriad practices;
the Bodhisattva’s mind of non-arising extensively cultivates the myriad practices, for all myriad practices are themselves non-arising.
Regarding the discussion of superiority and inferiority, it is further explained through another principle: the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas differ only in their beginning and end.

For the two vehicles, the beginning is the stage of *uṣmagata* (warmth) and the peak (*mūrdhan*), and the end is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). For the bodhisattvas, the beginning is the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*), and they proceed until reaching the Buddha-ground.
Since the end of the two vehicles is the beginning of the bodhisattvas, their superiority and inferiority are thus distinct. The Master said: "One must advance."

This immediately refutes the proponent’s own position because it contradicts the principle that "the non-different is different. Thus, while Bodhisattvas practice the contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpāda-aniruddha-vipaśyanā*), the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) practice the contemplation of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-vipaśyanā*). Since this distinction between their respective positions is not invalid, the Two Vehicles likewise practice the contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing, and Bodhisattvas do the same.

This refers to Prajñāpāramitā, which can extinguish great suffering and bestow great bliss, and furthermore, can universally uproot the great suffering of the six realms and bestow the great bliss of the six realms;

this is called a "great matter. Regarding the phrase "the arising of inconceivable matters," the following four praises all praise the inconceivable nature from the perspective of the Buddha’s fruition-merit—that is, these four dharmas. First, while sentient beings are long [immersed in delusion], the Tathāgata alone...
1. He is called a Buddha because he has awakened. 2. He has realized Prajñā just as the Buddhas of the past did; thus his name is Tathāgata, which is the same as that of all Buddhas in this land.

3. He is distinguished from the Śrāvakas by being spontaneous: while Śrāvakas attain awakening in the present through others, the Buddha attained awakening spontaneously in the present through causes cultivated in the past.
4. He is distinguished from the Pratyekabuddhas: Pratyekabuddhas likewise cultivated [the path] in the past...
Because one spontaneously awakens in the present to the fact that there is no "all-knowledge," it is through *prajñā* that one attains the four kinds of inconceivable names.
Regarding the arising of the inconceivable, there are three meanings for the arising of the unnameable:
first, because the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of *prajñā* is extremely profound and grave, whereas wisdom is light and thin; therefore, it cannot be [grasped] by light and thin wisdom.
1. It is called "profound" because it is a weighty Prajñā. 2. It is called "immeasurable" because its wisdom is vast and manifold, such that it cannot be measured even slightly.
3. It is called "immeasurable" because permanence and impermanence, emptiness and existence, cannot measure it; Prajñā is itself immeasurable.

Regarding "immeasurable," some say that "measuring" (*māna*) refers to calculation, while others say that "measuring" refers to grasping at signs (*nimitta*); since Prajñā cannot be grasped as a sign or as something to be attained, it is immeasurable.

It is also called "mind-measure" (*cittamātra*). Furthermore, the wisdom of these three types of persons—the ordinary worldlings, the followers of the two vehicles, and the bodhisattvas—is unable to measure the limits of *prajñā*.
This interpretation of *prajñā* indicates that it is not a cause. Regarding the term "unequaled" (*asama-sama*): among all phenomena, *nirvāṇa* is without equal;
because *prajñā* enables one to attain great *nirvāṇa*, it is equal to *nirvāṇa*. Second, [it refers to] the Buddha.
The power of the peerless *prajñā* among humans enables sentient beings to become equal to the Buddhas.
Subhūti said to the Buddha: "But [this applies] from the stage below the Buddha... This second explanation begins by addressing the doubts of beginners.
Beginners claim that only the four kinds of inconceivables are inconceivable, while all other dharmas are not; therefore, he uses the four dharmas of the fruition stage as an analogy for all things.
Because the Dharma is non-dual, one knows that there has never been cause and effect, nor have there ever been sentient beings or Buddhas.
This third doubt is removed. Regarding the realization of the Way, as explained in the text:

this chapter mostly clarifies inconceivable matters, and because those who hear them give rise to much faith and reverence, many laypeople attain the Way; for while the faculty of faith is strong in laypeople, their faculty of wisdom is weak.

Although there are many who attain the Way, it is only those who have attained the initial path who become renunciants; because their wisdom-characteristics (*prajñā-lakṣaṇa*) are strong, they attain Arhatship.
Discussing by way of gender, women attain the Way less frequently because their delusions are heavy, whereas men attain the Way more frequently because their delusions are light.

Fourth, herein it is not correctly stated that one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, in the Mahāyāna, those who attain the Way are few, while in the Hīnayāna, they are many.

The Path is manifold; furthermore, because the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is difficult to attain, it is rare, whereas the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is easy to attain, it is common.

Moreover, the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) pervades all four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), as these are the differing causes and conditions for awakening to the Path. Regarding those who can attain [enlightenment] during the Bhadrakalpa, there are two interpretations:

Regarding the phrase "going to other worlds," this should not be interpreted according to the previous explanation.

Chapter Fifty, "The Accomplishment" (*Sampadana-parivarta*), is titled as such because it praises the causal practices that accomplish Prajñā; this section consists of two parts, the first of which concerns Subhūti.
The previous praise of the two Buddhas was a response to the questions posed; why then is there now a further fivefold praise? It is because the Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep;

thus, there is no fault in praising it repeatedly. It is like a king who, upon hearing the parable of Śāriputra, hears it again and again without ever being satiated. Furthermore, the preceding praise extolled the Prajñāpāramitā as that which can bring about the merit of the fruition (phala-guṇa);
the present fivefold praise extols the Prajñāpāramitā as that which can accomplish one's own practice (sva-caryā), for its benefit is weighty.
Because it is beneficial, he sighs deeply once more.

In the Buddha’s exposition of the middle two [verses], there are first five praises based on the meaning of "containing" (*saṃgraha*), and second, an explanation of "containing" by citing non-attachment.
Regarding the first three—Dharma, analogy, and application—the *Śāstra* states: "One sūtra constitutes two types; the two vehicles are treated as one."

Regarding the two types of *śrāvakas*, one may also say that both are [the same]. However, the twelve *yānas* involve the contemplation of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), whereas the Great and Small Vehicles share the analogy of the non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpāda-aniruddha*) with the Bodhisattvas. If one type of *śrāvaka* is contrasted with another, when they are set against each other, it is said they possess the contemplation of arising and ceasing;
yet when they are granted [the higher perspective], it is said they practice the contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing. This is what the Buddha recounted.

The understanding is as stated in the text. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha; from here down through sixty-six chapters, three sections comprise thirty-five chapters which clarify the wondrous meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.
Four chapters clarify the preservation [of the teaching] herein; these fifty-five chapters and a half of the sutra collectively clarify that those who understand Prajñāpāramitā obtain [its benefits].
Regarding the subsequent discussion, the Master [Vasubandhu] retreats from the chapters to generate the three stages of exposition. First, it is said that when Prajñā is being taught, Māras arrive.

In the "Refutation of Prajñā," the first two sections clarify those who now clearly believe in and accept *prajñā*. These two sections clarify the dharma of *prajñā* and the fact that dharmas have both the heterodox and the orthodox;
the subtle meaning reveals the correct while setting aside the obstacles, which is to demonstrate the heterodox so that one may recognize the heterodox and the orthodox.

Therefore, regarding the belief in and acceptance of *prajñā*, since those who believe in *prajñā* must necessarily possess certain characteristics, it is necessary to clearly elucidate the marks of merit. Furthermore...

Above, the Prajñā was elucidated through the gate of dharmas; now, the Prajñā is explained through the gate of persons. Within the section on dharmas, both the heterodox and the orthodox are clarified.

Regarding the persons, the three superior types praise the person in two ways. From this point until the end of the "Non-attestation" chapter (*Aprativedha-parivarta*), Subhūti and the Bodhisattvas do not abandon any sentient beings;
this must be the eleventh chapter of the sūtra which correctly clarifies the three [aspects].
Chapter Two: The Characteristics of the Nature of the Faith of Persons of the Three Capacities. Following the "Non-Realization" chapter, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"I should not abandon all sentient beings. From the end of the "Emptiness" chapter downward, it clarifies exclusively the practice based on faith for persons of the three capacities.
The initial text is divided into two parts: first, this chapter briefly elucidates the merit of the faith of persons of the three capacities; second...

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that have not yet departed do not abide because they are illusory; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) do not abide either because they are shallow and devoid of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

If one can attain it by practicing form, then would one attain all dharmas by practicing?

Because the cessation of all views is called the Path, the assembly at that time attained awakening. The point at which the Buddha’s discourse on the Path for the assembly occurs can be understood from the text.
