The "Small" refers to the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*; because it is small and situated far [from the ultimate], it was subject to censure. However, as it is a person of expedient means (*upāya*), it is worthy of being entrusted.
"Accumulated" (*lei*) means to rely upon, to entrust, and to commission. The "Ten Teachings" (*shíjiào*) are precisely the teaching of the *prajñā* of the true aspect (*śūnyatā*).
This chapter is divided into two parts: first, because he is about to entrust [the Dharma], he first confirms and recounts what the two persons have said, showing that it does not violate the Dharma.
Section Two: Measuring and Revealing Superiority to Encourage Practice. This section consists of three parts: first, the seal of approval for the two individuals;
second, measuring and revealing superiority; and third, encouraging practice. This is the first part, which serves as a seal of approval for the Lord of Devas (Indra) and subsequently for Subhūti.
The reason the Lord of Devas speaks of himself is that he requests the Buddha’s seal of approval. As for why...

First, regarding those who request the printing: since the Lord of Devas (Indra) abides among the three vehicles and possesses only the lowest fruit among the fruits [of the path], his afflictions are not yet purified and his wisdom is not yet perfected;

therefore, it is possible that there may be errors. Second, within the assembly there are many *avaivartika* bodhisattvas, arhats whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*), and various devas free from desire;
they may doubt whether the Lord of Devas has truly attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and how he could possibly exhaust the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, he personally requests the Buddha to confirm his statement. From "Subhūti the bhikṣu" onwards is the second section, which praises what Subhūti has said;
that is, it constitutes the confirmation. In the Buddha’s narration, he merely recounts what [Subhūti] has understood, rather than confirming what he has said.
Since the praise for what was said has already been repeated several times above, [the Buddha] now merely recounts his internal realization—that is, his internal understanding.

Since the external words are profound and without error, this Bodhisattva wishes to proceed to the second stage of comparative evaluation, which is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the reason for attaining benefit;

herein, the comparison between the great and the small regarding the superiority or inferiority of their understanding is intended so that the eight hundred bhikṣus below may hear it, and though their [understanding] is small and inferior, they may attain realization through the superior greatness.
For this reason, and because one intends to entrust the *prajñāpāramitā*—which is the dharma of the bodhisattvas—it is necessary to manifest the bodhisattva’s profound understanding;

thus, one knows that *prajñāpāramitā* is a profound dharma. Furthermore, when people hear that *prajñā* is the wisdom of emptiness, they may claim there is no difference between the understanding of the Great and Small Vehicles;

therefore, it is necessary to distinguish them. Question: What is the difference between the two types of emptiness—the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—such that you speak of them?
The Śrāvakas do not equal the Bodhisattvas because the wisdom of the two vehicles is inferior, and thus their vision of emptiness is shallow;

the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas is profound, and thus their vision of emptiness is also profound. It is like a lamp illuminating objects: one cannot expect the objects to become clearly manifest through the lamp’s light alone.
Furthermore, the practice of the two vehicles is merely emptiness, whereas the Bodhisattva attains that which is not merely emptiness. Moreover, the two vehicles see only emptiness and do not see...

The Bodhisattva Amoghasiddhi perceives emptiness as both empty and non-empty. Furthermore, because the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) lack the support of emptiness and rely solely on the fixed state of existence, their emptiness is inferior.
The Bodhisattva, however, purifies the buddha-fields for the sake of sentient beings; by utilizing this emptiness to support existence, his emptiness is superior.

Moreover, the two vehicles lack the emptiness that is the very essence of the Middle Way; it is because of the Middle Way that there are provisional names, yet within the Middle Way, there is no [inherent] existence.
Thus, even by way of conventional designation, this is not lost. At that time, it rained flowers from the heavens.

Having heard of the supreme vows of the Bodhisattva’s practice, the second group who had attained benefit desired to practice them; as the flowers fell upon their robes, they immediately used them as offerings.

Because they made this internal offering of flowers, when they attain Buddhahood, their lands will always rain flowers. Due to the roots of goodness from past lives, these eight hundred people attained awakening simultaneously.
This is the Path.
Thus, following the third cause for Ānanda’s descent [from the heavens], it concludes that through practice one attains Great Bodhi.
Regarding the phrase "hearing [the Dharma] amidst death and birth among humans" and so forth: the previous sections on Rebirth and Faith and Slander have already been completed; now, once again...
The preceding section on "Accomplishment from Above," Chapter Fifteen, concludes the exposition on the characteristics of the three types of persons who clearly understand *prajñā*.
Now, as we are about to entrust [the teaching], it is further summarized: the eight hundred bhikṣus who have attained realization did not do so in isolation;
they came from among humans and devas. One should clearly understand that they practiced the six *pāramitās*; as for those who fear, it is said that they should simply practice them.
If one could attain liberation through the five perfections alone, what would be the use of Prajñā? Therefore, the present commentary explains:

although one practices the six perfections, if one does not exhaust the desire within the field of the Buddha, yet seeks the liberation of the three vehicles, this is a deluded practice; true practice is the thorough practice of the perfections.
Regarding the second section, "Entrusting You," which follows the preceding [section], it is correctly explained as being twofold: first, the entrustment for the circulation [of the teaching];

second, the circulation through practice. This is the first [part]. Regarding the ancient interpretation, it states: "The Prajñāpāramitā elucidated above is exhaustive and leaves nothing remaining; this is the entrustment. It further states:
"Because those present have already listened for a long time, they are weary and about to rise; therefore, [the Buddha] intends to stimulate their resolve."
Therefore, it is entrusted once again. The *Treatise* says: "Aside from the *Prajñāpāramitā*, losing the twelve divisions of the scriptures constitutes a minor offense;
however, if one loses the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the offense is great. Why is this so? It is because awakening to 'non-attainment' is itself the Way (*mārga*).
Thus, this scripture is precisely the scripture of the Way; if it is lost, there is no means by which one may enter the Way. For this reason, it is an offense."
Daya asked: "If that is so, then other sūtras should not lead to the realization of the Way. He replied:

"Those other sūtras that clarify how one attains awakening through non-reliance are all alternative names for Prajñāpāramitā. Within the text, four matters are raised to explain this: the loss and gain of great offenses.
First, if one receives and upholds it, one is receiving and upholding the Bodhi of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Second, if one makes offerings to it..."

This constitutes making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; thirdly, because one has faith and love for the Buddhas of the three periods, one must not lose this through negligence.
If a good man receives and upholds it, explains it to others, and practices it—this is the second [point], the propagation of the practice. Having already received it above...
Furthermore, it is maintained that this has not been forgotten and is now being circulated for those who have not yet heard it. The text is divided into four parts: first, exhorting others to speak;
second, resolving the doubts of the assembly; third, praising the absence of awakening; and fourth, manifesting the mark of the tongue to inspire faith in the great merits of Prajñāpāramitā.

This is the first discussion, which states that even if one were to teach three thousand great chiliocosms of sentient beings so that they attain Arhatship, such a person would be incapable of becoming a Buddha.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] does not understand how to teach others, nor does he possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), nor the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

He teaches the bodhisattvas that they should plant the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*). At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), the second doubt is resolved. The doubt is as follows:
"Since the Buddha is already free from attachment, why does he so earnestly entrust [the teaching] as if his mind were attached? To resolve this by citing an example, it says: "The four offenses."
There is nothing further to be seen, and that which my mind clings to is entirely due to my past vows and the compassion I have shown toward this world; thus, I entrust [this teaching] to you.
Furthermore, by citing these matters, it is shown that all things are ultimately pure and that the meaning of quiescence is beyond conceptualization.

If one wishes to attain the limit of Prajñā, the following third section praises the immeasurability of Prajñā, thereby explaining and establishing the meaning of the entrustment. Thus spoke the Buddha.
By extending his tongue so that it covered his face, he provided proof of his faith and understanding.

If the merit one obtains were not in vain, then because my parents gave birth to this body and I have maintained this tongue without ever speaking falsely, one who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā will certainly obtain its true benefit.

He did not manifest supernatural powers to make the tongue large, for had he done so, there would have been fear that the tongue was not truly large, or that it had been made large by the power of great supernatural penetration; therefore, he merely extended his tongue to cover his face.
Furthermore, worldly false speech is pursued for the sake of seeking fame and profit; yet the Buddha remains unattached amidst his myriad virtues and myriad practices, fearing such fame and profit.
Herein, it is said that *dhāraṇī* is a synonym for *prajñā*: in the context of the Śrāvakas, it is called the "factors of the path" (*mārga-aṅga*);
in the mind of a Buddha, it is *bodhi*; and in the case of a Bodhisattva, it is *ni*.
Chapter Sixty-Seven: On the Inexhaustible.

Herein begins the second section, which clarifies the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*). Prior to this was the path of wisdom (*prajñā-mārga*), whose arising was explained according to the treatise as being of two distinct types of wisdom.

One interpretation holds that practicing for oneself is the ultimate reality (*satya*) while transforming others is skillful means; another holds that all [practices] above [the stage of faith] are reality.
Wisdom that penetrates reality as it truly is without attachment is skillful means; wisdom that possesses the three types of clear knowledge regarding these matters is called true wisdom.
Regarding such phenomena, the absence of grasping and non-attachment is called skillful means.

Fourth, the thorough understanding of one's own practice as true wisdom, and the subsequent rejoicing and dedication of merit in common with all sentient beings, is called skillful means-wisdom. Furthermore—
It is said that what was previously taught was the *prajñā* common to the three vehicles; from here below, the *prajñā* exclusive to Bodhisattvas is taught.

This is intended to clarify that because the preceding *prajñā* is empty, quiescent, and truly illuminating, the two vehicles are able to enter it according to their respective capacities. From here below, there is a greater emphasis on the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*), which are collectively clever, marvelous, and wondrous in application; thus, these are the deeds of Bodhisattvas, for which the two vehicles have no share. Regarding the text itself: The previous section explained the *prajñā* shared by the three vehicles. From this point forward, the *prajñā* unique to Bodhisattvas is explained. This is to demonstrate that while the aforementioned *prajñā* is characterized by emptiness, stillness, and true illumination—thereby allowing the followers of the two vehicles to enter it according to their respective degrees—from here below, the focus shifts primarily to manifesting the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*), which are collectively ingenious, marvelous, and wondrous in their function. Therefore, these are the activities of Bodhisattvas, in which the followers of the two vehicles have no part. As for the text:
The first part consists of the twenty-three chapters from the beginning, which correctly elucidate the great function of the causes and effects of skillful means (*upāya*).

The second part consists of the two chapters on Sadāprarudita and Dharmodgata, which serve as an exhortation to practice. The reason for explaining the great function of the causes and effects of skillful means is that it is fundamentally intended to cause sentient beings to engage in practice;
thus, there is this second section. This first section is divided into three parts: the first extends from the beginning up to the chapter on Skillful Means.

Chapter Two: Praising the Essential Nature and Function of Skillful Means to Encourage Practice. This chapter has three sections. Chapter Three: The Ultimate Nature of the Three Wisdoms, Explaining the Arising of Practice through the Generation of the Bodhicitta.
From the section on the Four Noble Truths onwards, it explains attaining the fruit through skillful means. Within this, there are again three parts:

first, explaining that the essential nature of the wisdom of skillful means is subtle and exhaustively penetrates the reality of all phenomena; second, explaining that the function of the wisdom of skillful means leaves no evil uneliminated.
"Except for good, there is nothing that is not accumulated. This third section praises skillful means (*upāya*) and exhorts practice. Regarding the "Inexhaustible Chapter":
in the previous [section], the inexhaustibility of *prajñā* was already discussed; now, Subhūti asks again to clarify this meaning. The treatise states:

"If *prajñā* has harmony (*saṃyoga*) and accumulation (*caya*), then it has cessation (*nirodha*) and exhaustion (*kṣaya*). Because it lacks harmony and accumulation, it is without [cessation or exhaustion]."
Because extinction is inexhaustible, the Buddhas of the three periods of time attain Buddhahood by relying upon it. Subhūti had this thought:
"Bodhi is profound. The Treatise says: When Subhūti first heard the Buddha speak of ultimate exhaustion, he heard the entrustment that there is a dharma;
from the section "From the immeasurable in prajñā" downwards, it again clarifies ultimate emptiness. Thus we know that to grasp at the signs of existence is to lose [the truth].
If one grasps at the mark of emptiness through prajñā, one likewise loses prajñā. These five phrases are all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
therefore, one knows that prajñā is profoundly deep. Since its depth is inexhaustible and without limit or bottom, the Buddha has briefly explained the meaning of its inexhaustibility above;
thus, for now, we inquire into this inexhaustibility. As for how prajñā is generated: by means of this true prajñā, one universally delivers [beings] without end.
Since the Buddhas of the three periods of time arise from within it, we know that the wondrous principle is profound, unified, and inexhaustible.
Because one constantly desires to give birth to this within the spiritual treasury (*lingfu*), one asks about "giving birth.

Since form (*rūpa*) is inexhaustible, the arising of Prajñā is because Prajñā realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; thus, Prajñā arises. If form were to arise, it would necessarily have cessation; and that which ceases...

It is called "exhaustion" because form is unarisen and thus has no cessation; therefore, it is said to be inexhaustible. The same applies to emptiness and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

As for the twelve links of dependent origination being the unique teaching of the Bodhisattvas: if one contemplates them as empty based on their names, one falls into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
if one contemplates them as existent, one falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). Now, by contemplating dependent origination as profoundly deep, one attains wondrous awakening.
The Middle Way, which does not cling to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism, is the essence of expedient wisdom. That which is the unique dharma of the Bodhisattva is as follows:
ordinary beings directly follow the twelve [links of dependent origination] without seeking out what is right or wrong, nor what is deviant or correct;

the Two Vehicles merely recognize their faults and, having exhausted [the view of] self, desire to extinguish the "I" and enter into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, yet they do not exhaustively investigate the reality of causes and conditions. The Bodhisattva knows that these [phenomena] are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.

Because there is neither arising nor ceasing even now, it is not the practice of ordinary beings, nor the practice of noble ones; it is the practice of the Bodhisattva alone, and is therefore called "solitary.
Although one performs this contemplation prior to attaining the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is not yet clear;
only when one fully attains the understanding and clarity of the contemplation of non-arising is it said that one should contemplate thus while seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
It can eliminate all extremes and inverted views; this second section clarifies the wondrous function of skillful means, wherein no evil is not eliminated and no good is not accumulated.
This consists of two parts: first, no evil is not eliminated; second, no good is not accumulated. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the elimination of internal evils;
second, clarifying the elimination of external evils. Within the second section, there are five points: first, eliminating the various extremes and inverted views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Ordinary beings are largely attached to extremes such as annihilationism, eternalism, emptiness, and substantiality; they mostly perceive the body through the four inversions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity.
Now, the Bodhisattva contemplates internal conditions and finds no such faults. Second, he leaves behind the stage of the Two Vehicles. Third, he leaves behind the view of a self.
Fourth, he leaves behind the views of causelessness and false causes. Fifth, he leaves behind the view of dharmas. These passages are easy to understand. He does not see [them].
Regarding the statement that form is either permanent or impermanent, the ancient commentary explains: "The preceding [passage] clarifies the removal of various extremes and inversions;
it removes the four inversions, whereas now it fully removes the eight inversions. Thus, one should not say that this sutra does not clarify the removal of the eight inversions.

Furthermore, while the *Prajñāpāramitā* was not seen to clarify the exhaustion of conditions (*pratyaya-kṣaya*), here it clarifies the observation of purity (*śubha-vipaśyanā*). Therefore, at that time, when the Bodhisattva’s conditions and observations are both severed, the evil Māra [is unable to act].
"Great sorrow and poison are like arrows piercing the heart"—this refers to the second [section] on being born free from adverse conditions.

Regarding "endowed with generosity" (*dāna*), the second part clarifies the generation of the path, which is twofold: first, it clarifies how the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) attain fulfillment through the power of skillful means;
second, it clarifies how each individual perfection is endowed with all six perfections. Herein lies the attainment of non-... [text ends].

One who gives birth to skillful means fulfills the six perfections; yet, because they have never practiced giving within giving, nor ever observed precepts within precepts, the six paramitas are fully realized.

If one has not attained the skillful means of Prajñā, intermittent giving leads to attachment to existence, while intermittent giving of emptiness results in stagnation in emptiness, thereby establishing both permanence and annihilation. Conversely, if one perfects giving, then permanence and annihilation are not established.
Section Sixty-Eight: Subsuming the Five Categories.

This section below is the second [part], clarifying that within each individual practice all practices are fully present. When one has not yet attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), a single practice is not truly a single practice.
Once one gains faith and attains the patience of non-arising, because one is able to act without grasping at practices, all practices are fully present within a single practice.
Question: What is that which is subsumed herein? Answer: This is subsumed by way of mutual production (*anyonya-janaka*), for the root subsumes the branches.
The difference between the subsumption clarified here and that clarified previously in the "Chapter on Eloquence" (*pratibhāna-paṭala*) is as follows:

the former clarifies subsumption by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha*), intending to show how many practices, through their collective power, accomplish a great efficacy, thereby manifesting adornment with great majestic power.

Having shattered birth and death, one proceeds directly toward the Buddha-way; now it is clarified that within each and every vehicle (*yāna*), various practices are initiated to manifest skillful means (*upāya*).
Chapter Sixty-nine: On Skillful Means.

The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the reality while the three vehicles are expedient means; thus, it opens the gate of expedient means to reveal the meaning of the ultimate truth.
However, this supreme sūtra clarifies that the One Vehicle is a "great expedient means. If even the One Vehicle is still an expedient, how much more so must the Three Vehicles be expedients?

This statement must be discussed through both progressive and regressive analysis. If viewed from the perspective of the gateway to the Path, all three [vehicles] exist for the sake of conditions and are therefore all [expedient].
In the chapter on the Gate of Expedient Means, "The Three Are Never One," Subhūti rebukes Śāriputra, saying:
"Do you wish for there to be a single Buddha Vehicle? Śāriputra replies: "If even the three vehicles do not exist, how could there be a single vehicle?
Thus we know that both the three and the one are all expedient means. If, in relation to the three vehicles, they are expedient means, then the one vehicle is not an expedient means.
Furthermore, the present sutra states that "expedient means" (upāya) refers to illuminating emptiness as the reality while roaming in emptiness without attachment;

it involves engaging with existence without stagnation, employing skillful application, and is therefore called expedient means. In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the two types of wisdom are subsumed into the One Vehicle, such that both the expedient and the real are termed "expedient means.
Here, however, the One Vehicle is differentiated into the two types of wisdom; therefore, there is the "real" [wisdom].

Wisdom and skillful means are also explained as follows: in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the One Vehicle is clarified as the ultimate reality, whereas in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the One Vehicle is presented as skillful means;
both are general interpretations. Now, however, the One Vehicle is revealed as being itself skillful means, which constitutes the specific interpretation.
Having finished explaining above the essence of skillful means and the function of skillful means, this third section now praises and explains skillful means, exhorting students to practice it.

First, it clarifies the person who practices skillful means by praising their long-standing causes from the distant past; second, it praises the wondrous function of skillful means as being ultimately consummate and adept;

third, it praises the person who practices skillful means for attaining boundless merit, because they have planted causes over a long period, they attain wondrous function, and because they possess wondrous function, they attain boundless merit.

The first question and answer concerns the vehicle (*yāna*): because a Bodhisattva born with superior faculties (*adhimātra-utpanna*) possesses the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), they are able to practice a single deed while fulfilling all deeds;

thus, the cause is questioned regarding its duration. Although the time since the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) may be long, it does not necessarily mean that many Buddhas have been seen; thus, the number of Buddhas to whom offerings were made is questioned.

Although one may have seen Buddhas, there are those who remain among humans, devas, or the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), as well as those who have merely acquired roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*); thus, the planting of these roots is questioned.
"What are the roots of goodness? The Buddha answered: "The initial aspiration and ultimate fulfillment are not two;

therefore, the beginning is the end, and the end is the beginning. Since both the beginning and the end are complete, the end is also complete in the beginning. When one attains non-arising at the end, the beginning is immediately [non-arising]."
One also practices non-arising; if one does not practice non-arising at the beginning, how could one attain it later?

Since the beginning is not the end and the end is not the beginning, the beginning is not a cause of habituation. Therefore, as soon as the mind is generated, one performs the contemplation of non-arising, whereby the six perfections are fully realized.
For example, following the analogy of the sun and moon, the second section praises the wondrous efficacy of skillful means (*upāya*).

It consists of three parts: first, praising the skillful means of guidance and penetration; second, praising the skillful means of initiating practice; and third, praising the skillful means of firm clarity. Within the first part, there are three sub-sections:
first, praising *prajñā* as the foremost of all practices; second, praising *prajñā* for its capacity to guide and penetrate.
Regarding the three trainings and two analogies that conclude by extolling the excellence of the ultimate meaning of Prajñāpāramitā, there are ten analogies at the beginning.

The ancient commentaries state that these ten analogies are grouped in sets of three or two, and all serve to praise the three matters within the preceding "Inexhaustible" chapter. The first two metaphors represent:

(1) the substance that is capable of accomplishment, and (2) the name that is established; these correspond to the aforementioned capacity to accomplish meritorious qualities. The third and fourth clarify: (3) internal clarity and (4) external evil.
The second and third clarify the accomplishment of internal practice; this is intended to sever evil at its source.

The fifth and sixth clarify that one follows the cause by means of the first [wisdom] and exercises caution by means of the second [wisdom], thereby reaching the fruit. The seventh and eighth clarify the initial establishment by the first [wisdom] and subsequent caution by the second [wisdom].
The ninth and eleventh clarify its understanding; within this understanding, there is no further differentiation. This is based upon...

The treatise begins with the analogy of the sun and moon to represent the two types of wisdom of a bodhisattva, answering the question regarding the four modes of birth. Furthermore, it is like having eyes but lacking the sun and moon, whereby nothing can be seen;
likewise, although sentient beings possess worldly goodness, if they lack the *prajñā* of a bodhisattva, they do not perceive the true path.
Question: The five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*) are the stream of sentient beings, while *prajñā* is the great ocean; why, then, is *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) taken as the [destination]?
The *Dahai dalu* (Oceanic Response to Discourse) states: "Sarvajña (omniscience) is an alternative name for Prajñāpāramitā.
Because of Prajñā, the five perfections (pañcapāramitā) become non-abiding; thus, these five perfections enter into Prajñā and all become Prajñā.
When Sarvajña transforms, each enters into the Bodhisattva; likewise, the five perfections also transform according to Prajñā and enter into Sarvajña. [End of] Ancient Text.
Regarding the phrase "the hand is expedient," it is asked: if each of the six perfections possesses its own power, why is one expedient while another is not?
The final analogy compares the breaking of thieves by means of a wheel; [the wheel] remains in the air before the King’s palace, for the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) dwells in the void.

The "wheel" here is the Bodhisattva, and the "wisdom" (prajñā) is that which destroys the Māras, already abiding in the void of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Although the wheel guides, it has no mind of its own; likewise, although wisdom...
"Guidance itself has no object of guidance.
At that time, Subhūti [begins] the second section, which clarifies the capacity for guidance and attainment through skillful means; this is divided into two parts:

first, the formal clarification of the capacity for guidance and attainment; second, the clarification of gain and loss regarding the study of Prajñāpāramitā. First, he asks based on the preceding *pāramitās*...
"Regarding honey being like a wild horse, one should not practice in order to obtain its fruit. He replied: "The reason for performing actions is for the sake of sentient beings;

therefore, one practices until their exhaustion. The second question concerns the eighth analogy above: it asks why there is a distinction within the midst of non-distinction regarding existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, it states that one should comprehend that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas previously mentioned is empty and without differentiation.

Therefore, the answer states that the reason one attains this non-differentiation is due to the power of *prajñā*, just as when various colors reach a mountain, although they all become indistinguishable, it is because of the mountain that they are indistinguishable;
thus, it is the mountain that is praised. Regarding the third question, [the opponent] asks: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) ought not to be the supreme.

The answer is: "Because it is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya) that is supreme. [The opponent] asks: "Is it not the case that the non-conceptualization of *prajñā* is itself the ultimate truth? True.
Question: What is the supreme answer regarding the truths? Answer: To say "supreme" is a conventional expression. The Treatise states:
previously, it was called "emptiness" because one had not yet attained the Noble Path; now, because one has attained the emptiness of the Noble Path, it is called the fourth [truth].
Questioner: For what reason is Prajñāpāramitā supreme? Answer: Because it is able to grasp all dharmas and reach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

"If [the Bodhisattva] still remains above," Subhūti, this refers to the second section, which clarifies gain and loss, divided into two parts: first, clarifying loss; second, clarifying gain. Within the section on loss, there are four types of loss.

The first clarifies that even if one can perform the practices of the two kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*) as described above—namely, the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-prajñā*) and the wisdom of their meaning (*arthapravicaya-prajñā*)—it is still a loss.

Furthermore, to internally cling to a self and externally cling to emptiness, thinking, "I am able to practice the two kinds of emptiness regarding phenomena and birth," because there is no such thing as a phenomenon of birth, this constitutes the second [type of] clinging.
To break this clinging to emptiness is precisely Prajñā; yet, if one clings to Prajñā, that is itself clinging to emptiness.

Because of clinging to emptiness, one loses the third [stage]. When it says, "The Bodhisattva then thinks... and so forth, because one clings to the Bodhisattva path, one loses the first [stage], which was clinging to emptiness.
To hold the view that "emptiness" is a subsequent attachment, and even to hold the view that "emptiness of emptiness" is likewise a false view, is itself an error.

To claim that one who abides in *prajñāpāramitā* can fully accomplish the myriad practices—that this constitutes practicing the Bodhisattva path—is also a loss. This person believes that because of *prajñā*, one can fully accomplish the myriad practices;

although it is neither empty nor non-empty, they believe that ultimately there is a *prajñā* that can bring the myriad practices to fruition, and thus they err. This is the fourth error made by a Bodhisattva.
This thought—“I am an ordinary person in birth-and-death who has not yet realized non-arising, and therefore all that I have studied is lost;

only the Buddhas do not grasp at marks and are without fault”—is itself a loss. To think, “What I study is the Buddha’s knowledge, and I shall preach the Dharma for sentient beings according to what the Buddha knows,” is also a loss.
The Treatise says: “Because of attachment to the Buddha-way, one loses it. Now, regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, what Buddha is there?

Is it that one who is not a Buddha gives rise to the view of a Buddha? Since when has there ever been such a thing as awakening or non-awakening, that you say the ordinary person is unawakened while the Buddha is awakened?
This is merely seeing loss where there is none; all such views of loss are indeed losses. Seeing both awakening and non-awakening is itself non-awakening. How can there be no arising?
[This concludes] the second pair below, clarifying the loss of gain and loss. The four preceding sections were all losses; now they are not.
Because there is nothing to be attained, one asks: "How is it that there is no such fault? The Buddha replies:
"Because they do not grasp, for by realizing that all dharmas are non-existent, one is without grasping or attachment. One does not cling to emptiness, nor cling to the emptiness of emptiness;

one does not cling to the Bodhisattva path, nor to the Buddha. Because there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped, this is purity; therefore, there is no such fault as being 'supreme' [in a limited sense]."
Subhūti next asked: "Are you, who are the faultless and pure Prajñāpāramitā, devoid of self-characteristics?
If there were self-characteristics, there would be attachment; if there were no self-characteristics, what then would there be to practice? The Buddha replied:
"To fully comprehend all phenomena without loss is precisely not to perceive permanence or impermanence, nor persons or dharmas. How could one again give rise to a mind that creates [distinctions]?"

Although "existence" and "non-existence" are indeed existence and non-existence, it is like the third example cited below the wheel-turning king. This concludes the proximate connection to what was previously generated;
because one is thus able not to see [them] as either separate or inseparable, there is no fault in practice, and thus all practices follow the non-practice of Prajñāpāramitā.
From the second analogy, the doubt that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess their own inherent power is resolved; therefore, following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is explained:

"Just as a chariot, though it has the capacity to travel, requires a woman to drive it. Furthermore, this serves as a concluding exhortation regarding loss: if one follows a skillful driver, one will certainly not lose the way;
likewise, by following the skillful driving of *prajñā*, one does not lose the right path, and thus there is no supreme fault.

What is the Path? Second, the clarification of the skillful means for initiating practice, which is divided into three parts: first, clarifying that prior to practicing one must first rely on the path and avoid what is not the path;
second, discerning what is and is not the path so as to practice correctly; third, clarifying that through such practice one attains the fruit.

The first part has four sections: (1) distinguishing between what is and is not the path; (2) praising *prajñā* as that which can ride the path; (3) clarifying that although the path—though... [text continues].

To practice while remaining free from arising and ceasing is for the myriad practices to be perfected. Zhiyi (Sishiming) states that because the myriad virtues are perfected, he concludes by exhorting one to practice.
Here, first a question is posed and then answered. The question arises from what is near and far:

since the preceding sections have praised Prajñā as supreme, and we have recently heard that "non-apprehension" is the practice of Prajñā, we now wish to engage in its cultivation; therefore, we first inquire whether the path is correct or not.
Section Two, following the preceding: Subhūti, having heard that the Way is not a way, subsequently rejoices and praises that Prajñāpāramitā can serve as a vehicle;

this is indeed a great matter. Section Three, following the preceding: It clarifies that although the Way is without arising or cessation and is ultimately empty, it does not obstruct the practice of the myriad deeds of non-arising. How could this be considered an obstruction? For this reason, [the following section].
The fourth section is the exhortation.
[The interlocutor] asks the Buddha: "How does one practice *prajñā*? This is the second part, clarifying that because one has already mastered the Path through practice, one attains the Path.

In the Buddha’s response, first, he explains that practicing in a manner that is neither unified nor dispersed results in the presence of various afflictions (*kleśa*); whereas seeking by means of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) leads to non-attainment [of those afflictions].

In the current practice of "dispersal" (*saṃkṣepa*), one deeply cultivates *prajñā* and does not perceive this [distinction between] gathering and dispersal. Next, one practices "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*);
fearing that one might not perceive dispersal as being correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), and wishing to entrust the mind to abiding therein, one clarifies the practice of non-abiding.
The "Noble Son" (puruṣa) plants the seed of the Noble Son beneath the tree; this third section clarifies the attainment of the fruit, which is divided into two parts:

first, the attainment of the fruit itself, and second, further exhortation to practice. Regarding the first, the attainment of the fruit: the "Noble Son" is the Bodhisattva; the tree is the seed; the water is Prajñā;

and the five perfections (pañca-pāramitā) result in the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi. The Mahāyāna Sūtra takes sentient beings as the direct cause (hetu-pratyaya), while the six perfections serve as the contributing conditions.

Regarding the causes and conditions, this sutra takes Prajñā as the direct cause (nidāna) and divides the other five perfections as the contributory causes (pratyaya), thereby attaining the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* takes sentient beings as the direct cause and the six perfections as the contributory causes; within those six, it further designates the six perfections as the direct causes and the [remaining] five perfections as the contributory causes.
Next, the exhortation to practice follows the text.

The third section of the "Explanation of the Signs of Cultivating Contemplation" (Báifó Xiūguānxiàng xià) is the "Difficulties and Explanations on Attaining the Expedient Means of Illuminating Penetration.

Having attained these expedient means, one achieves clarity regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). This section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the illumination and penetration of the primary profound meaning and exhorting reliance upon its study;

second, clarifying that this gateway is unobstructed and that those who study it all enter therein. The first part contains three sections: first, clarifying the breadth and brevity [of the teachings] based on the scriptures.
Second, regarding the four dharmas, the three points clarify the exhortation to practice and study. As for why they are extensive or concise:
it is because the Great Illumination of the Buddha’s teachings does not transcend the extensive and the concise; one must fully comprehend both *prajñā* (wisdom) and *upāya* (skillful means).

The first interpretation states that the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma constitute the "extensive," while a single volume constitutes the "concise"; furthermore, even a single long discourse (*dīrgha-āgama*) is "extensive," whereas a single verse (*gāthā*) is "concise. The second interpretation [is as follows]:...
To say "brief" and "extensive" refers to the meanings of the general and the specific. To know that all dharmas are without arising and non-dual is "brief";

to know the two meanings of the non-duality and duality of all dharmas is "extensive. Regarding the six *pāramitās*, whether brief or extensive, there are already brief and extensive versions pertaining to the Three Vehicles;
here, we clarify the brief and extensive [practices] of what the Bodhisattva performs. Subhūti’s intention was as follows:

How is it known that the brief and extensive aspects follow? Second, the explanation of the brief and extensive by means of the four dharmas refers to the fact that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are neither conjoined nor dispersed—these are the four dharmas.

The reason for clarifying the brief and extensive by means of these is that only through awakening to suchness (tathatā) does one come to recognize the brevity and extensiveness of the Buddha’s teaching;
it is not that one understands the brevity or extensiveness within the four [categories] such as the nature of phenomena itself.
These four [points] clarify the breadth and brevity of the Buddha’s teachings and elucidate the four propositions regarding the four dharmas.

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) has no distinction between "this" and "that," it is said that there is no non-correspondence. Regarding the fourth proposition, "neither conjoined nor dispersed":

many people claim that the three dharmas—suchness and so forth—serve as objects; by awakening to these three dharmas, wisdom arises, and because wisdom and its object are conjoined, [wisdom] now clarifies that this is not the case.
"Combining and dispersing" is another name for the "brief compendium of Prajñā. This is the third section, which concludes by exhorting one to study the brief compendium of Prajñā.
Because one knows the four dharmas—such as "thusness" (tathatā) and so forth—one thereby knows both the brief and the extensive; this is called the "brief compendium of Prajñā.
Since one comes to know both the brief and the extensive through these four alone, is this not indeed the brief compendium of Prajñā?
Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who enter this gateway are the second type of people clearly awakened; they take the aforementioned four dharmas as their gateway.
It is for this reason that these demonic activities are about to arise.

This immediately extinguishes the three lower [stages]. Regarding the practice of skillful means (*upāya*), it is said that the person possesses great merit; this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying their merit, and second, clarifying the attainment of wisdom.
First, as the text states, "skillfully knowing the letter-gates" (*akṣara-mukha*); this second part clarifies that such a person possesses wisdom.
The "letter-gates" refer to the forty-two letter-gates, while the "non-letter-gate" refers to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—this should be understood as the principle (*tattva*).
It is called "knowledge" because it is taught [by the Buddha]. A single phrase that can clarify one meaning is called "one phrase";

the same applies to two, three, or four phrases. "Abandoning the path" means abandoning the lower stages; upon attaining a stage, one does not cling to joy, nor does one feel sorrow in abandoning the lower stages.
"Not abandoning the path" means abiding within this very stage. "Thoroughly knowing all views" refers to the views of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
"Skillfully knowing the aspects" refers to the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). A *srotāpanna* is a person on the path;

the path of the *srotāpanna* is the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*); and the fruit of the *srotāpanna* consists of the sixteen moments of mind and mental factors, as well as the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) and other such dharmas.
"Skillfully knowing the faculties" means knowing whether the faculties of others are complete or incomplete, and thus whether they can be delivered.

One who is capable of being delivered also knows for themselves whether their faculties are complete or incomplete, just as a fledgling bird knows for itself whether it has formed its own island or not.

"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to all-encompassing wisdom and collective wisdom. "Swift wisdom" (*kṣipra-prajñā*) refers to one who quickly understands all phenomena. Although some may understand quickly, their power of wisdom may be weak;
therefore, "powerful wisdom" (*balavatī-prajñā*) is taught. Although one may possess powerful wisdom, there may still be dullness; therefore, "sharp wisdom" (*tīkṣṇa-prajñā*) is taught.
Prajñā (wisdom) is that which extracts one from various difficulties and enables escape from the midst of afflictions;

it is called "extraordinary wisdom" (*viśeṣa-prajñā*). It is the wisdom that exhaustively investigates and thoroughly penetrates the Buddha-dharma; it is the wisdom of the path that pervades both the monastic and the laity, existence and non-existence, and so forth. It is the vast wisdom that enters deeply and is unimpeded.
Because it possesses all these aforementioned meanings, it is termed "Great Wisdom" (*mahā-prajñā*). Furthermore, because the Buddha is great, the Buddha's wisdom is also termed Great Wisdom.
Within *prajñā*, one does not even cling to *prajñā*. This explanation is sublime and beyond compare; it is called "unequaled wisdom" (*asamaprajñā*).

Like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), it can fulfill all heart's desires, and is thus called "true wisdom" (*bhūtaprajñā*). For those who wait upon sentient beings, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) all become their retinue.
Although a bodhisattva must wait for sentient beings to cross over birth and death together, even when attaining the Dharma of ultimate meaning, there is no [clinging].
Because one is able to skillfully understand speech, attain eloquence, and possess the joy of exposition, one knows the meaning; endowed with these four capacities, one can preach the Three Vehicles.

Herein, because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) were first explained extensively and later summarized, it was first stated that "one knows form" (*rūpa*) and subsequently said "one skillfully knows the aggregates, bases, and elements" (*skandhāyatana-dhātu*).
Herein, because the conditions (*pratyaya*) were first explained briefly and later expanded upon, it says: "the causal condition, the immediately preceding condition, and the predominant condition."
Thus ends [the section on] the third wisdom. Chapter Seventy-One:

First, the explanation of the essence of the wisdom of skillful means, including its praise and exhortation to practice, is completed. Now, second, the explanation of the cultivation of skillful means begins.

Regarding the two types of causal practice (*hetu-caryā*), the first three chapters concern the category of wisdom (*prajñā*). Before distinguishing the causal practices, I shall first clarify the model for the cultivation of practice.
From the second chapter, "The Tree of the Path" (*mārga-vṛkṣa*) onwards, the sūtras and śāstras do not explicitly name the three types of wisdom;

they simply speak of "the cultivation of *prajñā* arising from practice. If one takes *prajñā* to mean wisdom, this is consistent with the meaning. There are two [aspects] to the three types of wisdom.

Regarding the three—hearing, reflection, and cultivation—the former are generally discussed in terms of those without stages (*anupūrvika*) and those with stages (*ānupūrvika*), while the latter three—practice, birth, and cultivation—are mostly discussed in terms of those with stages and those without stages.
Thus, the Sūtra states: "From the first generation of the mind until sitting at the site of enlightenment, one should practice and cultivate.
However, the explanations of the Dharma Masters and the commentaries differ; some say that the thirty minds constitute the stage of practice (*caryā*).

Regarding the attainment of non-arising (*anutpāda*) as "arising" wisdom: this is because it was originally non-existent and now exists, and because what was previously unattained—non-arising—is now first attained;

thus, it is designated as "arising" wisdom. There are two interpretations regarding the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-jñāna*). One interpretation states that since the first stage (*bhūmi*) is already considered "arising," the second stage and those following belong to the wisdom of cultivation;

thus, according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the first stage constitutes the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the second stage belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The second interpretation holds that [the first stage] is the first stage... [text ends].
Reaching the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) constitutes "arising" (*janman*), while proceeding to the seventh stage and beyond constitutes "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). The *Śāstra* states:

Some say that the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) is "practice" (*caryā*), and attaining the non-arising (*anutpāda*) is "attainment"; thereafter, employing the *dhyāna-pāramitā* for perfuming and cultivation constitutes "wisdom through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

Others say that Emperor Liang’s interpretation holds that the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) possesses both practice and arising-cultivation; however, this is merely a conceptual exposition of three [stages]. Yet, the *Śāstra*...
The middle section directly explains the stage of liberation without a master; the latter section directly clarifies the absence of stages.
This meaning elucidates the three principles of possessing stages, lacking stages, and both.
Section Three: First, it clarifies the three wisdoms; second, it clarifies the three arisings; third, it clarifies prajñā. Initially, there are two cycles.

First, a brief explanation of the three types of wisdom; second, a detailed explanation of the three types of wisdom. Within the brief explanation, there are three parts: first, clarifying the essence of the three types of wisdom;

second, clarifying the timing for cultivating the three types of wisdom; third, clarifying the method for cultivating the three types of wisdom. Regarding the first [of these three], there is first the question and then the response. As for the origin of the question:
because the superior grade [of practitioners] praises the merit of *prajñā*, it is said, "One who well knows all dharmas"—the listeners delight in this.
Out of reverence for Prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti poses this question, to which the Buddha replies with three answers concerning the three realms.

In the first of these, four phrases are spoken; the first two clarify that the Bodhisattva has profoundly realized that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves *nirvāṇa* and quiescence (*śānti*).
The subsequent two phrases state that, having deeply realized the quiescence of the five aggregates, one then knows that all five aggregates within the triple world are illusory and false.

To thus comprehend [this] is called *prajñā*. Furthermore, another interpretation states that the first two lines refer to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the latter two lines refer to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
therefore, this is the practice of *prajñā*. Regarding the phrase "arising like space," this answers the second question concerning arising.
The Sāṃkhya school and other non-Buddhists [assert that] space is either eternal or a conditioned phenomenon (whether eternal or impermanent); now, it does not rely upon these.
This serves as an analogy for how emptiness is explained within the *Prajñāpāramitā*: it is neither existent nor non-existent, and its nature is eternally like that of *nirvāṇa*.
Now, it is clarified that when a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, they are likewise like empty space—neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor impermanent, and so forth.

Since this constitutes the arising of the *prajñā* contemplation, it is said that "they arise like empty space. However, empty space itself has no arising and no non-arising; it is merely a conventional designation.
The explanation of the arising of *prajñā* is likewise. Previously, the meaning of practice was clarified by means of the quiescence of the five aggregates;
now, regarding space, this is based on six aspects. To purify these six aspects so that they become unapprehendable is the meaning of the arising of practice.
Regarding "cultivating all mental states," this answers the third question concerning cultivation. The *Śāstra* says: "Once the Bodhisattva has attained *prajñā*, he enters..."
By means of the power of *prajñā*, one dwells in deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and observes that both the meditations and their objects of focus are unobtainable;
because one perceives neither distraction nor tranquility, nor the subject that cognizes nor the object that is cognized, one is said to "embrace all" as the cultivation of *prajñā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha: "Regarding the appropriate seasons, [the text] now proceeds to clarify the timing for cultivating the three types of wisdom.

As for the assembly, they say that all phenomena must necessarily have their appropriate seasons; therefore, Subhūti asks this question. The Buddha’s answer concerns those who first resolve to attain enlightenment and those who sit at the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This refers to the meaning of being without beginning and without end, yet it speaks in terms of beginning and end. The question begins from the initial resolution..."

Question: When one reaches the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one ought to practice the ten thousand practices (sāhasracaryā). Why, then, do you say that one practices Prajñā? Answer: The *Lunjie fangbian pin* (Exposition on the Skillful Means) states:
Some say that it is not necessary to fully cultivate all other practices to attain Buddhahood; rather, by merely hearing the Prajñā, one becomes a Buddha.
For example, in the world-system called Siṃhadundubhisvara (Sound of the Lion’s Drum), people merely hear of non-arising and signlessness and thereby attain realization of non-arising.
Furthermore, although there are people who practice such deeds as giving and precepts, because they have already practiced *prajñā*, we now inquire only about *prajñā*.
Moreover, Subhūti previously asked specifically about the impurity of *prajñā* and answered regarding *prajñā* throughout the three periods of time.

Since one practices the myriad practices with the mind of *prajñā*, and all myriad practices are subsumed by *prajñā*—as *prajñā* is the myriad practices—it is for this reason that attaining Buddhahood is explained specifically through [the cultivation of] *prajñā*.
At that time, because it is renamed "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā), the names of the three types of wisdom apply only up to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
[The text] asks the Buddha about the sequence; following the mind, the third section clarifies the method for cultivating the three types of wisdom so that other thoughts cannot enter.
This means obstructing all thoughts of apprehension (*upalambha*), destroying them as they arise so they do not enter, and [controlling] the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*).

"The Dharma does not function" is a statement used by those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to revile this [teaching]. Generally, regarding all mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*), they do not function; this refers to the four places of the Noble Ones' vows.

First, when one attains the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the mind does not attain the heaven of signlessness (*animitta-dhātu*). This means that while one selects the functioning of the mind, these causal minds do not function.

When a Sage attains the remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mind does not function; having entered [this state], it is without [mental activity].
Question: At other times, the mind also does not function; how then can it be said that the Bodhisattva’s mind never functions? The Master replies:

This statement—that the mind does not function—is made from the perspective of the Hīnayāna. Because the Mahāyāna differs from the Hīnayāna, it clarifies that all minds of a Bodhisattva do not function.
However, this clarifies that while other minds do not enter this dhyāna, they are all characterized by the attainment of something.
The mind does not function; it is clear that the mental factors do not function either. Only when a bodhisattva practices prajñā is there practice, yet in reality there is nothing practiced.
Master Rui’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The bodhisattva takes the Dharma-body as his body; though he dwells therein, he is not within the three realms.
He takes wondrous wisdom as his mind; though it engages with objects, it is eternally quiescent."

"Practicing Prajñāpāramitā oneself to attain Sarvajñā" concludes the second section, which extensively clarifies the three types of wisdom (*tri-vidyā*). This consists of three parts: first, clarifying cultivation; next, clarifying practice;

and finally, clarifying how practice gives rise to cultivation. Now, this section clarifies how cultivation gives rise to practice. Since one possesses all three types of wisdom from beginning to end, there is no distinction of depth or shallowness;
therefore, the treatise explains them such that they are without sequence. Second, it is due to the force of the textual structure as presented previously.
Regarding the superior cultivation of wisdom, because one does not apprehend the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), it is asked:

"Since they are not practiced, is it that by now cultivating *prajñā* one attains *sarvajñatā* (omniscience)? The Buddha answers: "This mind is constantly cultivated; one cultivates the mind and mental factors.
If they are not even practiced, how can there be cultivation, and how could there be *sarvajñatā*? If even cultivation cannot be apprehended, how much more so non-cultivation? Furthermore...

If one speaks of the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no cultivation; if one speaks of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is the contemplation of the mind. Therefore, it is said that cultivation exists.

Since both of these positions are erroneous, it is said that [the object] is likewise unattainable. This is the refutation of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) regarding the attainment of the meaning.

Now, having clarified the cultivation of wisdom above, since all four propositions concerning cultivation and non-cultivation are shallow, one should know that the same applies to the arising of knowledge. The subsequent question asks: "How then shall one attain it?"
This also destroys the notion of attainment; therefore, the question now concerns attainment. The Buddha answers: "As for the notion of suchness (*tathatā*), do you understand it?

There are four propositions regarding its attainment, yet it is not identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Subhūti does not understand suchness; he takes the realization of the limit of reality as his metaphor.
Since the limit of reality has four propositions, he subsequently does not understand the attainment of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) through the limit of reality. Thus it is said: "Suchness."
Question: The *dharmatā* asks Subhūti, "One should understand the *bhūtakoṭi*; why do you not explain it? Answer:

It is not that one does not understand the *bhūtakoṭi*, but rather that one understands *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) as being like the *bhūtakoṭi*. Question: It has always been said that the *bhūtakoṭi* is like the *dharmatā*;
why is it now asked whether the *bhūtakoṭi* is the *dharma*? Answer: Because this *dharmatā* is analogous to human nature (*puruṣatva*), it is deferred and placed later. Furthermore, regarding...

The followers of the Hīnayāna argue that one practices the path of learning (*śaikṣa-mārga*) in order to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), as in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
Since it is only after realizing the limit of reality that one subsequently penetrates the infinite nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they claim that the nature of phenomena exists only at the end.

Regarding the question, "Can the self-nature (*ātman) be apprehended? the answer is: "Even those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) do not perceive a self; how much less so an Arhat? The questioner asks: "Is the self ultimately non-existent?"

To "attain" is a false conceptualization (*parikalpa*) of a self; that one now "attains" *bodhi* is likewise a false conceptualization. [The Buddha] did not answer that there is something attained, for even "attainment" is a false conceptualization.
That which is now attained is non-attainment; taking the absence of self as a minor illustration, the Bodhisattva should train in this.
Following the section on form, the second part clarifies the practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*). This is divided into five sections; the first clarifies that there is nothing to be practiced.

This practice of Prajñā consists of: second, the practice of non-attainment; third, the practice of the unconditioned and the uncreated; fourth, the practice of non-abiding; and fifth, the practice of conventional designation.
Now, regarding this first practice of non-arising: as for the existence and non-existence of karma, the aforementioned arising and ceasing is the gate of signlessness (*animitta-mukha*);

here, the non-arising of the karma of existence and non-existence is the gate of the uncreated (*anabhisaṃskāra-mukha*). Below, it is the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

This is the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which does not give rise to the karma of existence or non-existence; "existence" here refers to the karma of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).

Ordinary people and non-Buddhists, being devoid of the correct contemplation of Prajñā, seek to extinguish the karma of the three realms of existence with a mind of false views; this is the arising of the karma of non-existence.
To speak in general terms, all minds that harbor either existence or non-existence are the karma of the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the first question, "How does one practice after the initial resolve? the second section clarifies the practice of non-apprehension. [Question 2 concluded. First: If there is no practice, this is the practice;
yet at the initial resolve, the mind is bewildered and confused. If there were a practice, its nature would belong to the present; how then is it so? The Buddha answers:
The present generation of the resolve is to study non-apprehension. That which is non-apprehension purifies all existence and non-existence.
Because of this observation, one master says that the study of the arousal of the bodhicitta consists in the contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing;
one cultivates the myriad practices based on a mind of non-arising, rather than—as others say—cultivating the myriad practices within existence and subsequently guiding them with emptiness.

Therefore, both now and previously, one must exhaust all grasping at a "mind that has attained" until ultimate emptiness is reached; only then does one cultivate the myriad practices. If one retains even a single [grasping],...
If one has a mind that grasps at something, one does not accomplish this practice; rather, this practice will instead result in grasping at something. [The disciple] said to the Buddha:
"Among those who grasp at something, there is that which is non-attainment. This is precisely asking about the meaning of attaining non-attainment within the realm of craving.
If one attains non-attainment through non-attainment, then this non-attainment is precisely the natural state of non-attainment for a bodhisattva."

To resolve that one should first practice with something to be attained and subsequently enter the state of non-attainment—this phrase "the permanence of the Buddha's meaning" cannot be derived from permanence, nor can the permanent be derived from the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the Buddha to be impermanent and yet function as permanent;

if he could be made so, he would be permanently making himself impermanent. The Buddha replied: "Both are impossible. You perceive both attainment and non-attainment, and thus you create [these dualities].
Question: If one perceives "non-attainment" as being dualistic, that is still an attainment; it is like the two dharmas mentioned before, which constitute having something attained.
Now, if one does not perceive even this "non-attainment," only then is there truly non-attainment.
When the attainment of others and non-attainment are equal, only then is there truly non-attainment. I now ask again: is equality attained through equality, or is it attained through inequality?
If one receives an answer of equality when asked such a question, it is still the same as the previous answer: your perception of both "equality" and "inequality" ultimately remains unequal.
The Buddha’s intention was to clarify that, based on the delusion or enlightenment of sentient beings, we provisionally designate "attainment" and "non-attainment.

How could there ever have been a fixed nature of attainment or non-attainment? If one penetrates the ultimate principle, even if there were something attained, one would ultimately never realize the Unattainable.
That which is attained arises precisely from emptiness; it is called "attainment" because one regards it as having attainment. How could there be anything that constitutes attainment?
[Subhūti] addressed the Buddha: "For what purpose does one practice *prajñāpāramitā*? This is the third section on practicing *prajñāpāramitā* through the unconditioned and the uncreated.

First, the question and answer correctly clarify that one practices *prajñāpāramitā* because there is nothing for which to act and nothing to be done. [Subhūti] addressed the Buddha: "In what manner..."

Regarding the division into three [vehicles] mentioned previously: since the intent of the question is that there is neither the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nor the uncreated (*akṛtaka*), how can one differentiate among the three vehicles?
In the Buddha’s response, he first confirms the question and clarifies that within the unconditioned and the uncreated, there is no differentiation of the three vehicles;
it is only within that which has something to be done or something to be performed that one differentiates them for oneself. Why is this? Because ordinary, foolish people disparage this goodness.

One should not give rise to doubt. Since ordinary persons who have not yet attained the Way are attached both to the five aggregates and to emptiness, they may give rise to the doubt that one should not differentiate the three vehicles.
Now that you have attained the Way and are attached to neither emptiness nor existence, why do you harbor this doubt?
When I say, "I did not attain bodhi by means of the five eyes," this further explains the reason why ordinary persons give rise to such doubts.
Furthermore, because I possess the five eyes, I do not see bodhi; moreover, as one who has attained bodhi, I do not see that bodhi can be attained.
That ordinary beings, who have not yet attained bodhi, say that bodhi can be attained—because ordinary beings have not yet attained bodhi and yet claim it can be attained—is truly most strange.
[Question: Since the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) perceives the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), can bodhi be seen?
Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom of the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), how can it be said that the five eyes do not see?

If you say that because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) negates the five eyes, they therefore do not arise and thus are not seen, this is also not the case. If the five eyes were negated, then the five eyes would not exist;

yet, we are currently confronting ordinary beings who lack the five eyes and are clarifying that the five eyes do exist. How then could the five eyes be negated? This is utterly inconsistent with the meaning of permanence.
To explain: the five eyes do not see that which is not seen by ordinary beings—that is, the bodhi perceived by ordinary beings.
All such instances are collectively referred to as follows: where could such a bodhi exist that it might be seen?
Yet ordinary beings, through their conceptualization, claim that there is such a bodhi to be seen; they conceptually assert that there is a bodhi to be seen. Furthermore, now...
Because one sees bodhi while seeing nothing that is seen, it is said that there is "no seeing.

For example, the passage beginning with "It is like another person" [refers to] the fourth section on the practice of non-abiding prajñā. By citing the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) that comes forth, it explains that because the Buddha has no place of abiding, he attains universal penetration;
this clarifies that because the bodhisattva likewise has no place of abiding, they practice prajñā. This is because it must be through transformation.

This extensively clarifies the activity of transformation (*nirmāṇa*). "The *śūnyatā* (emptiness) is mostly without origin but has traces" refers to the four propositions, which are easy to understand.
Furthermore, there are cases where the origin is long and the traces are short, and cases where the origin is short and the traces are long; this is precisely what is meant by those matters.

"The *śūnyatā* is mostly without origin but has traces" means that Śākyamuni has an origin but no [remaining] traces. "Origin and traces being simultaneous" is, for example, as when Śākyamuni accepted the offering of Cunda.
When the body and mind are received by others, both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku) are non-existent;
this very state of being both fundamental and manifested, yet neither fundamental nor manifested, is the fourth phrase. That which is "fundamental short and manifested long" refers to Śānta.

That which is "fundamental long and manifested short" is like Śākyamuni appearing at times through response; because this is fundamental long and manifested short, it is said that the matter is simply Śānta.

[The interlocutor] asks: "If it is said that by bowing to a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) one obtains the merit of a true Buddha, then by destroying a transformation Buddha one should also incur the sin of destroying a true Buddha.

The Master [Vasubandhu] replies: "If one destroys the body of a transformation Buddha with an evil mind, blood will flow from it, and one will indeed incur the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).

[The interlocutor] asks: "If that is so, why does the Vinaya state that there is no sin in destroying a transformation person? [The Master] replies: "In the Vinaya, this was stated for the purpose of establishing the formal rule (*saṃvara*)."

The precepts are established to protect the Buddha-dharma while conforming to worldly conventions; thus, this teaching was given. When people see the slaughter of oxen, sheep, and other animals, they do not hold them in deep reproach, and therefore [the act] is considered without fault.
However, if the intention to kill is genuine and no different [from that of a formal execution], the offense incurred is of the same degree.
"This true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena should not be harbored as a conceptual attachment" refers to the fifth provisional designation of practice.

This is like the *Daharaputra-parivarta* (Chapter on the Boy), which states that there is no fault in following conventional language; although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are non-existent, they speak using conventional provisional designations.

"To be attached to existence is also to be attached to emptiness" is an explanation intended to dispel doubt, for one might fear that if speech follows conventional provisional designations, [then...]

Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas should adhere to conventional designations (*prajñapti*), it is explained that they "adhere to conventional designations. If one were to adhere to conventional designations, then emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would likewise have to adhere to emptiness.
Since emptiness does not adhere to emptiness, how could a name possibly adhere to a name?
At that time, Subhūti [begins] the third section, which clarifies the three knowledges as two: first, it clarifies the relative superiority and inferiority of the knowledges;

second, it clarifies what is abandoned and what is not. This is the first part. Subhūti asks: "From the aforementioned Buddha’s response within the practice of the bodhisattva path, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
therefore, it is clarified that if one were previously fixed [in the stage of a śrāvaka], the Buddha would not speak of all-knowledge. All.

"Knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā) refers to knowing both the internal and the external; "external" refers to the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya), and "internal" refers to the six sense faculties (ṣaḍindriya).
The followers of the Two Vehicles know these twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana) as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self, yet they cannot employ all modes and all paths.
Because they cannot regard meditative concentration (samādhi) as truly existent, it is said that they lack all modes; thus, they cannot employ all paths to deliver sentient beings.
It is also said that the knowledge of the modes of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is the wisdom of the bodhisattva. By means of the four paths, the bodhisattva delivers sentient beings:

namely, the path of humans and devas for the sake of merit and happiness, and the paths of the three vehicles. While those of the two vehicles and the path of humans and devas act only for the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha-path is for one's own sake.
Second, regarding the clarification of abandonment: it clarifies only the abandonment of the two vehicles and does not clarify the abandonment of the bodhisattva.

In the Hīnayāna, it is not clarified that Bodhisattvas possess abandonment; since this inquiry is made from the perspective of the Hīnayāna, the Buddha answers only regarding the abandonment of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s abandonment of afflictions through the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is roughly the same as that of the two vehicles;

this is as explained in the context of the Bodhisattva’s patience of non-arising within the section on the two knowledges (*dvi-jñāna*). Question: How does the wisdom of a Bodhisattva differ from that of the two vehicles? Sūtra: [The sūtra states: "The wisdom of a Bodhisattva is distinct from that of the two vehicles."
Regarding the question, "How is it that there is a difference at the time of attainment, yet no difference after it has been severed? the treatise states:

Because the wisdom of the Buddha and that of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) differ in sharpness and dullness, there is a difference at the time of severance; however, after the severance, both are equally free from the underlying propensities (anuśaya), and thus there is no distinction after the severance.
As for the statement that "ordinary people and fools incur fault by doing so," the treatise explains that this refers to the two ways in which ordinary people perceive and hear [the Dharma].

The habitual tendencies of those who ride the vehicle are like this: for example, when Śāriputra saw [the Buddha] become angry, he remarked that Piṅgala had insulted the Ganges out of his own habitual tendency;

thus, it is said that even sages commit offenses due to anger and pride. In this context, first the distinctions among the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are clarified, based on the fact that the unconditioned realized is without difference—the unconditioned is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*). Subsequently, the differences among the various sages within the unconditioned are clarified.

This is the wisdom capable of awakening. Regarding the statement that the Path severs the fetters and explains the "subsequent limit" (*paścimā koṭi*): because the Noble One has severed all fetters, they attain the state of "no remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*);
this "no remainder" is precisely the subsequent limit.
The third explanation of the text on *prajñā* is divided into four parts; the first clarifies that because *prajñā* can reach the other shore, it is named *prajñā*.
The second [section] clarifies the function of *prajñā* in producing the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome;
the third clarifies the meaning of how *prajñā* can accomplish all contemplations; and the fourth clarifies the abandonment of both the non-true and the non-beneficial, thereby elucidating *prajñā*.

This is divided into three parts: first, elucidating the *pāramitā* by way of the practice of wisdom; second, furthermore, elucidating it by way of the merit of the fruit; and third, [the remaining section].
Regarding the third *pāramitā*, there is another sequence: first, the *pāramitās* are elucidated by way of their objects;
