1. A voice responded with two cries of lamentation, moving the Buddha to manifest in the air; 2. He attained samādhi, whereby the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared before him.
Now, the first two instances of "response" clarify that because he internally forgot his own body and life and externally renounced worldly fame and profit, he was able to evoke such responses.

Within the section on the responses, "do not look back" is an admonition, while "proceed eastward from here" is an instruction. "Maintain wholesome thoughts" and what follows are instructions. Admonitions.

Do not dwell upon the internal or the external; the external refers to the five sense objects, and the internal refers to one's own body. Since both the internal and external lack intrinsic nature and are empty, they should not be dwelled upon.

Do not destroy the characteristics of the body—this is a subtle admonition. This means that all views regarding the body as being either identical to or different from [the elements], or as being existent or non-existent, destroy the characteristics of the body.
One must not destroy the specific characteristics of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Question: In the midst of emptiness, who should this voice belong to?
Regarding the response from Śrāvaka: The first interpretation states that it was a dust mote, manifested because the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and others took pity [on him].
The second interpretation states that this was a yakṣa created by Sadāprarudita’s spiritual friend; furthermore, this yakṣa sought the Buddha-way and instructed him.
This is like the case where the spiritual friend, the yakṣa, instructed Sudatta to go and see the Buddha.
In response to the voice from the sky, he made three vows: first, that for all sentient beings fallen into the darkness of ignorance, he would kindle the light of great wisdom;
second, that for all sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he would gather all medicinal herbs of the Dharma;
third, that for all sentient beings fallen onto deviant paths, he would now seek the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] on their behalf.
Regarding the fourth stage of the Path, within the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), there are two initial stages: first, the Dharma; second, the Honored Person.

Within the stage of the Dharma, one first contemplates the three emptinesses (*tri-śūnyatā*) to give rise to faith, and subsequently contemplates the conceptual mind (*nimitta-citta*) to seek [liberation].

If one is separated from Prajñā, there are two types of emptiness; when combined with Prajñā, they constitute the three emptinesses. Because the two emptinesses are the essential means for entering the Path, they are explained first. [The term] "separated" [refers to the preliminary stage].

In the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the long-standing inquiry has clarified only the dissociation from the mark of persons (*pudgala-nimitta*); the commentary fully clarifies the dissociation from both the marks of persons and phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*).
Regarding the passage "One should draw near to spiritual friends" and below, the second section, the "Venerable Explanation," is divided into two parts: first, the contemplation, and next...

Regarding the "Admonition" (誡): within the Dharma, one simply contemplates that which is not admonished. Because the initial inspiration in the middle stage arises from the intention of admonition, there is no need for further elaboration here.

Within the contemplation, one first contemplates drawing near to virtuous friends; from this true goodness, the signs of its arising must lead to hearing the Dharma. Next, it clarifies the benefit gained by drawing near to the virtuous.
One contemplates the desire to repay the debt of gratitude as described in the text. Regarding the worldly benefits, [the text] proceeds from the lowest to the first.

This is the admonition. First, regarding the admonition against worldly gain: once one has observed that those who are closely associated with it will surely extinguish their fame and profit, one must clearly understand that although Śāriputra initially sought the Dharma, he later yielded to fame and profit. Next, observe the awakening to Māra; herein there are two types of teachers.
The first is when Māra manifests as the five desires to disturb the teacher’s preaching of the Dharma; when the disciple sees this, they should take only the Dharma and nothing else.
Seeing that the Master accepts sensual desires, one might think it surpasses the heavens; however, it is for the sake of the Dharma that he causes the recipient to accept them.
It is Māra who manifests as the five desires to create disorder between master and disciple, falsely posing as the Dharma to induce acceptance.

As for the Bodhisattva preaching the Dharma and entering the gate of the true Dharma, this refers to those of high practice who manifest the acceptance of the five desires to benefit sentient beings, yet remain without any attachment.
"You must not intentionally engage in impure mental conduct toward your teacher. Later, when you realize it was the work of Māra, this shall be the third admonition.
Even if you are not accepted by a teacher who is liberated from heavy burdens, abides in high renown, and possesses profound virtue, do not harbor resentment.

You should instead shatter your own pride and reproach yourself, thinking: 'It is because of the retribution for my sins in past lives that I am a person of low station, and thus the teacher does not accept me.'"
This recording is not the fault of the Master.
At that time, Sadāprarudita’s second response to the stimulus consists of four phrases, meaning two stimuli and two responses.

Within the first stimulus, there are three parts: the Dharma, the analogy, and the application. As for the phrase "Why do I not [hear] the voice in the sky?", the preceding section merely recorded [the Master's words].
Regarding the admonitions and exhortations, there are three matters asked about that differ from the others: first, the distinction between near and far;

second, not asking where [the son] was located; and third, not asking who he followed. As for why these were asked falsely, it is because he had previously experienced great joy, and thus asked falsely.
In the parable, the "only son" precisely illustrates *prajñā*. The *Śāstra* states that it is illustrated by means of three meanings. First:
Just as a lover grows old without gaining strength from their beloved, so too does the power of Prajñāpāramitā lead one to attain *avaivartika* [non-retrogression] and the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, O son of good family, just as filial conduct toward one's father remains unchanged throughout one’s life, so too is Prajñāpāramitā never far from a bodhisattva until they attain Buddhahood.
Moreover, just as parents rejoice greatly upon seeing their child, so too does the Bodhisattva rejoice greatly upon seeing Prajñāpāramitā.
This is indeed so; however, the general meaning here takes the metaphor of undergoing transformation without abandoning [the practice] as its basis.
Within this response, there are two parts: first, praising the peace; second, answering the three questions. This is the first part. As for why the response occurs only after seven days:

when one has practiced for a short time, one’s diligence is not yet deep; when one encounters many [distractions], anxiety and hindrances arise. Therefore, the response to the question occurs after seven days.
Question: Since the Buddha has already manifested in the sky, why does he not immediately preach the *Prajñāpāramitā*? Answer:

Because that person and the Dharma still possess deep and heavy karmic conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), the Buddha is unable to deliver them. Question: What kind of Buddha is it that appears in the sky? Answer:

One interpretation states that this is not the true Buddha, but rather the bodies of various transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) or great Bodhisattvas who have manifested as Buddhas to take [beings] across.
The clouds are indeed the True Buddha. Therefore, he cites the past practices as a means of guidance and consolation;

this is because his own remorse for his grave transgressions was such that they hindered his progress in cultivating merit. From there he traveled eastward, answering the three questions in succession.
He departed from here five hundred *xiūn* (yojanas) to answer the question regarding the distance of his journey. There is a city named Saṃghagandha.

To explain where they go and to inquire about their differences: the Eastern Orthodox (Dongzheng) school asks, "To which land do you go? and thus provides this answer. The text is divided into two parts:
first, an introduction to the land; second, an elucidation of the people. It must be understood that this wisdom is *prajñā* (wisdom), which is neither the provisional nor the ultimate;
rather, both the provisional and the ultimate modes of skillful means (*upāya*) are themselves *prajñā*. Do not say that this is merely the "Chapter on Prajñā."
This mind and these people here are all the functioning of *prajñā*. Because one practices *prajñā*, one attains this retribution;

do not say that *prajñā* is empty and devoid of fruit. Regarding the locations, there are two parts: first, explaining the general location by discussing the City of Fragrance (*Gandhavatī*); second, explaining the specific location, which is the passage concerning the destruction of Dharmodgata’s house—this part is easy to understand.

Question: [The City of] Fragrance... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "Question: 眾" (Question: [The City of] Fragrance). The translation reflects the content available up to that point.)
"Where is the City of Fragrance? He replied: "After the past Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, before his bequeathed Dharma had yet ceased, the Buddha-dharma was not yet spread throughout Jambudvīpa;
therefore, within Jambudvīpa, there was a separate land called the Land of Universal Fragrance."

Dharmodgata, together with sixty thousand court ladies, descends [from the second heaven]. This first clarifies the manifestation of objects; having first clarified the reception of worldly pleasure, it next clarifies the experience of bliss.
The intent here is to reveal that Prajñāpāramitā can produce both mundane and supramundane bliss, and because it differs from worldly pleasure, one experiences its fruit.
By preaching the Dharma, one practices the Dharma; thus, one cultivates the cause. Furthermore, this serves to attract sentient beings. By practicing Prajñā, one fully attains worldly [bliss].
Regarding the two supramundane joys, sentient beings who hear the Prajñāpāramitā and obtain only mundane joy will not immediately practice and receive it.
"You, son of good family," [the Buddha] replied to the third question below: "From whom should one hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"

At that time, Sadāprarudita... [The second section clarifies the response of the Buddha]. First, regarding the "response" (*saṃgati*), there are three parts: the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Within the analogy, the one struck by a poisoned arrow represents those with wrong views; "poison" refers to false views, and the "arrow" refers to doubt.

Because the poisons of afflictions such as greed and hatred have been removed, it is said they will surely lose their physical body and their life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). By seeing the good and giving rise to it, one preaches *prajñā* to extract [the arrow] and sever [the afflictions].
Regarding the attainment of the mind named "Severing All Existences" (*sarvabhavaccheda*), at that time, Sadāprarudita should immediately attain the benefits of all samādhis;
this is what is meant by "should. First there is response through sound, then response through form, and also response through the Dharma;

since these are also responses of the mind, form, sound, and mind are all means of benefiting sentient beings. The Treatise states that he attained sixty thousand samādhis. [This concerns] the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

The Samādhi of Contemplation is the realization that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing; the Samādhi of the Unattainability of the Dharma-nature is likewise non-attachment even to the contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing.
The Samādhi of the Destruction of Ignorance is so called because by destroying ignorance, one attains the aforementioned samādhis.
There are many grades of ignorance to be destroyed, and thus [the destruction] is also manifold. Furthermore, the subduing of ignorance is also termed "destruction."
The Samādhi of Departing from Darkness (Vimalaprabhā) refers to having previously destroyed light ignorance (*avidyā*) and now destroying heavy ignorance.

The Samādhi of Non-Continuity (Anuccheda) means that because the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) continue in a similar manner from moment to moment throughout a single lifetime, they are said to be without difference;

if the characteristics of birth and death were different, the continuity would be severed, which is what is meant by "difference. Because it destroys the obstacles to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), it is called the Vajra Samādhi.

Those who are deluded are the subjects of Māra and constantly desire to see the Bodhisattva; they always seek to encounter him, and thus their constant seeing of the Bodhisattva is a favorable circumstance.
Abiding within these various samādhis—this is the third [section] on resonance and response—because samādhi is capable of inducing [the Buddhas], the Buddhas of the ten directions [appear].
This is appropriate. Regarding the first point of consolation within the "Appropriate" section: his original practice of the bodhisattva path was just as it is today;
therefore, you must not consider yourself to be of little merit. Next, concerning "not seeing him enter samādhi":

since Sadāprarudita has already attained various samādhis, this now serves to shatter his attachment to them, which is a brief exposition of Prajñāpāramitā. One should have faith in the Buddha-dharma below this point.
Re-examining the honoring of the Honored One and the honoring of the Dharma: because of [abiding in] samādhi, there is no further [need for such honoring].
Regarding the section "Seeing the Buddhas" below, this is the second major division, which further exhorts one to seek good friends and seek Prajñā.

There are five points: first, because one has not seen the Buddha, doubt arises; second, having received a body, one makes offerings to others and acts as their companion in order to sever that doubt; third... [text continues].
1. Because he sold his body, he obtained wealth through the kindness of a good friend; because of that wealth, he set out specifically to seek a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*).
2. A list of the places he visited. 3. Two kinds of offerings. 4. Upon seeing the spiritual teacher, he expressed his sincerity in seeking the Dharma and made a request.

5. He then presented his doubts. Now, this is a beneficial inquiry: since the Buddha’s doubts have already been resolved, why does he not enter *samādhi*? [The text] requests the Buddha regarding these doubts.

Answer: Since it is stated that even the Buddhas of the ten directions were his spiritual friends when he went to them, one should inquire whether [this practice] is not even comparable to seeking the Dharma.
Furthermore, the second reason for selling one's body to make offerings—as expressed in the passage "He further thought..."—is that one must make offerings for the sake of others.
Seeing that he had come from afar empty-handed and possessed nothing, [Sadāprarudita] did not give rise to a joyful mind;
therefore, [Mañjuśrī] provided him with the requisites for worship. Second, he wished to guide the multitude: if even those who are poor can prepare such offerings, why should one not do so?

Second, he wished to clarify that *dāna* (generosity) is the foremost of the *pāramitās*, and to question Sadāprarudita regarding his attainment of sixty thousand samādhis and his vision of ten [Buddhas].

Question: For what reason was the Buddha poor? Answer: First, although that person had the conditions to see the Buddha, because he had committed few sins in the past, he was born into a poor family and thus lacked wealth and goods.
Second, although he was born into a wealthy family, he left home to study the Way in the deep mountains far away, and therefore did not take wealth or goods with him.
Question: To whom did he sell his body and belong so that he might provide for his virtuous friend? (1)
The commentary offers two interpretations: one states that this refers to offering oneself to others;

the other states that although this physical body belongs to others, it is permitted to offer it first, and upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, one returns [to the original state]. Now, I say: when selling one’s body in the marketplace, everyone is moved by its extraordinariness;
at such a time, one will inevitably attract wealth and gain the hearts of friends. For this reason, he sold his body. Why did he question Māra?
Therefore, why did he not kill Sadāprarudita and disturb him? Answer: Māra was not moved by his extraordinary resolve; he merely sought to destroy his aspiration for Buddhahood.
Furthermore, according to the Dharma of the devas, no human being may be harmed unless they have committed a great transgression.

This serves as an expedient means for treating delusions. One should hear the explanation that once the realization of emptiness is perfected, if there is no application of expedient means, four kinds of delusion arise:
doubt, wrong views, the inclination toward the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle, and the claim that one has already become a Buddha.
If there is the application of expedient means, these doubts and wrong views will not arise, and one will not enter [the limited state].
Nirvāṇa is the definitive realization of attaining Buddhahood. If there are skillful means to treat doubt—whether it be three or more—it may be asked:

"For what reason did the Buddha entrust [the teaching] for its circulation? The answer is: Out of compassion, he gathers in sentient beings; why wait to ask? If even the Buddha broke his own body to benefit others, how much more so the Jewel of the Dharma?
Furthermore, the previous discourse used emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to refute existence (*bhāva*); now, what does this belong to that refutes emptiness? It is intended to demonstrate...
Question: Since the entrustment is made because of the Middle Way, and knowing that there is benefit in this entrustment, why is it not entrusted to a Bodhisattva but rather to Ānanda?
Ānanda is a Śrāvaka, whereas Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma of Bodhisattvas. Answer: It is because one wishes to cause sentient beings to have faith.
Ānanda has attained a comprehensive understanding of the Buddha; he is a disciple from among the followers, serves as an attendant, and is also a brother in the Dharma of the Buddha.
The Three Masters said: "As for Śāriputra, he was indeed a second Buddha; however, because they knew his lifespan would be short, they did not entrust [the Dharma] to him.
Therefore, everyone believes and accepts what Ānanda has taught, as is fully explained in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra. Bodhisattvas all bear heavy responsibilities:
they personally subdue their own retinues in the city of Vaiśālī, yet they err in being unable to propagate [the teaching] when people do not believe."

Because [the Buddha] had already received [the teaching], he did not entrust it to the Bodhisattvas; the Bodhisattvas themselves, knowing the profound virtue and grace of Prajñāpāramitā, widely proclaimed it, so there was no need for it to be entrusted to Ānanda. Those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) do not know the grace of Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, the Buddha entrusted it to them. Question: If that is so, why were the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts entrusted to Bodhisattvas such as Pūrṇa? Answer: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) can become Buddhas. It is for this reason that it was entrusted to them. Furthermore, because the Dharma-gate of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is extremely profound and difficult to understand, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas so that they might protect and uphold it. Moreover, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the ultimate Dharma-gate, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas so that they might propagate it throughout the ten directions. Therefore, although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is entrusted to the Bodhisattvas, this does not contradict the principle that the Prajñāpāramitā was not entrusted to them. This is because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the root of all dharmas; it is the most supreme and profound, and thus it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. However, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the final teaching of the Buddha’s lifetime, and because its meaning is vast and profound, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas so that they might protect and uphold it. Thus, there is no contradiction between these two cases. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the initial teaching, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the final teaching. Because the initial teaching is subtle and difficult to understand, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the final teaching is vast and profound, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the Śrāvaka vehicle, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna. Because the Śrāvaka vehicle is narrow and limited, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the Mahāyāna is vast and expansive, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the provisional teaching, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the definitive teaching. Because the provisional teaching is incomplete, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the definitive teaching is complete, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya), while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya). Because the emptiness of phenomena is subtle and difficult to realize, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the emptiness of persons is easier to understand, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the practice of non-attachment, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the practice of compassion. Because the practice of non-attachment is difficult to cultivate, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the practice of compassion is easy to cultivate, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga). Because the path of seeing is subtle and difficult to enter, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the path of cultivation is vast and extensive, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the fruit of Arhatship, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the fruit of Buddhahood. Because the fruit of Arhatship is limited, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the fruit of Buddhahood is supreme and ultimate, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the Lesser Vehicle, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the Greater Vehicle. Because the Lesser Vehicle is inferior, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the Greater Vehicle is superior, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the past, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the future. Because the past is already gone, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the future is yet to come, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the present, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the ultimate. Because the present is fleeting, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the ultimate is eternal, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the provisional, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the true. Because the provisional is deceptive, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the true is real, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the cause, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the fruit. Because the cause is difficult to accomplish, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the fruit is easy to attain, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the wisdom of emptiness, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the wisdom of existence. Because the wisdom of emptiness is subtle and difficult to fathom, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the wisdom of existence is manifest and clear, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the negation of all dharmas, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the affirmation of all dharmas. Because the negation of all dharmas is difficult to accept, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the affirmation of all dharmas is easy to believe, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-gate of the extinction of suffering, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-gate of the cessation of suffering. Because the extinction of suffering is subtle and difficult to realize, it was not entrusted to the Bodhisattvas; because the cessation of suffering is vast and profound, it was entrusted to the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is
The Buddha is the secret Dharma, while Prajñāpāramitā is the manifest Dharma. Manifest dharmas are easy to employ, whereas secret dharmas are difficult to employ.
A minor physician uses medicinal herbs as medicine, but a great physician uses poison as medicine. Furthermore, there are two types of Prajñāpāramitā:
the common and the uncommon. The uncommon Prajñāpāramitā is entrusted to Bodhisattvas, while the common is entrusted to Śrāvakas.
Question: How many verses of this Prajñāpāramitā-samādhi are there that were entrusted [to Ānanda]? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* consists of one hundred thousand verses;

the present version consists of twelve thousand verses. Question: When it was entrusted to the Tripiṭaka-master Ānanda, where was the Prajñāpāramitā compiled during the council held by Kāśyapa on Mount [Gṛdhrakūṭa]? Answer: It is not known whether Mañjuśrī led Ānanda in the compilation.
Regarding the location: first, it is said to be still within the mountains; second, it is said to be at the edge of the Cakravāḍa Mountains. Question:

Why was the Prajñāpāramitā not compiled immediately within the Tripiṭaka? Answer: The Tripiṭaka properly contains three hundred thousand verses and nine million nine hundred thousand words, whereas the Mahāyāna is immeasurable.
There are the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Nāga Kings*, the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Asuras*, and so forth, numbering ten [such works].

The Buddha did not speak these hundreds of millions of verses in a single lifetime; rather, he spoke them throughout immeasurable lifetimes. Since they have already been spoken, how could they be included within the minor teachings of the Tripiṭaka?
Furthermore, because the names of the teaching gates differ and the Great and Small Vehicles are distinct, their compilation is likewise separate.

This chapter is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching]; second, the great assembly’s joyful practice and observance. Regarding the first part, there are three sections:
first, the earnest entrustment to ensure respect and veneration; second, the entrustment to Ānanda to ensure the uninterrupted circulation [of the teaching];
third, the explanation of the intent behind the entrustment. This is now the first section. Question: The Buddha knows that Ānanda is his disciple.
"Why do you ask only now? He replied with two points: first, to distinguish between the genuine and the spurious.

There were spurious disciples of the Buddha, such as Sunakṣatra, who falsely claimed to be disciples for the sake of wealth and treasures; because the Buddha did not preach the Dharma for them, they in turn violated the precepts and declared themselves no longer disciples.
Furthermore, there was Susīma, who acted as a disciple for the purpose of stealing the Buddha's teachings. For these reasons, [he asks now].

Question: This second section clarifies doubts. Various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that Ānanda’s original practice was that of a non-Buddhist ascetic who wore grass garments and sought immortality;
they further assert that because the Buddha was his relative and had entrusted him with instructions, he entered the Buddhist path out of necessity, yet his heart truly lacked faith.

Therefore, this current inquiry in the text is intended to resolve the doubts of these non-Buddhists. For example, [the text notes] that while he employed evil karma of body, speech, and mind, he possessed disciples whose speech was virtuous.

If one’s mind is not virtuous, or if the mind is virtuous but one does not practice meditation through body and speech—Ānanda, because these three karmas are fully present, you should serve me with these three karmas now;
after my parinirvāṇa, you should serve the Prajñāpāramitā with these three karmas. As for the second and third [categories], the Buddha-dharma does not exceed these three matters.
One who does not accept the Buddha’s words is a person of rebellion, and the Vajra-devas shall then slay them.
Furthermore, if there is too much, it becomes excessive; if there is too little, it is insufficient. Therefore, there are only these three.

Do not forget, do not lose them—this first entrustment commands that they be circulated without interruption. For a son who cannot inherit his family’s legacy is considered the most shameful of those who sever the lineage.
Now, if you can circulate the Prajñāpāramitā even slightly, the Buddha's sutras will reside within your own person.
The above [section] concludes that this is also a major error. Following that for a certain period of time is the third point, the entrustment;
it is an entrustment because there is a profound benefit.
"When the Buddha had spoken this sutra" and so forth is the second section, the practice and upholding. Question: Are freedom from sorrow and freedom from joy the merits of an Arhat?

Question: If even virtue does not fail to bring joy, why speak of "Great Joy" (mahāmuditā)? Answer: An Arhat has no doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths, yet they still harbor doubts concerning all other phenomena.
Now, by means of Prajñā, these various states of doubt are shattered; this is "Joy," which is exhausted here without remainder.
